true_positives.matched_candidate:
Add-guests emails ignore the event type's disableStandardEmails settings

Every neighboring sender in this file (sendLocationChangeEmails, sendRescheduledEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts eventTypeMetadata and skips host/attendee emails via eventTypeDisableHostEmail/eventTypeDisableAttendeeEmail. sendAddGuestsEmails takes no metadata and the calling handler never reads eventType.metadata, so organizers who disabled standard emails for an event type still have 'guests added' emails sent to themselves, their team, and all attendees — violating a user-facing event-type setting.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Adding guests to seated bookings bypasses seat tracking

For event types with seatsPerTimeSlot, attendees are supposed to be backed by BookingSeat reference rows; this handler inserts plain Attendee records via createMany without creating seat references and without checking remaining seat capacity. The occupied-seat count for the slot is therefore not incremented, so the slot can be overbooked beyond seatsPerTimeSlot, and the new attendee cannot be managed through seated-booking flows (e.g. cancelling an individual seat via seatReferenceUid). Either create the seat references and enforce capacity, or reject add-guests for seated event types.

Any attendee can add an unbounded number of guests to a booking

The permission check allows anyone whose email appears on the booking — including guests who were themselves added through this feature — to add further guests, and ZAddGuestsInputSchema places no upper bound on the guests array. A single request can therefore create hundreds of Attendee rows and trigger an email to every one of them through Cal.com's mail infrastructure (a spam/abuse vector), and it discloses the meeting location/video link to arbitrary addresses without the organizer's involvement. Consider capping the number of guests per request/booking and reconsidering whether attendees (rather than only the organizer/team admins) should have this ability.

Attendees are persisted before calendar/email side effects with no transaction or idempotency

`prisma.booking.update({ ..., attendees: { createMany } })` commits the new attendees first; only afterwards are the calendar event updated (line 165) and emails sent (line 168). If anything after the DB write fails (calendar API error, missing credential, process crash), the API returns an error even though the guests were added, and because the uniqueness filter at line 76 then treats them as existing attendees, the user cannot simply retry — the guests remain on the booking without calendar entries or invitation emails. The operation should be idempotent or the side effects performed in a way that can be recovered.

Calendar update uses the requester's credentials instead of the booking organizer's

The handler builds EventManager from `ctx.user` and `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` — the person clicking 'add guests' — but the booking's calendar reference and destination calendar belong to `booking.user` (the organizer, whose credentials were even fetched in the booking query at lines 35-40 but go unused). When anyone other than the organizer adds guests (an attendee, or a team admin/owner managing someone else's team booking), `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` cannot find the calendar credential that owns the event, so it throws or silently skips the update. Because the attendee rows were already committed at line 92, the guests end up saved in the DB while the calendar event is never updated and the mutation returns an error; retrying then fails with 'emails_must_be_unique_valid' because the guests already exist.

No tests for the new addGuests mutation

The PR introduces a new authenticated mutation with non-trivial authorization logic (organizer vs team admin/owner vs attendee), dedupe/blacklist filtering, calendar updates, and email fan-out, but adds no tests. Handler tests over the permission matrix and error paths would have caught regressions such as the && / || mix-up in isTeamAdminOrOwner and the wrong-credential EventManager construction.

No validation of booking status or time before adding guests

After loading the booking the handler checks only permissions; it never verifies that the booking is still active. Guests can be added to CANCELLED or REJECTED bookings, and to bookings whose endTime is in the past (the UI even offers the action on past confirmed bookings via the Edit menu in BookingListItem). In those cases the handler inserts attendees and sends emails plus an ics with status CONFIRMED and method REQUEST for an event that is cancelled or already over, leaving attendees and calendars in a misleading state. The handler should reject cancelled/rejected (and probably past) bookings.

Team members are never notified because evt.team is never populated

sendAddGuestsEmails contains a loop over `calendarEvent.team?.members` to send each team member an OrganizerAddGuestsEmail, but the CalendarEvent constructed in this handler has no `team` property, so that loop is dead code and team members of collective/round-robin events never receive the guests-added notification.

Untranslated 'Remove email' tooltip string

The remove-button tooltip uses the hardcoded English string "Remove email" instead of t(...) with a key in the locale files (the component otherwise uses useLocale), so it renders in English for every locale and is not pickable by the translation tooling.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount deletion branch is not scoped to SMS reminders

In the cleanup `deleteMany`, the new second OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method` (or `scheduled`) filter, so it matches every row in WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 — including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders. The first OR branch is explicitly limited to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, showing the SMS-only intent of this cron, but the retryCount branch is table-wide. Today only this file writes retryCount so there is no immediate data loss, but retryCount is a column on the shared WorkflowReminder model; if any other reminder type ever sets it (e.g. a similar retry mechanism for email), this SMS cron would silently delete those reminders. The condition should be `AND: [{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]` (and probably `scheduled: false`).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

false_positives.candidate:
No tests cover the new retry increment and deletion threshold

The PR adds branching logic that permanently deletes data (retryCount > 1 cleanup) and increments retryCount on two different failure paths (scheduleSMS returning falsy, and exceptions), but no tests were added or updated. A regression here either leaves users receiving duplicate SMS attempts indefinitely or silently deletes legitimate reminders. At minimum the behavior 'failure increments retryCount once per run', 'reminder is deleted on the run after the second failure', and 'successful scheduling leaves retryCount untouched' should be covered.

Reminders that never reach the Twilio call never get their retryCount incremented

The retry-count increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. When a reminder fails before reaching `twilio.scheduleSMS` — e.g. the booking has no `smsReminderNumber` so `sendTo` is null, or the resolved message is empty — the guard fails, no SMS is attempted, and no retryCount increment happens. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0, so it is re-fetched and fully reprocessed (template rendering, profile lookup, etc.) on every cron run until `scheduledDate` passes. That is exactly the repeated-rescheduling behavior this PR is meant to stop, and a missing/invalid phone number is the failure mode called out in the PR description. There should be an `else` that increments retryCount (or otherwise marks the reminder) so the two-strike deletion applies to these reminders too.

Unawaited-safe DB write inside catch can throw and abort the entire cron run

The catch block now performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` without its own error handling. The try block itself contains prisma calls (`prisma.profile.findFirst`, the update marking a reminder scheduled, and the new else-branch increment), so a database error lands in this catch where the update is likely to throw again. Additionally, if the reminder row is deleted concurrently (e.g. by a booking-cancellation flow between the findMany at the top and this update), the update raises Prisma P2025 'record not found'. In both cases the exception propagates out of the handler: the request returns 500 and the for-loop aborts, so every reminder after the failing one is skipped for the run. Before this PR the catch only logged the error, so this is a new failure mode. Wrap the increment in a nested try/catch (and consider using `retryCount: { increment: 1 }`).

Caching behavior tests removed while caching logic remains in the service

The entire `describe("Caching", ...)` block (which verified that repeated calls to `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()` return the cached result) was deleted rather than ported to the new `Prisma.Sql` format, yet the service still implements caching via `cachedAuthConditions`/`cachedFilterConditions` (including the subtle `undefined`-vs-`null` sentinel logic for filter conditions). true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' syntax is macOS-only and fails on GNU/Linux

The script updates GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with `sed -i '' -E "s|...|..." "$ENV_FILE"`. The `-i ''` form (separate empty-string argument for the backup suffix) is BSD/macOS-only; on GNU sed (Linux dev machines, CI containers) the empty string is parsed as a filename and the command fails with "sed: can't read : No such file or directory", so the .env file is never updated. Use a portable form (e.g. `sed -i.bak -E ... && rm -f "$ENV_FILE.bak"`) or detect the platform.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Handler throws a generic Error, surfacing as HTTP 500 instead of 404/403

When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, deleteCacheHandler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC a plain Error is reported to the client as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500), which is wrong for a not-found/authorization failure and will also pollute server error monitoring. The codebase convention is to throw a TRPCError with an explicit code, e.g. `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: ... })` or FORBIDDEN, so clients get the correct status code.

Cache timestamp is hardcoded to en-US formatting, ignoring the user's locale

Every user, regardless of their configured locale, will see US-style dates (e.g. 7/15/25, 3:04 PM), which is confusing for locales that use DD/MM/YYYY or 24-hour times. Use the user's locale (e.g. navigator.language or the i18n locale from useLocale) instead of the hardcoded "en-US" string.

ENV_FILE="../.env" resolves relative to the caller's working directory and can write outside the repo

The script hardcodes ENV_FILE="../.env", which is only correct when the script is invoked from inside the scripts/ directory. deleteCache success does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status on screen

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Marking reminders as cancelled is fire-and-forget (previously the reminder deletion was awaited)

The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` / `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` inside nested `forEach` loops without awaiting the returned promises. Before this PR, the workflowReminder rows were removed via `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany(...)` promises that were awaited in `Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(remindersToDelete))`. Now the entire fix depends on a DB write (`cancelled: true`) that is never awaited: in a serverless environment (Next.js API route on Vercel) the response can be sent and the invocation frozen before the update commits, so reminders intermittently never get flagged and the emails for cancelled bookings are still sent. Errors are also invisible since the inner functions swallow them. The cancel calls should be collected and awaited (e.g. `await Promise.all(...)`) before the handler returns.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path cancels in SendGrid but leaves the WorkflowReminder row untouched (not deleted, not marked cancelled)

When `immediateDelete` is true and `referenceId` is set, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` POSTs the cancel to SendGrid and returns without deleting or updating the DB row. For the caller in `handleNewBooking.ts` (reschedule, line 968) the old booking is kept (status CANCELLED), so its reminder rows linger with `scheduled: true` and `cancelled: null` until their scheduledDate passes (only then does the cron's first deleteMany remove them). Two concrete consequences: (1) the SendGrid cancellation is issued immediately even when the email is scheduled up to 72 hours out, so the pending cancellation sits in SendGrid for days — this re-introduces the accumulation toward SendGrid's 100 pending-cancellation cap that this PR identifies as the root cause, via repeated reschedules (and via workflow/step deletions which use the same path); (2) when the `requestReschedule` tRPC flow ran first, the row still has `cancelled: true` from that flow, so the cron will POST a second cancellation for the same SendGrid batch that handleNewBooking already cancelled. After a successful immediate cancel the row should be deleted (mirroring `deleteScheduledSMSReminder`), or the reschedule path should use the `cancelled`-flag flow like the others.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellation of the old booking's workflow reminders is fire-and-forget and the surrounding try/catch cannot catch their errors

The new block `originalRescheduledBooking.workflowReminders.forEach((reminder) => { deleteScheduledEmailReminder(...); deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...); })` never awaits the async functions it calls, and the `try/catch` around the `forEach` can therefore never catch failures from them (it only looks protective). Since these are the only calls that cancel the previous booking's reminders on reschedule, an unawaited invocation in a serverless request can be cut short when the response is sent, meaning the SendGrid cancellation (and the DB row deletion for SMS / the eventual cleanup for email) never happens and the old booking's reminder emails are still sent — the exact issue this PR is meant to fix. The promises should be collected and awaited inside the try block.

One failing SendGrid cancellation aborts the whole batch and silently drops the queued DB deletes

In the new cancellation block of the cron handler, the try/catch wraps the entire `for (const reminder of remindersToCancel)` loop, and the `prisma.workflowReminder.delete(...)` promises collected in `workflowRemindersToDelete` are only executed by a single `await Promise.all(...)` after the loop. A PrismaPromise does not run unless it is awaited, so if `client.request(...)` throws for any reminder (e.g. SendGrid returns 404 for an unknown or already-cancelled batch_id, or a transient 5xx), then: (a) every reminder after the failing one is skipped for this run, and (b) all delete queries gathered so far are discarded — rows whose SendGrid cancellation already succeeded stay in the DB with `cancelled: true` and will be cancelled again on the next run. Worse, a persistently failing row is never deleted, so it is retried on every cron run and aborts the loop at the same point, blocking all later reminders. Because the cancellation window is only 1 hour (~4 cron runs), blocked reminders can miss their window and their emails will be sent for cancelled bookings — the exact bug this PR fixes. The try/catch should be inside the loop (per reminder), and each reminder's row should be deleted right after its own successful SendGrid cancel.

requestReschedule marks reminders cancelled without awaiting, a regression from the previously awaited deletion

In the `requestReschedule` mutation the old code pushed `prisma.workflowReminder.deleteMany(...)` promises into `remindersToDelete` and awaited them with `await Promise.all(remindersToDelete)`. The new code calls `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` (which performs the critical `cancelled: true` update) and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(...)` inside a `forEach` without awaiting any of the promises. In a serverless tRPC invocation the response can complete and the process freeze before these DB updates finish, so the reminders for the rescheduled booking may never be marked cancelled and the workflow emails will still go out. The calls should be awaited before the mutation continues/returns.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
requestReschedule: calendar deletions are now fire-and-forget behind an un-awaited dynamic import

In the `requestReschedule` mutation the PR changed the booking-reference cleanup loop from a synchronous `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => { const calendar = getCalendar(...); return calendar?.deleteEvent(...); })` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })`. `forEach` does not await async callbacks and nothing else awaits them, and there is no surrounding try/catch. Before this change `calendar.deleteEvent(...)` was invoked synchronously, so the provider API calls were in flight before the mutation sent the reschedule email and returned; now each callback suspends at `await getCalendar(...)` (the dynamic import) and the deletion only starts later, possibly after the response has been sent — on serverless platforms the function can be frozen before `deleteEvent` ever runs, leaving stale events on the organizer's calendar. Failures inside the callback (import or deleteEvent rejection) become unhandled promise rejections instead of surfaced errors. Fix by awaiting the work: `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

requestReschedule: calendar deletions are now fire-and-forget behind an un-awaited dynamic import

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded

Each value in the appStore map is now a promise created when this module is evaluated (e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`). `import()` begins loading the target module immediately, so all 28 app packages are still fetched/parsed as soon as anything imports `@calcom/app-store` — the loading is not deferred to first use, which defeats the stated purpose of the PR. To get real lazy loading the values must be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites doing `await appStore[key]()`. Additionally, these module-scope promises float until a caller awaits them: if one of the dynamic imports ever rejects (failed/missing chunk) and that app key is never awaited, Node raises an unhandled promise rejection, which terminates the process by default on Node >= 15.

Recurring-cancel path: awaiting getCalendar inside fire-and-forget forEach defers deleteEvent past the end of the request

In the branch that cancels all remaining occurrences of a recurring event, the code does `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... await calendar?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId); ... })`. The `await getCalendar(...)` added by this PR makes each callback suspend on the dynamic import before `deleteEvent` is ever invoked; previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so every `deleteEvent` HTTP call was started synchronously while the forEach ran. Nothing awaits the forEach callbacks, and the pushes into `apiDeletes` happen only after those callbacks resume — i.e. after the handler already executed `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (which snapshots the array) and returned success. The net effect is that deleting the calendar events for all future occurrences of a cancelled recurring booking may never start before the request completes (and may never run at all on serverless), leaving cancelled occurrences on users' calendars. Collect the promises (e.g. with `map`) and include them in the final `Promise.all`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Copy-paste bug: `end` is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

In the working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` computation — it was clearly meant to use slotEndTime. As a result `end > workingHour.endTime` can only fire when the slot's start is already past the end of working hours, and a slot that starts within working hours but ends after the host's availability end is treated as available. Example: fixed host works until 17:00, a round-robin co-host works until 19:00, and a 60-minute slot starts at 16:45 (aligned to the co-host's schedule) — the fixed host gets booked 16:45–17:45 despite being unavailable after 17:00.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`===` comparison between two Dayjs objects is always false (dead blocked-day branch)

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares object references, so it is never true — the author presumably meant `.isSame()`. This branch is meant to detect a fully blocked day (an override whose start equals its end, typically midnight, which is how "unavailable" date overrides are stored). Because it never fires, blocked days are only rejected incidentally via the surrounding before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the start==end timestamp of a blocked-day override (e.g., exactly 00:00 UTC) is reported as available on a day the host marked unavailable.

false_positives.candidate:
Date-override containment check accepts slots that only partially overlap the override

The new override-range logic only rejects slots that are entirely outside the override: it returns "not within" when slotEndTime <= override.start or when slotStartTime > override.end. Two cases slip through and are treated as within the override (and therefore available): (1) a slot that starts before the override start but ends inside it, because slotStartTime.isBefore(override.start) is never checked; (2) a slot that starts before the override end but ends after it, because the end-side check is the strict `slotStartTime.isAfter(override.end)` — a slot starting at 17:30 with an override ending 18:00 (and even a slot starting exactly at 18:00, since isAfter is not inclusive) passes. Hosts with non-aligned schedules (e.g., fixed host override 14:00–18:00, co-host hours starting at :30) can be booked partially or fully outside their override window. The check should require the slot to be fully contained: slotStartTime >= override.start && slotEndTime <= override.end.

No test covers the headline fix: date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin events

The PR's primary change is the new fixed-host/loose-host availability enforcement in checkIfIsAvailable (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts), but the only added test exercises a single-user event with a date override viewed from a different invitee timezone. There is no ROUND_ROBIN scenario with an isFixed host that has a date override, and no scenario where a host with a date override also has busy times/bookings on the override day — which is why the regression where the busy check is skipped on override days (the `dateOverrideExist` early return) is not caught: the new test would pass even with that bug. Please add tests for a round-robin event with a fixed host override (including timezones where organizer/invitee dates differ) and for a host with an override plus a conflicting booking on the same day.

Slots inside a date override return early and skip the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a host has a date override on the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the new `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` returns "available" before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom of the function ever runs. checkIfIsAvailable is the only place busy times (calendar events and existing bookings) are consulted — getTimeSlots never sees them. Consequence: for any host with a date override on a given day (fixed hosts via the new fixed-host filter, round-robin hosts via the loose-host filter, and single-user events since users default to isFixed), all of their existing bookings and calendar conflicts on that day are ignored, so the slot is offered and the host can be double-booked. Before this PR the busy check always ran, so this is a regression. The override-branch should fall through to the busy check instead of returning true.

Timezone conversion of date overrides drops the date component; overrides land on the wrong invitee day when timezones straddle midnight

The new conversion shifts the stored override time by (inviteeOffset - organizerOffset) and then reads only `.hour()`/`.minute()`, discarding any day rollover, and the `activeOverrides` filter (line 207) still matches the override's stored-as-UTC date against the invitee's calendar day. When the organizer's and invitee's local dates differ, the override is applied on the wrong invitee day and never on the correct one. Concrete example: organizer in Honolulu (UTC-10) with an override Mar 10 08:00–09:00, invitee in Auckland (UTC+13). The true window is Mar 11 07:00–08:00 Auckland time, but the code offers Mar 10 07:00–08:00 Auckland (offset +1380 min rolls 08:00 to 07:00 the next day, and .hour() truncates it back onto Mar 10), while for inviteeDate Mar 11 the filter no longer matches the stored Mar 10 date so the override is missing entirely. The same happens for e.g. Tokyo organizer / Los Angeles invitee. This is the timezone-adjustment scenario the PR sets out to fix, still broken for large timezone gaps.

Working-hours gate fails open when the host has no working hours on the slot's day

The new working-hours check treats a slot as "within working hours" whenever `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined. The find callback only returns true when a workingHour entry matches the slot's UTC day AND the slot is outside its range; if the host has no working-hour entry at all for that weekday (their day off), the callback returns undefined for every entry, find returns undefined, the `return false` is skipped, and the host is considered available. For round-robin events, slots are generated from the union of all hosts' hours, so a slot on a fixed host's day off (generated from a round-robin host who works that day) passes the fixed-host filter and becomes bookable — exactly the kind of booking this PR is meant to prevent. The check should fail closed: if no workingHour covers the slot's day, the slot should be unavailable.

dayjs.tz(override.timeZone) silently falls back to the server's timezone when timeZone is undefined

TimeRange.timeZone is optional (packages/types/schedule.d.ts marks it `timeZone?: string`), and getSlots is a shared library function, but the new code calls `dayjs(...).tz(override.timeZone)` unconditionally. When timeZone is undefined, dayjs.tz does not throw — it falls back to the runtime's local timezone (typically UTC on servers/containers). The offset calculation then becomes inviteeOffset - serverOffset instead of inviteeOffset - organizerOffset, silently shifting the override's slots for any caller that passes date overrides without a timeZone. Either make the field required for date overrides or handle the undefined case explicitly.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError crash when an existing Integration has no "sender" in metadata

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when an Integration row exists for the installation_id but has no OrganizationIntegration, the new verification does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. The "sender" key is only written into metadata by the installation webhook; `build_integration` adds it only when the pipeline state contains "sender", and nothing in the pipeline ever binds that key, so every integration created through the pipeline path (e.g. when the webhook was delayed or lost) lacks it, as do older rows created before the webhook recorded the sender. No test covers the sender-match success path of the new verification

true_positives.golden_comment: The AssignmentSource dataclass uses queued: datetime = timezone.now() as a default field value, which evaluates timezone.now() once at class definition time and shares that single datetime instance across all objects.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`queued` default is evaluated once at module import, not per instance

In the `AssignmentSource` dataclass, `queued: datetime = timezone.now()` executes `timezone.now()` a single time when the class body is evaluated (at module import). Every `AssignmentSource` created without an explicit `queued` — which is all of them, since `from_integration` and the test constructors never pass it — shares the timestamp of process startup/module import rather than the time the assignment actually originated. The field's apparent purpose (recording when the assignment was queued) is therefore defeated, and any future consumer reading `queued` would get a wrong, potentially days-old value. true_positives.golden_comment: to_dict() returns a datetime for queued; if this dict is passed in task kwargs (e.g., via apply_async), JSON serialization may fail depending on the serializer, which can cause enqueue errors.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`from_dict` performs no type coercion/validation, so `queued` round-trips as a string through the task queue

`to_dict()` emits `queued` as a `datetime`, but the dict crosses the Celery boundary as the `assignment_source_dict` kwarg, where Sentry's JSON-based task serialization converts datetimes to ISO-8601 strings. `from_dict` then blindly splats the payload into the constructor (`cls(**input_dict)`), and dataclasses do not enforce type annotations, so after every real round trip `queued` is a `str` in a `datetime`-typed field — the class invariant is silently broken (the eager test runner does not serialize kwargs, so the tests don't catch this). The same lack of validation means a wrong-typed `integration_id` (e.g. a string after a future serialization change) would construct successfully and then never equal `org_integration.integration_id` in `IssueSyncIntegration.should_sync`, failing open and re-opening the exact sync cycle this PR exists to prevent. `from_dict` should parse `queued` back into a datetime (or the field should be dropped) and coerce/validate `integration_id`.

false_positives.candidate:
test_dedupe builds the expected occurrence with the wrong group key, so its assertion fails

In TestEvaluateGroupKeyValue.test_dedupe, the expected occurrence is built via build_mock_occurrence_and_event(handler, "val1", 6, PriorityLevel.HIGH), but the DetectorEvaluationResult it is compared against is produced by calling evaluate_group_key_value with group_key="group_key" (expected_result.group_key is passed in). build_mock_occurrence_and_event embeds handler.build_fingerprint(group_key) into the IssueOccurrence, so the expected occurrence has fingerprint ["<detector_id>:val1"] while the actual occurrence has ["<detector_id>:group_key"].
