true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metrics tag keys: "shard" vs "shards", and comma-joined multi-shard tag values

The new per-process metrics tagging is inconsistent: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185) and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 196) are tagged with key `"shard"`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199) uses key `"shards"`, so dashboards or monitors grouping/filtering by `shard` will silently miss the wait_produce timer. Additionally, when `max_processes < len(assigned_shards)` a process handles multiple shards and the tag value is a comma-joined list like "0,2,4", whereas `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` (line 243) emits one data point per individual shard integer — two different conventions for the same dimension that cannot be correlated in metrics queries.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep

`test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at the top of the test (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change" provides no synchronization whatsoever. The test still depends on the racing flusher thread observing `current_drift.value = 9000` and completing a flush+produce before `step.join()` sets `stopped.value`; if the flusher thread's next loop iteration starts after `stopped` is set, it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails on an empty list. If the intent was to deflake the test, this doesn't do it — the flusher's completion needs to be awaited deterministically (e.g., poll `messages` with a real timeout loop, since the fake sleep also makes the flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` a hot spin).

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process is always False for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed

`isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is never true for the processes this class creates. The flusher uses `multiprocessing.get_context("spawn")`, whose `Process` class is `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess` — a sibling of `multiprocessing.Process` (which is the fork-context flavor), not a subclass of it. The type annotation on `self.processes` (`SpawnProcess | threading.Thread`) even acknowledges this. Consequences: (1) In `_ensure_processes_alive`, when a flusher process is deemed unhealthy due to a hang, `process.kill()` is silently skipped before the replacement process is started — previously the kill was unconditional, so this is a regression. The hung process keeps running indefinitely: it keeps flushing the same shards as its replacement, and because the restart reuses the same shared `healthy_since` Value for that process slot, a still-looping zombie can keep refreshing `healthy_since` and permanently mask the hang from the health check. (2) The same wrong check at line 346 means `join()` never calls `terminate()` on spawn processes that outlive the deadline. Fix by checking `not isinstance(process, threading.Thread)` or by calling `kill()`/`terminate()` unconditionally as before.

true_positives.golden_comment: Sleep in test_consumer.py won’t actually wait because time.sleep was monkeypatched above; consider restoring sleep or using a different sync to ensure the flusher has time to process.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep

`test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at the top of the test (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change" provides no synchronization whatsoever. The test still depends on the racing flusher thread observing `current_drift.value = 9000` and completing a flush+produce before `step.join()` sets `stopped.value`; if the flusher thread's next loop iteration starts after `stopped` is set, it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails on an empty list. If the intent was to deflake the test, this doesn't do it — the flusher's completion needs to be awaited deterministically (e.g., poll `messages` with a real timeout loop, since the fake sleep also makes the flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` a hot spin).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Breaking out of the loop when the deadline has elapsed can skip terminating remaining flusher processes, potentially leaving them running after shutdown; consider ensuring termination is attempted even if the deadline is exceeded.

false_positives.candidate:
--flusher-processes is not validated; 0 is silently treated as per-shard and a negative value crashes startup with KeyError

The new `--flusher-processes` option (and `SpanFlusher`'s `max_processes`) accepts any integer without validation. Passing 0 is silently treated as "one process per shard" because `0 or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` takes the shard count. Passing a negative number is worse: `self.num_processes = min(-1, len(shards))` is negative, so `process_to_shards_map` is built from `range(-1)` and is empty, and the very first shard assignment `self.process_to_shards_map[0].append(shard)` raises a bare `KeyError`, crashing the consumer at startup with no useful message. The option should be validated as `>= 1` (in the click callback or the constructor) and 0 should either be rejected or documented.

Dead method _create_process_for_shard left over from per-shard design

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is never called anywhere: the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards(process_index, shards)` directly. This leftover single-shard helper is misleading (it suggests per-shard restarts are possible when a restart actually recreates the whole multi-shard process) and should be removed.

Unset max_processes defaults to one process per shard instead of preserving old single-process behavior

`self.max_processes = max_processes or len(buffer.assigned_shards)` makes an unset value mean "one process per shard", the most aggressive setting. The new `--flusher-processes` click option defaults to 1, which preserves the previous single-flusher-process behavior, but any construction path that does not pass the new parameter gets the aggressive behavior: for example an ops override of the `process-spans` entry in `SENTRY_KAFKA_CONSUMERS` that still uses the old `click_options` shape (the ops repo is deployed independently of this code), or any direct Python instantiation of `ProcessSpansStrategyFactory`/`SpanFlusher`. Such deployments would silently go from 1 flusher process to N spawned processes and N Kafka producers per consumer on upgrade, contrary to the PR's stated gradual-rollout intent. The default for `flusher_processes=None` should be 1, with per-shard scaling opt-in via the option.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts the opposite of the implemented behavior and races the 1s commit thread

The test mocks the result processor to raise on the first of two messages and then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, i.e. that nothing is ever committed. That contradicts both the implementation and the test's own docstring ('errors in processing don't block offset commits for other messages'): OrderedQueueWorker.run marks the failed item's offset complete in its finally block, so once the strategy's commit thread wakes on its 1-second tick it will commit offset 102 for the partition. The test only passes because the assertion usually runs before the commit thread's first 1s iteration; on a slow CI worker the commit fires first and the test fails nondeterministically. The test should instead wait on a commit and assert the real intended semantics — that the processing error did not prevent the partition's offsets (including the failed message's, which is skipped) from being committed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

false_positives.candidate:
Shutdown drops queued work without draining or a final offset commit, causing duplicate processing on every rebalance/deploy

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on 'while not self.shutdown', so each worker exits immediately after its current item and never drains the remaining queued items — the immediate=False 'graceful' drain is dead code. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() never waits for queued work (wait_until_empty exists but is unused) and performs no final commit after workers finish: the commit thread is joined before the pool is shut down, and its last pass races with in-flight items. The result is that on every deploy or partition revocation the queued backlog plus roughly the last commit-interval's worth of completed-but-uncommitted work is redelivered by Kafka and processed a second time. join(timeout) should drain the queues within the timeout and then stage a final commit of all completed offsets.

Strategy close() kills the factory-shared queue pool; after any rebalance all messages are silently dropped but their offsets are committed

The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (result_consumer.py, mode == 'thread-queue-parallel') and the same pool object is handed to every strategy built by create_with_partitions. However, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets worker.shutdown=True, shuts down every queue, and joins the worker threads. Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and joins the current strategy on every partition revocation and creates a new one on the next assignment, so after the first routine consumer-group rebalance (deploy, autoscaling, another group member joining) the new strategy is built on a dead pool. From then on every submit() reaches work_queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches that with a broad 'except Exception', logs it, and then calls offset_tracker.add_offset + complete_offset for the message. The commit thread therefore commits offsets for messages that were never enqueued or processed, and since this consumer has no DLQ configured the data is silently lost until the process is restarted. Nothing recreates the pool (ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() is never invoked by the StreamProcessor). Fix by creating the pool per create_with_partitions call (or not shutting it down from the strategy), and by not marking offsets complete when the work item was never actually queued.

Unbounded queues and no backpressure despite docstring claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy never applies backpressure: submit() always enqueues immediately and poll() only emits a gauge (arroyo strategies signal backpressure by raising MessageRejected from poll/submit). The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but put() on an unbounded queue never blocks, so the Kafka consumer thread keeps polling and buffering messages in memory no matter how far behind the workers fall. A single slow group — the exact scenario this mode is built to tolerate — grows its queue without bound and the partition's entire backlog accumulates in the process heap, eventually OOM-killing the consumer pod. The queues should be bounded (maxsize) and/or poll() should raise MessageRejected when total depth exceeds a threshold.

test_different_groups_distributed is flaky due to per-process string hash randomization

The test submits 20 group keys and asserts len(queue_indices) == 3, i.e. that they cover all 3 queues. Queue assignment is hash(group_key) % num_queues, and CPython randomizes str hash values per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so each test run is effectively a random draw: the probability that 20 keys land in only 1–2 of 3 buckets is about 0.09% (3*(2/3)^20). With no code change at all, roughly 1 in 1100 CI runs will fail this assertion. Use a looser assertion (e.g. indices are within range and ordering per key is stable), pin the hash seed, or mock hash().

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Deny-cache test does not actually prove the denial cache short-circuits

In TestService_CacheCheck/'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry', the permission cache is seeded with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} and the comment claims this 'allows access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked'. A scope-map value of false does not allow anything, so the test returns Allowed=false even if the denial-cache logic were removed entirely: the cached perms would deny, the DB fallback (empty fakeStore) would also deny, and the assertion would still pass. To prove the denial cache is consulted, the cached value must be true — then the test would fail if the permDenialCache check in Check were removed or bypassed.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache can persist denials computed from stale data and is never invalidated

In Check, when the DB fallback still denies, the denial is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and short-circuits all later checks for that (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple. Two problems follow: (1) The deny decision may depend on the cached folder tree (checkInheritedPermissions -> buildFolderTree uses folderCache, also 30s TTL), which the DB fallback does NOT refresh. If a teammate of a folder creator checks a dashboard inside a folder created seconds ago, the fresh permission re-query returns the same scopes (e.g. only folders:uid:<grandparent>) and the stale tree has no ancestors for the new folder, so the request is denied and that deny is now cached for another 30s — extending the deny window up to ~60s after folder creation, longer than before this change, for exactly the 'newly created folder' scenario this PR is meant to fix. (2) When the fallback re-fetch does update permCache with fresh scopes, any pre-existing denial entry for a resource covered by those fresh scopes is not deleted, so the stale denial still wins over fresher permission data. Consider refreshing/invalidating the folder tree (or skipping denial caching) when the deny relied on folder-tree evaluation, and/or keying denials so a fresh allow can supersede them.

Every denied check for a distinct resource name now triggers a full DB permission fetch

With the new fallback, whenever the cached permission map does not contain the requested scope, Check unconditionally re-queries the full permission set from the database (getIdentityPermissions -> getUserPermissions -> permissionStore.GetUserPermissions). The denial cache only deduplicates repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parentFolder) tuple, so a caller that polls N distinct resources it cannot access (dashboard listing integrations, scanners, a user clicking through an org where most content is restricted) now issues N full permission queries per 30s window, where before this change the permission cache answered all of them with a single query per user/action. Singleflight only collapses concurrent identical user+action fetches, not sequential distinct names. Consider bounding the fallback (e.g., a short 'permissions fresh as of' marker per user/action so repeated denials on different names within a few seconds don't each hit the DB).

Permission-cache hits that result in denial are recorded as cache misses

When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission map (cache hit) but checkPermission returns allowed=false, execution falls out of the if-block and reaches s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...) — recording a cache miss even though the permission cache was hit. Denied checks are precisely the traffic pattern this PR optimizes, so this mislabeling systematically skews the cache hit-rate metric downward and makes the new caching behavior look less effective than it is. The hit/miss label should be recorded based on whether the cache lookup succeeded, before evaluating the allow/deny outcome.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a key in the filtered rule list

In the rules.map switch, the 'grafana' branch returns `<GrafanaRuleListItem rule={...} .../>` without `key={key}`; the replaced GrafanaRuleLoader had key={key}, and the sibling 'datasource' and 'default' branches still pass key. React will emit a missing-key warning, and mixing keyed and unkeyed siblings in the same list can cause React to mis-associate per-item component state (e.g. RuleActionsButtons' silence drawer / delete modal state) when the list updates.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Silence notifications" menu item is shown but does nothing in the new rule list

In the new list view, GrafanaRuleListItem renders RuleActionsButtons with only promRule (the `rule` prop is undefined). AlertRuleMenu now derives the Silence ability from the Prometheus rule via useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, so the "Silence notifications" menu item renders enabled and clicking it calls handleSilence -> setShowSilenceDrawer(true). However, the drawer is gated on `{rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer && <SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer rulerRule={rule} .../>}`; with `rule` undefined the drawer never mounts, so clicking the menu item is a silent no-op. The new GrafanaGroupLoader test only asserts that the Silence menu item exists, never that clicking it opens anything. The silence flow needs to be driven from the prom rule/identifier, or the item should be hidden when no ruler rule is available.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete and Pause actions no longer appear in the list view rule menu

AlertRuleMenu gates the Delete item on `canDelete && rulerRule` (line 165) and the Pause item on `canPause && rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rulerRule)` (line 123). The new list view (GrafanaRuleListItem -> RuleActionsButtons.V2) never passes a rulerRule, only a GrafanaPromRuleDTO, so even though canDelete/canPause can now be satisfied through useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities, the Delete and Pause items never render. Previously the list passed the ruler rule and both actions were available. The updated GrafanaGroupLoader test codifies the regression by asserting exactly 4 menu items (silence, duplicate, copy link, export) with no delete. Users of the new list view can no longer delete or pause rules from it, which is a functional regression beyond the stated goal of removing ruler API requests.

Duplicate menu item becomes enabled for data-source rules based on Grafana-internal create permission

canDuplicate now ORs the ruler-based ability with the result of useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities. For a non-Grafana (Mimir/Cortex/Loki) rule, promRule fails prometheusRuleType.grafana.rule so skipToken is passed, producing useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities(undefined). With rule undefined, loading=false makes duplicateSupported=true, and the allowed side is checked against getRulesPermissions('grafana').create (alert.rules:create). A user who has Grafana-managed rule create permission but lacks alert.rules.external:write will now see the "Duplicate" menu item on cloud rules; before this change only the ruler-based ability (which requires the external write permission) was consulted. The backend still enforces permissions, but the UI now advertises an action the user cannot complete.

Federated rule groups lose their edit/delete immutability protection

useAllAlertRuleAbilities (which backs useAlertRuleAbility/useAlertRuleAbilities used across the old list view and detail views) previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and treated federated rules as immutable, hiding Update/Delete/Pause/Restore/DeletePermanently. This PR rewrites it to delegate to useAllRulerRuleAbilities, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false` with a TODO. As a result, for Mimir/GEM federated (cross-tenant, source_tenants) rule groups, those actions now report as supported whenever permissions allow, rendering Edit/Delete/Pause buttons that were previously suppressed; attempted operations will fail at the ruler API or mutate a group the UI previously treated as read-only.

Grafana recording rules lose the Export menu item in the list view

The new prom-based ability gates ModifyExport on prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) (`[AlertRuleAction.ModifyExport]: [isAlertingRule, exportAllowed]`), whereas the ruler-based path used rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule), which also matches recording rules. In the new list view only the prom-based path runs (no rulerRule is fetched), so Grafana-managed recording rules no longer show the "Export / With modifications" menu entry even though they did before and modify-export is valid for recording rules.

JSDoc still claims the group is loaded from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints

The comment above GrafanaGroupLoader says "Loads an evaluation group from Prometheus and Ruler endpoints", but this PR removed the ruler query (useGetGrafanaRulerGroupQuery) — only the Prometheus endpoint is queried now. The expectedRulesCount prop comment also still references the ruler response. These stale comments misdescribe the component's behavior after the change.

Rule view link drops the returnTo parameter

The previous GrafanaRuleListItem (in the deleted GrafanaRuleLoader.tsx) built the href as createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo }) using createReturnTo(), so navigating back from the rule detail page returned the user to the filtered list. The new component uses createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`) with no returnTo, breaking return-to-previous navigation for rules opened from the new list and filter views.

Stale comment and variable name referring to ruler rule preloading

After removing the alertRuleApi getGrafanaRulerGroup prefetch, the comment "This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX..." and the variable name `cacheAndRulerPreload` are stale — the block now only upserts the Prometheus groups cache. The comment should be updated so readers don't think ruler preloading still happens here.

true_positives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No test coverage for ad hoc filters (request.filters) through the split/shard query paths

This change newly threads request.filters into datasource.applyTemplateVariables in runShardSplitQuery (previously it called interpolateVariablesInQueries with only scopedVars, so ad hoc filters were never applied to sharded queries) and in runSplitQuery (which previously did not interpolate targets at all). None of the added or updated tests set request.filters and assert the resulting selector — they only cover replacement of variables in expr and step. Because the shard path now invokes applyTemplateVariables multiple times per target (the updated 'Interpolates queries before running' test expects 5 calls for one query), a duplication or loss of ad hoc matchers in the final LogQL selector would go unnoticed. A test passing request.filters through both splitting paths and asserting the final expr would close the gap.

false_positives.candidate:
Sharded queries are interpolated N+1 times: once in runShardSplitQuery and again in every runSplitQuery sub-request

runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts:49-52) now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before grouping by stream shard, and then executes each shard group by building a subRequest and calling runSplitQuery. With this change, runSplitQuery also maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables (the new .map here), so in the shard-splitting flow each query is interpolated once up front plus once per shard-group sub-request. The updated test 'Interpolates queries before running' in shardQuerySplitting.test.ts now expects applyTemplateVariables to have been called 5 times for a single target (1 upfront + 4 shard batches), which bakes this redundancy into the test suite. Variable substitution ($var, $__auto, step) is effectively idempotent so this mostly wastes work, but request.filters is passed on both calls, so ad hoc filters are appended to the stream selector twice unless applyTemplateVariables dedupes them — producing duplicated label matchers in the LogQL selector sent to Loki. Consider interpolating in only one place (e.g. let runSplitQuery skip interpolation when the caller already interpolated, or have the shard path rely on a single interpolation point).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID silently dropped from "Plugin Request Completed" log lines

The previous implementation of logRequest explicitly appended the trace ID to the log params via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false). This PR removes that block and instead relies on m.logger.FromContext(ctx), which only picks up the contextual attributes stored by ContextualLoggerMiddleware.instrumentContext (endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, uname). instrumentContext does not add a traceID attribute, so the traceID field is silently lost from these log lines, breaking log-to-trace correlation for plugin requests. This is a behavioral regression in a PR described as a rename-only chore. Fix: add the trace ID back, either by including tracing.TraceIDFromContext in the attributes added by instrumentContext or by continuing to append it in logRequest.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a fresh recorder, making contextual logs invisible to tests

TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), a brand-new instance with its own empty Logs fields. Code under test that logs via FromContext — notably the updated LoggerMiddleware, which now calls m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) — will record calls on a throwaway instance, so any test passing a TestLogger and asserting on its InfoLogs/WarnLogs/ErrorLogs counters will observe zero calls and cannot verify log output. The fake should return the receiver itself (or a logger that shares the same recording state) so contextual logging remains observable in tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
Doc comment on Logger.FromContext is a copy of New's and describes the wrong contract

The comment on FromContext reads "returns a new contextual Logger that has this logger's context plus the given context", which is copied verbatim from New(ctx ...any) and describes New's semantics. FromContext takes a context.Context and returns a logger enriched with the log attributes previously stored in that context (via infra/log.WithContextualAttributes), falling back to the base logger when none are present. As written the comment misleads implementers about what the method must do.

LoggerMiddleware now silently depends on ContextualLoggerMiddleware running earlier in the chain

logRequest no longer derives pluginId, endpoint, dsName, dsUID and uname from the request's PluginContext; those fields only appear in the "Plugin Request Completed" log if NewContextualLoggerMiddleware was registered before NewLoggerMiddleware in the middleware stack. Both constructors are exported and nothing documents or enforces this ordering, so any other wiring that uses NewLoggerMiddleware without the new middleware (tests, alternate client decorators, downstream projects) will silently emit logs missing those fields. Consider documenting the dependency on both constructors or having the logger middleware fall back to the request's PluginContext when no contextual attributes are present.

New ContextualLoggerMiddleware has no test coverage

The PR adds ContextualLoggerMiddleware (instrumentContext plus the four wrapped client methods) but adds no test for it. Nothing verifies that QueryData/CallResource/CheckHealth/CollectMetrics attach the endpoint/pluginId/dsName/dsUID/uname attributes to the context, or that the nil DataSourceInstanceSettings and nil User branches behave correctly. Since LoggerMiddleware's log output now depends entirely on these attributes (the inline logParams were removed), a regression here would silently strip fields from plugin request logs without any test failing.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check-then-insert is not atomic; concurrent new devices can exceed the limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running CountDevices and then, only if count < deviceLimit, executing the INSERT. These are two separate statements with no transaction or locking. Concurrent anonymous requests carrying distinct new device IDs — or requests landing on different Grafana replicas in an HA setup — can all observe a count below the limit and then all insert, so the stored device count can exceed deviceLimit by an arbitrary margin under a burst of new devices (e.g., bot/scraper traffic). If the limit is meant to be a hard cap, the count-and-insert must be done atomically (single transaction with locking), or the overshoot should be explicitly accepted and documented.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache is set before the limit check, so a retry bypasses the device limit entirely

tagDeviceUI writes the device key into the local cache (29-minute TTL) before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the configured device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a new device and Anonymous.Authenticate (client.go) rejects the request — but the cache entry has already been written and is never removed. Any subsequent request from the same device within 29 minutes hits the cache in tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds, even though the device was never persisted and is never counted toward the limit. A brand-new device therefore only has to send its request twice to get anonymous access past the limit, and this is repeatable after each cache expiry (first request fails, then ~29 minutes of access). The cache key should be set only after a successful store call, or explicitly deleted when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.
The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
New device_limit option is not documented in defaults.ini/sample.ini or the admin docs

readAuthSettings adds support for device_limit under [auth.anonymous], but the option is not added to conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, where every other auth.anonymous key is listed with an explanatory comment, and the configure-grafana documentation is not updated either. Operators have no discoverable way to learn the setting exists or that the default of 0 means the limit is disabled. The PR's own checklist requires docs to be updated for new configuration.

No test for the allowed path: existing device must still be updated when the limit is reached

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only asserts that a new device is rejected once the limit is reached. The complementary and more important branch — a device that already exists in anon_device must still be updated via updateDevice and allowed in while count >= deviceLimit — has no test, and neither does the propagation through Anonymous.Authenticate in client.go, which now fails authentication on ErrDeviceLimitReached. A regression in updateDevice's WHERE clause (for example a wrong updated_at window) would lock out every existing anonymous device as soon as the limit is hit, and nothing in this PR's tests would catch that.

anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined infers the property type as undefined

In GrafanaBootConfig, the new field is declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` with no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the class property's type as `undefined` (the `implements GrafanaConfig` clause does not widen inferred member types). Any frontend code reading config.anonymousDeviceLimit will see the type `undefined` and cannot compare or otherwise use it as a number without a cast, which defeats the purpose of exposing the value to the frontend. It should be declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined;`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags contain six r.log.Error calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) that log normal, successful operation: "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Tags to clean", "cleaned tags". These fire on every batch of every cleanup run even when nothing is wrong (the "err" kv is always nil at those points), and they log the complete slice of IDs to be deleted, which can be up to the configured AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize entries in a single line. Combined with the cleanup ticker being changed to 1 minute in this PR, this floods error-level logs during healthy operation, breaks any alerting based on error logs, and can produce enormous log lines for large batch sizes. These are leftover debug statements and should be r.log.Debug at most, and probably should not dump the raw ID list.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, running all cleanup jobs 10x more often

The Run loop ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. clean() does not only run annotation cleanup — on every tick it runs the entire job list: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, expiring user invites, deleting stale short URLs, two query-history enforcement queries, and re-scanning the temp file directories. This change therefore multiplies the database and filesystem load of all background cleanup jobs by 10, yet the PR description (about avoiding MySQL deadlocks in annotation cleanup) never mentions it. If the intent is to keep annotation cleanup batches small and frequent, that should be scoped to the annotation job or at least called out explicitly; as written this is an undocumented behavior change affecting every cleanup task.

false_positives.candidate:
Parameter-limit guard only covers SQLite; large batch sizes break on Postgres

deleteByIDs only sidesteps bind-parameter limits when the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999; every other database gets a `DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` statement with one placeholder per ID. Postgres rejects statements with more than 65535 bind parameters, and very large placeholder lists can also hit MySQL's max_allowed_packet. Since AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable and the PR itself tests a value of 32767, a batch size above 65535 on Postgres would make the delete fail on every cleanup cycle (the job errors out and nothing is cleaned). Consider chunking the ID list into fixed-size DELETE batches for all dialects instead of special-casing SQLite.

SQLite literal IN-list built with O(n^2) string concatenation

In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback for batch sizes over 999 builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over ids. Each iteration allocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building the list is quadratic in the number of IDs. With the batch size exercised in the new test (32767 IDs) this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch, and it runs on every batch iteration of the cleanup loop. Use a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-converted strings) to make it linear.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete stores the unenriched logger in the context

Delete builds an enriched logger (`log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method)`) but then stores the base logger in the context: `ctx = klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log)`. Anything downstream that calls `klog.FromContext(ctx)` loses the name/kind/method fields. It should pass `log`, as the other methods do.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete passes the object name as the kind label to recordStorageDuration

On a successful delete, `d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage)` passes the object's name as the third argument, where every other call site passes `options.Kind`. That argument is the resource/kind label of the duration metric, so this both mislabels the series and creates unbounded Prometheus label cardinality — one time series per deleted object name — which can seriously degrade the metrics endpoint and Prometheus server. It should be `options.Kind`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and will be canceled immediately

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135 and DeleteCollection at line 163), the goroutine performing the asynchronous legacy write builds its context from the incoming request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. The dual writer returns immediately after spawning the goroutine, and the HTTP request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, so the derived context is already (or almost immediately) canceled when the legacy write actually runs. The legacy store will therefore fail with context.Canceled in the common case, silently defeating the purpose of mode 3 ("write to legacy as a safe measure") — unified storage will have the data but legacy will not. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (keeping the log values) before applying the 10s timeout so the legacy write survives request completion.

Create error test registers the storage failure on the legacy mock and only works via the shared mock instance

In TestMode3_Create's case "error when creating object in the unified store fails", the failing Create expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` on the legacy mock, but mode 3 calls unified storage first and the legacy expectation is never used intentionally — the test only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage Create call accidentally matches the legacy-registered expectation. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, the storage Create call will panic as unexpected. Register the failing expectation on the storage mock (setupStorageFn) so the test models what it claims to test.

Create records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails

In the error path of Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never contacted and the measured start time belongs to the unified-storage call. This should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`; as written, unified-storage create failures pollute the legacy-storage error/duration metrics and the actual storage failure is never recorded, which will mislead the dashboards this mode is meant to feed.

Delete no longer cleans up legacy storage when unified storage returns NotFound

The previous Mode 3 Delete tolerated a NotFound error from unified storage (`apierrors.IsNotFound`) and still attempted the legacy delete; the new code returns immediately on any storage delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy (e.g., written before the unified copy existed, or whose unified copy was lost during migration) can now never be deleted through the API: unified returns NotFound, the client sees a failure, and the stale legacy record is left behind, where it will resurface if the installation rolls back to a legacy-first mode. The NotFound special-case for proceeding with the legacy delete should be preserved.

DeleteCollection records the legacy delete result as a unified-storage metric

Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Errors and durations of the legacy delete-collection are therefore attributed to unified storage, masking real legacy failures and inflating storage timings in the metrics.

Mode 3 integration subtests assert synchronous legacy visibility of async legacy writes

The new subtests "with dual write (file, mode 3)" and "with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)" reuse doPlaylistTests, which asserts that objects written via the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy REST API (the `/api/playlists` list comparison in "Do CRUD via k8s" and the legacy GET in getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously in a goroutine with no synchronization point, so there is no guarantee the legacy store has caught up when those assertions run — these subtests will be flaky under CI load (and, given the request-context cancellation bug in the async writer, may fail consistently). The mode-3 runs need polling/eventually-style assertions against the legacy API.

No draining of in-flight async legacy writes on shutdown

The async legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines with a 10s timeout, and `Destroy()` does not wait for any of them. On pod shutdown or rollout, every legacy write still in flight is silently abandoned, so the legacy copy can diverge from unified storage exactly during deploys — the window in which the "legacy as a safe measure" guarantee matters most. Consider tracking in-flight writes with a WaitGroup and draining them in Destroy.

Unit tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes

None of the new mode-3 unit tests (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the legacy write or assert that it happened — e.g., TestMode3_Create registers a legacy Create expectation but never blocks on the goroutine nor calls `m.AssertExpectations`. The tests pass even if the legacy write is never executed, so the core behavior this PR adds (async dual write to legacy) is effectively untested at the unit level; a regression that drops the legacy call entirely would go unnoticed.

Update records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails

In the error path of Update, when `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. The legacy store was never called and the duration measured is the unified-storage call's, so unified-storage update errors are misreported as legacy-storage errors in the dual-writer metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock (double-checked locking)

After taking the exclusive lock, GetWebAssets does not re-check whether another goroutine already populated entryPointAssetsCache. At startup (or whenever the cache is empty), every concurrent request observes a nil cache under the read lock, then queues on the write lock; each one in turn re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json from disk (or fetches it over HTTP if the CDN path at line 56 is ever enabled) and overwrites the cache, with all but the last result discarded. This is the standard double-checked-locking pattern with the second check missing. Adding `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock avoids the redundant serialized I/O.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock held across manifest I/O serializes all callers

The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer) for the entire recompute, including the disk read of assets-manifest.json and, if enabled, the CDN HTTP fetch. While any writer holds it, all other callers block on the initial RLock at line 41. In dev mode the cache is deliberately bypassed on every call, so every request to GetWebAssets is now serialized through this single global mutex plus a disk read. The same happens in non-dev mode whenever the manifest read persistently fails, because the cache then stays nil and every request retries under the exclusive lock, turning a missing-file misconfiguration into a global serialization point for index page loads. Consider doing the read outside the lock and taking the write lock only to publish the result (combined with the re-check from the previous point).

Race fix ships without a regression test exercising concurrent access

This PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test. Nothing guards the new synchronization: if someone later removes the mutex or accesses the global without it, nothing in the test suite would catch it. A simple test that calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines (against a temp assets-manifest.json) and is run under `go test -race` would fail if the synchronization regresses and would document the concurrency contract of this function.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing SQL expression tests are left in place and will now fail against the "not implemented" stub

This PR makes DB.RunCommands and DB.QueryFramesInto unconditionally return errors.New("not implemented"), which means sql.TablesList (pkg/expr/sql/parser.go) and NewSQLCommand (pkg/expr/sql_command.go) now fail for every input. The repository already contains tests that exercise these paths and expect them to work: pkg/expr/sql/parser_test.go calls TablesList with valid SQL and asserts on the returned table names, and pkg/expr/sql_command_test.go calls NewSQLCommand/Execute with valid SQL and asserts successful results. None of these test files are updated, skipped, or removed in this PR, so they will fail with "not implemented" / "error reading SQL command" and turn CI red. The tests should be removed or rewritten in this PR to assert the new disabled behavior.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading — the feature is deliberately disabled

When a dashboard or alert rule contains a SQL expression, the query now fails with the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature is in fact implemented but has been intentionally disabled in response to CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI), which is exactly the situation users and support staff will need to understand when previously working SQL expressions start failing. The message text is wrong and will generate confusion; it should say something like "SQL expressions are disabled" (ideally referencing the security advisory) instead of claiming the feature does not exist.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dropping the build-wide lock makes GetIndex+BuildIndex non-atomic; same key can be built concurrently

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for its entire duration; it now only locks while inserting the finished index into b.cache. The check in GetIndex and the build/insert are therefore not atomic: two goroutines building the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event handled via handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex racing a concurrent Search for a namespace that was not pre-built at startup, or two concurrent Searches for a cold namespace) will both build a complete index. One result then silently overwrites the other in the cache, leaking the losing index (for file-backed indexes, an open bleve index whose handles are never closed). Worse, when size > FileThreshold both goroutines call bleve.New on the same on-disk directory, and the second open fails on the store's directory lock, so one caller gets an error even though the index is being built. Consider a per-key lock, singleflight, or an inflight-builds map so concurrent builders for the same key share one build while different keys still build in parallel.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu and now runs concurrently with cache writes

TotalDocs loops over b.cache without taking cacheMu. This PR adds a new caller: searchSupport.init now logs s.search.TotalDocs() (search.go) immediately after starting the watch-event goroutine, and that goroutine can concurrently trigger BuildIndex via handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex, which writes to b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. An unsynchronized map iteration racing a map write causes a fatal, non-recoverable 'concurrent map read and map write' runtime panic. TotalDocs should acquire b.cacheMu.RLock() for the duration of the iteration.

false_positives.candidate:
Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks already-initialized resources

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err without any cleanup: the cancellable context created a few lines above is never cancelled (cancel is otherwise only invoked via Stop), the lifecycle backend initialized by lifecycle.Init (e.g. the SQL backend's open DB) is never stopped, and if the failure occurs in initWatcher after search.init succeeded, the watch goroutine started inside search.init runs on context.Background() and keeps polling forever. The error path should call s.cancel() and, when lifecycle was initialized, lifecycle.Stop (or otherwise unwind the partial initialization).

Stop() no longer blocks requests: handlers dropped the Init/initErr check

Every gRPC handler previously began with `if err := s.Init(ctx); err != nil { return ... }`, which surfaced s.initErr — including the 'service is stopping/stopped' values written by Stop(). With those guards removed, s.initErr is never read after construction, so Create/Update/Delete/Read/List/Search/PutBlob keep serving against the backend even after Stop() has been called; the stopped-state logic in Stop() is now dead code (and its unsynchronized writes to initErr race with any concurrent Init). Either restore a cheap initErr check in the handlers or remove the initErr mutation from Stop to avoid implying a shutdown guard that no longer exists.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup in testCacheIDPForLogin registers removal of a literal IdP named "alias" instead of the created providers

In testCacheIDPForLogin the creation loop does getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) with the literal string "alias" (same again at line 425 for idp-alias-20). No identity provider with alias "alias" exists, so the 21 providers the test creates (idp-alias-0 .. idp-alias-20, ten of them linked to orga) are never cleaned up, and the deferred remove() call will hit a 404 during cleanup. Because the test realm is shared across the class, the leftover org-linked IDPs contaminate other tests that assert exact counts — e.g. testCacheIDPByOrg asserts orga's cached IDP list has exactly 6 entries, which fails if testCacheIDPForLogin ran first and left 10 more IDPs linked to orga. The cleanup should reference the actual alias created in each iteration (and "idp-alias-20" for the later one), e.g. by capturing final String alias = "idp-alias-" + i and using get(alias).

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache invalidation is skipped for IDPs whose organization is disabled, leaving stale entries after the org is re-enabled

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate compares getLoginPredicate() on the 'original' and 'updated' models to decide whether the .idp.login caches must be invalidated. The 'original' model comes from getById() (line 91), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The cached login ID sets, however, are built from the JPA query which only looks at the raw flags (enabled, hideOnLogin, linkOnly, BROKER_PUBLIC). So an org-linked IDP with enabled=true in a disabled org IS present in the cached login sets, yet predicate(original) is false. If an admin then updates that IDP so it no longer qualifies for login (sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or BROKER_PUBLIC=false, or moves it to another org), predicate(updated) is also false and no invalidation is registered (the early return at line 405-407). When the organization is later re-enabled (an org update does not invalidate these caches), the stale cached ID set is served: getById returns the fresh model whose org-aware isEnabled() is now true, and the only consumer-side re-check added in this PR (OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean) filters on isEnabled() only, so an IDP that should be hidden, link-only, or private to an org is displayed on the login page. The predicate for the 'original' state should be evaluated against the unwrapped/raw stored model (as remove() already does with idpDelegate.getByAlias) so the comparison matches what is actually in the cache.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JDK keystore provider, not BouncyCastle

The CryptoProvider contract documents this method as '@return BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider', but this implementation returns KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider(), i.e. whatever JDK provider implements the default keystore type (typically SUN/SunJSSE), never BouncyCastle. Consequently CryptoIntegration.getProvider().getBouncyCastleProvider() (and hence BouncyIntegration.PROVIDER) yields a non-BouncyCastle provider; any consumer that passes it to a JCA getInstance(..., provider) call for BC-only algorithms will fail, with no error pointing at the real cause. If this module intentionally ships without BouncyCastle, returning null (as WildFlyElytronProvider does) or explicitly documenting the deviation would be less misleading.

true_positives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dead leftover encoder writes in concatenatedRSToASN1DER

Lines 114-115 create two ASN1Encoder instances, write rBigInteger and sBigInteger into them, and then discard the results; the actual return statement immediately below builds brand-new encoders. This has no functional effect but performs pointless allocation and DER encoding on every signature conversion and looks like leftover scaffolding from development. The two statements should be deleted.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

CryptoProvider gains a new abstract method order(). Any existing third-party or custom CryptoProvider implementation compiled against the previous version of this interface will now fail at runtime with AbstractMethodError, because detectProvider invokes order() on every discovered provider during sorting (even when only one provider is present), and implementations fail to compile against the new interface. Declaring it as a default method (e.g. 'default int order() { return 100; }') would preserve backward compatibility while still allowing ordering.

false_negatives.golden_comment: When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
Creating an AuthzClient now installs the minimal provider as JVM-global CryptoIntegration state

AuthzClient.create(Configuration) now calls CryptoIntegration.init(...), which sets the static JVM-global cryptoProvider if it is not already set. In an application that embeds the authz client and later calls CryptoIntegration.init(...) itself (expecting to install a fully functional provider), that later init is silently a no-op, and every CryptoIntegration.getProvider() caller in the JVM receives AuthzClientCryptoProvider, which throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.") for nearly all methods (getSignature, getPemUtils, getKeyPairGen, getX509CertFactory, ...). If this global side effect is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise consider initializing lazily only when crypto is actually needed or scoping the provider to the client.

Multiple crypto providers no longer fail fast; ties in order() are resolved arbitrarily

Before this change, detectProvider threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath. Now it silently sorts by order() descending and takes the first. All built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) use order 200, so a misconfigured classpath containing, for example, both keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402 — previously a clear startup error — now results in an arbitrary winner (stable sort keeps ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order, which varies by environment), with the losing provider only mentioned in a debug log. Consider restoring fail-fast behavior when the highest order is shared by more than one discovered provider.

Round-trip test only proves the two converters are consistent inverses of each other

The test asserts only that asn1derToConcatenatedRS followed by concatenatedRSToASN1DER followed by asn1derToConcatenatedRS returns the same bytes (rsConcat equals rsConcat2). Both methods could be wrong in complementary ways and the test would still pass — in the extreme, if both were identity functions the assertion holds while every ES256/384/512 signature produced or verified through them would be invalid. The test should validate against an independent reference: e.g. check rsConcat has the expected raw length and content relative to the JDK-produced DER signature, verify the re-encoded DER with java.security.Signature.verify(), or use a known test vector.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
No cleanup of FGAP v2 client resources and permissions when a client is deleted

setPermissionsEnabled here throws UnsupportedOperationException, and the AdminPermissions.registerListener cleanup hook that used to invoke it on ClientRemovedEvent is now skipped whenever the v1 feature flag is off — i.e., in the standard v2-only setup. As a result, deleting a client that has fine-grained permissions leaves the resource created for it in the admin-permissions resource server (named by the client's internal id, created via AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource when a permission targets that client) and all permissions referencing it orphaned. These stale entries remain visible in permission listings and are still returned by getClientsWithPermission, so callers that resolve the returned names via session.clients().getClientById get nulls for deleted clients. A v2 cleanup path for client removal (deleting the resource and its referencing permissions) is missing.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing null check on the 'Clients' all-resource leads to NullPointerException in per-client permission checks

In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no client-specific resource exists, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking the result. getResourceTypeResource can return null — it does so whenever the 'Clients' resource is absent from the resource server (e.g., realms whose admin permissions client was initialized before the Clients type was added to the schema, since init() never runs again for them) or when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false. findByResource then dereferences resource.getId() and throws a NullPointerException, so every per-client permission check (canView/canManage/canConfigure/canMapRoles for a specific client) performed by a delegated admin returns a 500 instead of denying or granting access. Guard the null (return false) and/or ensure the resource is created on upgrade.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

false_positives.candidate:
getResourceName not extended for the Clients resource type

getResourceName resolves friendly resource names only for the Users type (returning the username, or "All users" for the all-resource). Resources of the newly added Clients type fall through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set for resources created by getOrCreateResource, so REST/admin-console representations of client permissions will render an empty or null name instead of the client's clientId, and the 'Clients' all-resource gets no equivalent of the "All users" label. Mirror the Users branch for CLIENTS: return "All clients" for the all-resource and resolve the client via session.clients().getClientById(realm, resource.getName()) to return its clientId.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:
Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance

false_positives.candidate:
New and changed exit codes (3 and 4) are never asserted

This PR makes the exit code the documented, stable contract of the update-compatibility tool (the guide explicitly tells users to rely only on exit codes for automation), changes the recreate exit code from 4 to 3 in CompatibilityResult, and introduces a new exit code 4 for 'feature disabled' — but no test asserts any of these codes. testFeatureNotEnabled only asserts the error message and never checks that the process exits with code 4; testWrongVersions never asserts exit code 3 for the recreate outcome; testCompatible asserts exit code 0 only for the metadata command, not for the subsequent check command; and the feature-disabled path of the check subcommand is not exercised at all. This contract was already wrong once (RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE returned 4 while the docs said 3), so a wiring mistake in picocli.exit(...) or a wrong constant would again ship undetected: CI would stay green while user automation and the operator, both of which consume these exit codes, would break.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() returns true for view-only permission, allowing group creation

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), i.e. it is satisfied by the 'view' scope on the Groups resource type. canManage()/requireManage() is what guards GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup (POST /admin/realms/{realm}/groups), so an admin who was granted only view permission on groups can create top-level groups — a privilege escalation. It is also inconsistent with canManage(GroupModel) in the same class (MANAGE scope only), with UserPermissionsV2.canManage() (MANAGE only), and it inverts the scope hierarchy used everywhere else in this code (MANAGE implies VIEW, not the reverse). The javadoc added to GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() documents the same incorrect contract ('permission to VIEW or MANAGE groups'). Only the MANAGE scope should satisfy canManage().

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission collects authz resource IDs instead of group IDs and never evaluates per-group permissions

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 121-125) the findByType callback calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and adds groupResource.getId() to the granted set. Both are wrong. hasPermission looks resources up by *name* (resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId)), and for the Groups resource type each resource is named with the group's ID (see AdminPermissionsSchema.resolveGroup/getOrCreateResource), so passing the authz resource ID never matches and every check silently falls back to the 'all-groups' resource — the per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions this method is meant to collect are never actually evaluated. Additionally, the returned set is documented and consumed as group IDs: UsersResource and BruteForceUsersResource put it into the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute and UsersResource.getUsersCount passes it to session.users().getUsersCount(realm, ..., groupIds), all of which compare against real group IDs, so an authz resource ID matches no group. Consequences: (a) an admin with an all-groups view-members/manage-members permission gets a non-empty set containing a bogus ID, so user search returns zero users even though they can view members of every group; (b) an admin with only per-group view-members permissions gets an empty set, so no DB-level group restriction is applied — users/count returns the count of ALL users instead of only visible ones, and user-search pagination is applied at the database before permission filtering. The method should evaluate the resource it already has (as V1 GroupPermissions does) and collect groupResource.getName(), which holds the group ID.

false_positives.candidate:
No upgrade path for existing admin-permissions clients: missing 'Groups' resource/scopes cause NPE and 500s

AdminPermissionsSchema.init() creates the scopes and the per-type 'all resources' resources only when the realm has no admin-permissions client yet (it returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null), and nothing in this PR backfills the new 'Groups' resource or the manage-membership/manage-members/view-members scopes for realms that already enabled admin permissions (ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2) before this change. For such realms every V2 group permission check fails: GroupPermissionsV2.hasPermission (lines 144-147) falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, "Groups"), which returns null because that resource was never created, and the next line calls policyStore.findByResource(server, null), throwing a NullPointerException — turning all group admin endpoints into 500s. Likewise AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource throws ModelException("No scopes found.") when a group permission is created, because the new scopes do not exist in the store. A migration/initialization path that adds the new scopes and the 'Groups' type resource to existing admin-permissions clients (plus a null guard before findByResource) is needed.

Tests never exercise the DB-level group filter or users/count for group-scoped admins

The new GroupResourceTypeEvaluationTest never exercises the database-level group filter that UsersResource/BruteForceUsersResource install via the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute populated from auth.groups().getGroupIdsWithViewPermission(). In the tested scenarios (per-group VIEW_MEMBERS / MANAGE_MEMBERS) that set comes back empty, so searchForUserStream runs unfiltered and the assertions pass only because of the in-memory usersEvaluator::canView post-filter — which is why the resource-ID bug in GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission slips through. There is also no test of users/count for a group-scoped admin (currently returns the count of all users) and no test of user search for an admin holding an all-groups view-members/manage-members permission (currently returns zero users). Adding tests for filtered counts and for the all-groups member-visibility scenario would catch this regression.

false_positives.candidate: Diff-snippet computation can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of reporting the violation In the "Illegal HTML" reporting branch, start (common prefix length) and end (common suffix length) are computed independently, so they can overlap: when the sanitizer output contains the entire input as a prefix and also shares its tail (e.g. input value "" that the sanitizer normalizes to "" yields start=3 and end=2), then value.substring(start, value.length() - end) is invoked with begin (3) > end (1) and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Instead of the intended "Illegal HTML in key …" message, the verification aborts with an unhandled exception and a bare stack trace, and no further keys/files are checked. JS console bundles switched from i18next {{0}} to Java MessageFormat {0}/{2,choice,...} syntax

The keycloak.v3 account console and keycloak.v2 admin console localize server error keys in the browser with i18next, whose interpolation syntax is {{0}} — every sibling error key in this file uses it (e.g. error-username-invalid-character='{{0}}' contains invalid character., error-empty=Please specify value of '{{0}}').
