true_positives.golden_comment: In AccessTokenContext constructor, the fourth Objects.requireNonNull validates grantType twice instead of validating rawTokenId, allowing null rawTokenId values to pass validation.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Constructor validates grantType twice and never checks rawTokenId for null

The constructor has `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null grantType not allowed")` immediately followed by `Objects.requireNonNull(grantType, "Null rawTokenId not allowed")` — the second check was clearly meant to validate rawTokenId but re-checks grantType. As a result, an AccessTokenContext with a null rawTokenId is accepted despite the error message claiming otherwise, and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.encodeTokenId() will then silently concatenate null into the token ID, producing something like "onrtac:null" instead of failing fast. Change the second requireNonNull to check rawTokenId.

true_positives.golden_comment: In isAccessTokenId, the substring for the grant shortcut and the equality check look inverted: the grant shortcut occupies indices 4–5 (substring(4,6)), and a match should return true (combined with UUID check), not false.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New isAccessTokenId matcher never actually verifies the grant-type shortcut (inverted condition and wrong character offsets)

The matcher added in this PR contains two mistakes in one line: `if (items[0].substring(3, 5).equals(expectedGrantShortcut)) return false;`. First, the condition is inverted: it returns false (no match) when the extracted shortcut EQUALS the expected one, instead of when it does not. Second, the offsets are wrong: in the 6-character prefix (2 chars session type, 2 chars token type, 2 chars grant type) the grant shortcut occupies indexes 4-5, so it should be substring(4, 6); substring(3, 5) takes the second token-type character and the first grant-type character. Net effect: for real token IDs the extracted two characters essentially never equal the expected shortcut, so the matcher degrades to only checking that the part after ':' is a UUID, and expectCodeToToken/expectRefresh/expectDeviceCodeToToken/expectAuthReqIdToToken pass regardless of whether the encoded grant type is correct. If someone later fixes only the offsets, every one of those assertions will start failing because of the inverted equals. The whole purpose of these updated event assertions — verifying the new encoded context — is therefore not tested at all.

true_positives.golden_comment: Javadoc mentions "usually like 3-letters shortcut" but some implementations use 2-letter shortcuts ("ac", "cc", "rt", "te", "pc", "ci", "ro"). Consider updating documentation to reflect actual usage pattern.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getShortcut() javadoc suggests 3-letter shortcuts, but the codec requires exactly 2 characters

The javadoc says the shortcut is "usually like 3-letters", yet every built-in implementation returns 2 characters and DefaultTokenContextEncoderProvider.getTokenContextFromTokenId() hard-codes a 6-character context prefix (2 chars each for session type, token type, grant type) and rejects anything else with "Expected length of 6". A grant implementation that follows the javadoc and returns a 3-character shortcut would produce token IDs that cannot be decoded later, and nothing in DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() validates the shortcut length (it only checks uniqueness). The contract should state that shortcuts must be exactly 2 characters and postInit should enforce it, or the codec should be made length-agnostic.

true_positives.golden_comment: Catching generic RuntimeException is too broad. The implementation throws IllegalArgumentException specifically - catch that instead for more precise testing.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
testIncorrectGrantType passes because of a NullPointerException, not the intended validation error

The test builds the factory by hand and never calls postInit(), so the factory's sessionFactory field is null. When decoding "ofrtac:5678", getGrantTypeByShortcut("ac") does not find "ac" in the hand-built map and falls through to sessionFactory.getProviderFactoriesStream(...), which throws a NullPointerException. The test catches the broad RuntimeException, so it goes green for the wrong reason and never exercises the intended path (unknown grant shortcut -> IllegalArgumentException "Unknown value 'ac' for grant type"). Catch IllegalArgumentException specifically and provide a stub/empty KeycloakSessionFactory so the real validation logic is tested.

false_positives.candidate:
Access tokens issued together with an offline refresh token get the wrong ("online") session-type prefix in their ID

initToken() encodes the token ID, including the session-type prefix, from the user session that exists at token-creation time. For an authorization-code or direct-grant request with scope=offline_access that session is the ONLINE session, so the ID gets the "on" prefix. However, afterwards TokenManager.AccessTokenResponseBuilder.generateRefreshToken() creates the offline user session and re-points accessToken.sessionState to the offline session (OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse even removes the online session for first-time offline access, which only works because the access token has been re-bound to the offline session). The result is that an access token bound to an OFFLINE session carries the "on" (online) prefix until the next refresh (refresh-minted tokens correctly get "of"). This corrupts exactly the data this PR exists to provide: a consumer relying on the session-type prefix to pick the right session lookup (follow-up #37662) would search online sessions, miss the offline session, and either reject a valid token or need the old fallback lookup anyway. The session type must be determined after the offline-session switch, or the token ID re-encoded when generateRefreshToken() rebinds the token to the offline session.

Context.setFormParams() leaves the cached grantType field stale

The Context constructor now derives the grantType field from formParams (`formParams.getFirst(OAuth2Constants.GRANT_TYPE)`), but the existing public setter setFormParams() replaces the formParams map without recomputing grantType. Any caller that swaps the form parameters after construction will have getGrantType() return the value from the original params, and that stale value is exactly what OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse() stores into the ClientSessionContext under Constants.GRANT_TYPE and what ends up encoded into the access-token ID. Either recompute grantType in setFormParams() or drop the cached field and read it from formParams in getGrantType().

New abstract getShortcut() method breaks existing custom OAuth2 grant providers with AbstractMethodError at server startup

Adding a non-default method to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface is a hard breaking change for any deployment with a custom grant type: DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates ALL registered OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut() on each of them during server startup, so a custom factory compiled against the previous version of the interface will throw AbstractMethodError and prevent the server from booting. This should be a default method (e.g. deriving a shortcut from the factory id, or returning null that the encoder factory tolerates). Note also that a custom implementation returning null would currently kill startup as well, because ConcurrentHashMap.put() throws NullPointerException for the null shortcut in postInit().

true_positives.golden_comment: Unsafe raw List deserialization without type safety. Calling Optional.get() directly on the Optional returned by RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user) without checking isPresent() can lead to a NoSuchElementException if the Optional is empty.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recovery-code login 500s for user-storage users unless the provider overrides the optional getCredentials with a fully-formed hashed model

This bean (and `RecoveryAuthnCodesFormAuthenticator`) now resolve the credential via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential(user)`, which for federated users relies on `CredentialInputValidator.getCredentials` — a default SPI method that returns an empty stream — and then calls `credentialModelOpt.get()` without handling the empty case. A user storage provider that opts into recovery codes the way the SPI documentation suggests for password/OTP — implementing `supportsCredentialType`, `updateCredential` (which receives a plain JSON array of the raw codes as the `UserCredentialModel` challenge response from `CredentialHelper.createRecoveryCodesCredential`), and `isValid` — but does not override `getCredentials` will make every recovery-code login page render throw `NoSuchElementException` (HTTP 500). If the provider instead returns the raw `CredentialModel` it stored from `updateCredential`, `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromCredentialModel` throws `IllegalArgumentException` because `secretData` is null and `credentialData` holds the raw JSON array rather than the hashed `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialData`/`SecretData` structures. The test provider only works because it re-builds the model through `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel.createFromValues`, re-hashing the raw codes on every read — a requirement that is undocumented and inconsistent with the shape handed to the provider on write. The read-side contract for `getCredentials` should be enforced or documented, and the consumers should degrade gracefully when no credential is returned.

false_negatives.golden_comment: After creating the RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialModel, consider setting its id from the stored credential (e.g., myUser.recoveryCodes.getId()); otherwise getId() will be null and downstream removal by id (e.g., removeStoredCredentialById in the authenticator flow) may not work.

false_positives.candidate:
Recovery codes stored in user storage are never consumed and remain reusable

When the recovery-codes credential lives in a user storage provider (the new federated path introduced by this PR), a successful `credentialManager().isValid(...)` here delegates to the provider's `CredentialInputValidator.isValid`, which can only return true/false. The local `RecoveryAuthnCodesCredentialProvider.isValid`, by contrast, removes the used code from the stored credential as part of validation. Nothing in this authenticator (or anywhere else) marks the used code as consumed for the federated case: the subsequent `allCodesUsed()` check re-reads the credential from the user storage via `RecoveryAuthnCodesUtils.getCredential`, which still contains all the codes, so a used recovery code stays valid forever and can be replayed any number of times. Recovery codes are designed as one-time credentials, so this silently downgrades their security whenever they are stored in user storage, and the 'all codes used -> remove credential and force re-configuration' flow never triggers. The new test `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once with a single code and never asserts that the same code is rejected on a second login, so the regression is not caught. Either the authenticator must consume the code through the SPI (e.g. re-write the credential without the used code) or the SPI contract must clearly require providers to consume one-time codes inside `isValid`, with test coverage for code reuse.

true_positives.golden_comment: The reader thread isn’t waited for; flipping deletedAll to true and asserting immediately can race and miss exceptions added just after the flag change, making this test flaky.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reader thread is never joined, so the new regression test can pass even when the NPE still occurs

In createMultiDeleteMultiReadMulti the main thread sets deletedAll.set(true) and immediately asserts caughtExceptions is empty, without joining the reader thread. A read iteration already in flight when the flag is set can still hit the NPE the test is meant to catch and add it to caughtExceptions after the assertion has executed, producing a false negative — the test can go green while the bug reproduces. The Thread reference is also discarded: if any group removal throws, deletedAll is never set and the non-daemon reader thread spins forever issuing requests past test teardown. The test should keep the Thread reference, set the flag in a finally block, and join() the thread before asserting on caughtExceptions.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Returning null from getSubGroupsCount() violates the GroupModel contract (Javadoc says it never returns null) and may lead to NPEs in callers that expect a non-null count.

false_positives.candidate:
Paginated getSubGroupsStream overloads still NPE on the same concurrent-delete race

The fix null-checks the delegate model only in getSubGroupsCount(). The three paginated overloads getSubGroupsStream(String, Integer, Integer) (line 256), getSubGroupsStream(Integer, Integer) (line 262) and getSubGroupsStream(String, Boolean, Integer, Integer) (line 268) still dereference modelSupplier.get() directly. Under the exact race this PR targets — a GroupAdapter created from a still-valid cache entry whose database row was concurrently deleted — modelSupplier.get() returns null and these methods throw the same NullPointerException, e.g. when GET /admin/realms/{realm}/groups/{id}/children?first=0&max=10 is issued right after the group is removed while the cached entry is still valid. The same null handling applied to getSubGroupsCount (e.g. return Stream.empty() when the delegate is null) should be applied here so the fix is complete.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the SpanFlusher flush loop, metric tags inconsistently use 'shard' (e.g., in spans.buffer.flusher.produce and spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes) and 'shards' (in spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce) for the same shard identifier value. This prevents correct metric aggregation across flush stages — dashboards and alerts filtering by tag 'shard' will miss data tagged as 'shards' and vice versa.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Inconsistent metrics tag keys: "shard" vs "shards", and comma-joined multi-shard tag values

The new per-process metrics tagging is inconsistent: `spans.buffer.flusher.produce` (line 185) and `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes` (line 196) are tagged with key `"shard"`, while `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce` (line 199) uses key `"shards"`, so dashboards or monitors grouping/filtering by `shard` will silently miss the wait_produce timer. Additionally, when `max_processes < len(assigned_shards)` a process handles multiple shards and the tag value is a comma-joined list like "0,2,4", whereas `spans.buffer.flusher_unhealthy` (line 243) emits one data point per individual shard integer — two different conventions for the same dimension that cannot be correlated in metrics queries.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly identifies the exact same inconsistency in metric tag keys ('shard' vs 'shards') across the exact same metrics (`spans.buffer.flusher.produce`, `spans.buffer.segment_size_bytes`, and `spans.buffer.flusher.wait_produce`) and explains the same impact on dashboards/monitors.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because the test monkeypatches time.sleep

`test_basic` monkeypatches `time.sleep` to a no-op at the top of the test (`monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)`), so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` with the comment "Give flusher threads time to process after drift change" provides no synchronization whatsoever. The test still depends on the racing flusher thread observing `current_drift.value = 9000` and completing a flush+produce before `step.join()` sets `stopped.value`; if the flusher thread's next loop iteration starts after `stopped` is set, it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails on an empty list. If the intent was to deflake the test, this doesn't do it — the flusher's completion needs to be awaited deterministically (e.g., poll `messages` with a real timeout loop, since the fake sleep also makes the flusher's own `time.sleep(1)` a hot spin).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: `test_basic` calls `time.sleep(0.1)` expecting it to wait, but `time.sleep` was monkeypatched earlier in the test to be a no-op (`lambda _: None`), making the sleep call ineffective.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process is always False for spawn processes, so hung flushers are never killed

`isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` is never true for the processes this class creates. The hung process keeps running indefinitely: it keeps flushing the same shards as its replacement, and because the restart reuses the same shared `healthy_since` Value for that process slot, a still-looping zombie can keep refreshing `healthy_since` and permanently mask the hang from the health check. (2) The same wrong check at line 346 means `join()` never calls `terminate()` on spawn processes that outlive the deadline. In hasPermission(ClientModel, String), when no client-specific resource exists, the code falls back to AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and immediately calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without checking the result. getResourceTypeResource can return null — it does so whenever the 'Clients' resource is absent from the resource server (e.g., realms whose admin permissions client was initialized before the Clients type was added to the schema, since init() never runs again for them) or when supportsAuthorizationSchema is false. findByResource then dereferences resource.getId() and throws a NullPointerException, so every per-client permission check (canView/canManage/canConfigure/canMapRoles for a specific client) performed by a delegated admin returns a 500 instead of denying or granting access. A migration/upgrade step that adds the missing scopes and the Clients all-resource to existing admin-permissions resource servers is needed, otherwise the new feature is broken (with 500s) for every realm that adopted v2 earlier.

In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission (lines 121-125) the findByType callback calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and adds groupResource.getId() to the granted set. CryptoProvider gains a new abstract method order(). false_positives.candidate:
Multiple crypto providers no longer fail fast; ties in order() are resolved arbitrarily

Before this change, detectProvider threw IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was found on the classpath. Now it silently sorts by order() descending and takes the first. All built-in providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) use order 200, so a misconfigured classpath containing, for example, both keycloak-crypto-default and keycloak-crypto-fips1402 — previously a clear startup error — now results in an arbitrary winner (stable sort keeps ServiceLoader/classpath discovery order, which varies by environment), with the losing provider only mentioned in a debug log. Consider restoring fail-fast behavior when the highest order is shared by more than one discovered provider.

Round-trip test only proves the two converters are consistent inverses of each other

The test asserts only that asn1derToConcatenatedRS followed by concatenatedRSToASN1DER followed by asn1derToConcatenatedRS returns the same bytes (rsConcat equals rsConcat2). Both methods could be wrong in complementary ways and the test would still pass — in the extreme, if both were identity functions the assertion holds while every ES256/384/512 signature produced or verified through them would be invalid. The test should validate against an independent reference: e.g. check rsConcat has the expected raw length and content relative to the JDK-produced DER signature, verify the re-encoded DER with java.security.Signature.verify(), or use a known test vector.

Creating an AuthzClient now installs the minimal provider as JVM-global CryptoIntegration state

In an application that embeds the authz client and later calls CryptoIntegration.init(...) itself (expecting to install a fully functional provider), that later init is silently a no-op, and every CryptoIntegration.getProvider() caller in the JVM receives AuthzClientCryptoProvider, which throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported yet.") for nearly all methods (getSignature, getPemUtils, getKeyPairGen, getX509CertFactory, ...). If this global side effect is intentional, it should be documented; otherwise consider initializing lazily only when crypto is actually needed or scoping the provider to the client.

true_positives.golden_comment: get_item_key assumes a numeric key, but the paginator is used with order_by=-datetime in the audit logs endpoint; calling math.floor/ceil on a datetime will raise a TypeError.

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key crashes with TypeError on the datetime ordering the endpoint uses

OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint wires this paginator in with order_by="-datetime", but get_item_key does math.floor/math.ceil on getattr(item, "datetime"), which is a datetime object. math.floor/math.ceil raise TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime (DateTimePaginator exists precisely to convert datetimes to epoch-millis first). build_cursor calls get_item_key(results[0]) via _build_next_values/_build_prev_values, so any request to GET /organizations/{slug}/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true from an authorized admin 500s on the very first page as soon as the queryset returns a row. false_positives.candidate:
BasePaginator change makes negative cursor offsets silently return page one for forward cursors while prev cursors still 500

The changed slicing in BasePaginator.get_result uses start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset. A crafted forward cursor with a negative offset (e.g. 0:-5:0) is now silently clamped to 0 and returns the first page instead of being rejected, while a prev cursor with a negative offset (0:-5:1) still reaches the queryset slice and raises Django's uncaught AssertionError "Negative indexing is not supported" -> 500. The added comment ("the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions") is incorrect for the is_prev case, and the two directions now handle malformed cursors inconsistently. Negative offsets should be validated and rejected with BadPaginationError for both directions instead of clamped or passed through.

No tests for the new paginator, the negative-offset path, or the endpoint's optimized branch

The PR adds a new OptimizedCursorPaginator class, a user-reachable branch in the audit log endpoint, and a behavioral change to BasePaginator.get_result that affects all cursor-paginated endpoints, but adds no tests. Both new code paths fail on first use (the datetime TypeError in get_item_key and the negative-slice AssertionError), which a single happy-path test of GET /organizations/{slug}/audit-logs/?optimized_pagination=true would have caught, and the BasePaginator change has no coverage for prev/negative-offset cursors either.

New Cursor comment falsely advertises negative offsets as a supported pagination feature

The added comment claims negative offsets are allowed "for advanced pagination scenarios" and "enable efficient reverse pagination from arbitrary positions in large datasets", but nothing in Cursor changed (int(offset) always accepted negatives), and the paginators that consume offsets either explicitly reject negatives (OffsetPaginator, ChainPaginator, CombinedQuerysetPaginator raise BadPaginationError on negative offsets) or crash on them (Django disallows negative queryset slicing). This documents a contract the rest of the pagination code does not support and could mislead future callers into emitting negative-offset cursors.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dropping the build-wide lock makes GetIndex+BuildIndex non-atomic; same key can be built concurrently

BuildIndex previously held cacheMu for its entire duration; it now only locks while inserting the finished index into b.cache. The check in GetIndex and the build/insert are therefore not atomic: two goroutines building the same NamespacedResource (e.g. a watch event handled via handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex racing a concurrent Search for a namespace that was not pre-built at startup, or two concurrent Searches for a cold namespace) will both build a complete index. One result then silently overwrites the other in the cache, leaking the losing index (for file-backed indexes, an open bleve index whose handles are never closed). Worse, when size > FileThreshold both goroutines call bleve.New on the same on-disk directory, and the second open fails on the store's directory lock, so one caller gets an error even though the index is being built. Consider a per-key lock, singleflight, or an inflight-builds map so concurrent builders for the same key share one build while different keys still build in parallel.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same concurrency issue: moving the `cacheMu` lock in `BuildIndex` from protecting the whole function to only protecting the final cache assignment allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the index for the same key.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates b.cache without holding cacheMu and now runs concurrently with cache writes

TotalDocs loops over b.cache without taking cacheMu. This PR adds a new caller: searchSupport.init now logs s.search.TotalDocs() (search.go) immediately after starting the watch-event goroutine, and that goroutine can concurrently trigger BuildIndex via handleEvent -> getOrCreateIndex, which writes to b.cache under cacheMu.Lock. An unsynchronized map iteration racing a map write causes a fatal, non-recoverable 'concurrent map read and map write' runtime panic. TotalDocs should acquire b.cacheMu.RLock() for the duration of the iteration.

false_positives.candidate:
Init failure in NewResourceServer leaks already-initialized resources

When s.Init(ctx) fails, NewResourceServer returns nil, err without any cleanup: the cancellable context created a few lines above is never cancelled (cancel is otherwise only invoked via Stop), the lifecycle backend initialized by lifecycle.Init (e.g. the SQL backend's open DB) is never stopped, and if the failure occurs in initWatcher after search.init succeeded, the watch goroutine started inside search.init runs on context.Background() and keeps polling forever. The error path should call s.cancel() and, when lifecycle was initialized, lifecycle.Stop (or otherwise unwind the partial initialization).

false_positives.candidate:
Strategy close() kills the factory-shared queue pool; after any rebalance all messages are silently dropped but their offsets are committed

The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (result_consumer.py, mode == 'thread-queue-parallel') and the same pool object is handed to every strategy built by create_with_partitions. However, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets worker.shutdown=True, shuts down every queue, and joins the worker threads. Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and joins the current strategy on every partition revocation and creates a new one on the next assignment, so after the first routine consumer-group rebalance (deploy, autoscaling, another group member joining) the new strategy is built on a dead pool. From then on every submit() reaches work_queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches that with a broad 'except Exception', logs it, and then calls offset_tracker.add_offset + complete_offset for the message. The commit thread therefore commits offsets for messages that were never enqueued or processed, and since this consumer has no DLQ configured the data is silently lost until the process is restarted. Nothing recreates the pool (ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() is never invoked by the StreamProcessor). Fix by creating the pool per create_with_partitions call (or not shutting it down from the strategy), and by not marking offsets complete when the work item was never actually queued.

Unbounded queues and no backpressure despite docstring claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up'

FixedQueuePool creates plain queue.Queue() instances with no maxsize, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy never applies backpressure: submit() always enqueues immediately and poll() only emits a gauge (arroyo strategies signal backpressure by raising MessageRejected from poll/submit). The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but put() on an unbounded queue never blocks, so the Kafka consumer thread keeps polling and buffering messages in memory no matter how far behind the workers fall. A single slow group — the exact scenario this mode is built to tolerate — grows its queue without bound and the partition's entire backlog accumulates in the process heap, eventually OOM-killing the consumer pod. The queues should be bounded (maxsize) and/or poll() should raise MessageRejected when total depth exceeds a threshold.

Shutdown drops queued work without draining or a final offset commit, causing duplicate processing on every rebalance/deploy

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on 'while not self.shutdown', so each worker exits immediately after its current item and never drains the remaining queued items — the immediate=False 'graceful' drain is dead code. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() never waits for queued work (wait_until_empty exists but is unused) and performs no final commit after workers finish: the commit thread is joined before the pool is shut down, and its last pass races with in-flight items. The result is that on every deploy or partition revocation the queued backlog plus roughly the last commit-interval's worth of completed-but-uncommitted work is redelivered by Kafka and processed a second time. join(timeout) should drain the queues within the timeout and then stage a final commit of all completed offsets.

test_different_groups_distributed is flaky due to per-process string hash randomization

The test submits 20 group keys and asserts len(queue_indices) == 3, i.e. that they cover all 3 queues. Queue assignment is hash(group_key) % num_queues, and CPython randomizes str hash values per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so each test run is effectively a random draw: the probability that 20 keys land in only 1–2 of 3 buckets is about 0.09% (3*(2/3)^20). With no code change at all, roughly 1 in 1100 CI runs will fail this assertion. Use a looser assertion (e.g. indices are within range and ordering per key is stable), pin the hash seed, or mock hash().

The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is defined as `toInt64(sum(Column("sample_weight")))`. In snuba, `sample_weight` on the errors/discover storage is Nullable and is only populated for error events that carry a client sample rate; error events ingested before a project was allowlisted, from SDKs that don't sample, or server-side have NULL `sample_weight`. ClickHouse `sum()` ignores NULL rows and returns NULL if every row is NULL, so (a) any unsampled error events are silently excluded from the returned count (e.g. 10 unsampled errors + 1 error sampled at 0.1 returns 10 instead of the correct 20), and (b) a time bucket containing only unsampled events returns NULL/0 instead of the true count. The added tests never exercise events without a client_sample_rate, so this is not caught. The aggregate should treat missing weights as 1, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`; the code comment's assumption that sample_weight always exists for allowlisted projects is not guaranteed by the schema.

This substring test ignores search semantics: a discover query like `!event.type:error` (the standard way to select transaction-like events) contains the substring and will be treated as error-focused, so its `count()` is rewritten to sum(sample_weight) over non-error rows that have no sample_weight — returning NULL/incorrect counts. A free-text search such as `message:"event.type:error"` also false-positives. For allowlisted projects this silently returns wrong data on common discover queries; the check should parse the query and inspect the actual event.type filter (including its negation) rather than doing a substring match.

Denial cache can persist denials computed from stale data and is never invalidated

In Check, when the DB fallback still denies, the denial is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and short-circuits all later checks for that (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple. Two problems follow: (1) The deny decision may depend on the cached folder tree (checkInheritedPermissions -> buildFolderTree uses folderCache, also 30s TTL), which the DB fallback does NOT refresh. If a teammate of a folder creator checks a dashboard inside a folder created seconds ago, the fresh permission re-query returns the same scopes (e.g. only folders:uid:<grandparent>) and the stale tree has no ancestors for the new folder, so the request is denied and that deny is now cached for another 30s — extending the deny window up to ~60s after folder creation, longer than before this change, for exactly the 'newly created folder' scenario this PR is meant to fix. (2) When the fallback re-fetch does update permCache with fresh scopes, any pre-existing denial entry for a resource covered by those fresh scopes is not deleted, so the stale denial still wins over fresher permission data. Consider refreshing/invalidating the folder tree (or skipping denial caching) when the deny relied on folder-tree evaluation, and/or keying denials so a fresh allow can supersede them.

Every denied check for a distinct resource name now triggers a full DB permission fetch

With the new fallback, whenever the cached permission map does not contain the requested scope, Check unconditionally re-queries the full permission set from the database (getIdentityPermissions -> getUserPermissions -> permissionStore.GetUserPermissions). The denial cache only deduplicates repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parentFolder) tuple, so a caller that polls N distinct resources it cannot access (dashboard listing integrations, scanners, a user clicking through an org where most content is restricted) now issues N full permission queries per 30s window, where before this change the permission cache answered all of them with a single query per user/action. Singleflight only collapses concurrent identical user+action fetches, not sequential distinct names. Consider bounding the fallback (e.g., a short 'permissions fresh as of' marker per user/action so repeated denials on different names within a few seconds don't each hit the DB).

Permission-cache hits that result in denial are recorded as cache misses

When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission map (cache hit) but checkPermission returns allowed=false, execution falls out of the if-block and reaches s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...) — recording a cache miss even though the permission cache was hit. Denied checks are precisely the traffic pattern this PR optimizes, so this mislabeling systematically skews the cache hit-rate metric downward and makes the new caching behavior look less effective than it is. The hit/miss label should be recorded based on whether the cache lookup succeeded, before evaluating the allow/deny outcome.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock (double-checked locking)

After taking the exclusive lock, GetWebAssets does not re-check whether another goroutine already populated entryPointAssetsCache. At startup (or whenever the cache is empty), every concurrent request observes a nil cache under the read lock, then queues on the write lock; each one in turn re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json from disk (or fetches it over HTTP if the CDN path at line 56 is ever enabled) and overwrites the cache, with all but the last result discarded. This is the standard double-checked-locking pattern with the second check missing. Adding `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock avoids the redundant serialized I/O.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same issue: the GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern by failing to re-check if the cache was populated by another goroutine after acquiring the write lock.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock held across manifest I/O serializes all callers

The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer) for the entire recompute, including the disk read of assets-manifest.json and, if enabled, the CDN HTTP fetch. While any writer holds it, all other callers block on the initial RLock at line 41. In dev mode the cache is deliberately bypassed on every call, so every request to GetWebAssets is now serialized through this single global mutex plus a disk read. The same happens in non-dev mode whenever the manifest read persistently fails, because the cache then stays nil and every request retries under the exclusive lock, turning a missing-file misconfiguration into a global serialization point for index page loads. Consider doing the read outside the lock and taking the write lock only to publish the result (combined with the re-check from the previous point).

Race fix ships without a regression test exercising concurrent access

This PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test. Nothing guards the new synchronization: if someone later removes the mutex or accesses the global without it, nothing in the test suite would catch it. A simple test that calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines (against a temp assets-manifest.json) and is run under `go test -race` would fail if the synchronization regresses and would document the concurrency contract of this function.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, running all cleanup jobs 10x more often

The Run loop ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. clean() does not only run annotation cleanup — on every tick it runs the entire job list: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, expiring user invites, deleting stale short URLs, two query-history enforcement queries, and re-scanning the temp file directories. This change therefore multiplies the database and filesystem load of all background cleanup jobs by 10, yet the PR description (about avoiding MySQL deadlocks in annotation cleanup) never mentions it. If the intent is to keep annotation cleanup batches small and frequent, that should be scoped to the annotation job or at least called out explicitly; as written this is an undocumented behavior change affecting every cleanup task.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same change (the cleanup job ticker changing from 10 minutes to 1 minute) and the same underlying concern (a 10x increase in frequency leading to increased database/system load across all cleanup tasks).

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite literal IN-list built with O(n^2) string concatenation

In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback for batch sizes over 999 builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over ids. Each iteration allocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building the list is quadratic in the number of IDs. With the batch size exercised in the new test (32767 IDs) this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch, and it runs on every batch iteration of the cleanup loop. Use a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-converted strings) to make it linear.

Parameter-limit guard only covers SQLite; large batch sizes break on Postgres

deleteByIDs only sidesteps bind-parameter limits when the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999; every other database gets a `DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` statement with one placeholder per ID. Postgres rejects statements with more than 65535 bind parameters, and very large placeholder lists can also hit MySQL's max_allowed_packet. Since AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable and the PR itself tests a value of 32767, a batch size above 65535 on Postgres would make the delete fail on every cleanup cycle (the job errors out and nothing is cleaned). Consider chunking the ID list into fixed-size DELETE batches for all dialects instead of special-casing SQLite.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and will be canceled immediately

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135 and DeleteCollection at line 163), the goroutine performing the asynchronous legacy write builds its context from the incoming request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. The dual writer returns immediately after spawning the goroutine, and the HTTP request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, so the derived context is already (or almost immediately) canceled when the legacy write actually runs. The legacy store will therefore fail with context.Canceled in the common case, silently defeating the purpose of mode 3 ("write to legacy as a safe measure") — unified storage will have the data but legacy will not. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (keeping the log values) before applying the 10s timeout so the legacy write survives request completion.

Delete no longer cleans up legacy storage when unified storage returns NotFound

The previous Mode 3 Delete tolerated a NotFound error from unified storage (`apierrors.IsNotFound`) and still attempted the legacy delete; the new code returns immediately on any storage delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy (e.g., written before the unified copy existed, or whose unified copy was lost during migration) can now never be deleted through the API: unified returns NotFound, the client sees a failure, and the stale legacy record is left behind, where it will resurface if the installation rolls back to a legacy-first mode. The NotFound special-case for proceeding with the legacy delete should be preserved.

Create records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails

In the error path of Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never contacted and the measured start time belongs to the unified-storage call. This should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`; as written, unified-storage create failures pollute the legacy-storage error/duration metrics and the actual storage failure is never recorded, which will mislead the dashboards this mode is meant to feed.

Update records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails

In the error path of Update, when `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. The legacy store was never called and the duration measured is the unified-storage call's, so unified-storage update errors are misreported as legacy-storage errors in the dual-writer metrics.

No draining of in-flight async legacy writes on shutdown

The async legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines with a 10s timeout, and `Destroy()` does not wait for any of them. On pod shutdown or rollout, every legacy write still in flight is silently abandoned, so the legacy copy can diverge from unified storage exactly during deploys — the window in which the "legacy as a safe measure" guarantee matters most. Consider tracking in-flight writes with a WaitGroup and draining them in Destroy.

Mode 3 integration subtests assert synchronous legacy visibility of async legacy writes

The new subtests "with dual write (file, mode 3)" and "with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)" reuse doPlaylistTests, which asserts that objects written via the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy REST API (the `/api/playlists` list comparison in "Do CRUD via k8s" and the legacy GET in getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously in a goroutine with no synchronization point, so there is no guarantee the legacy store has caught up when those assertions run — these subtests will be flaky under CI load (and, given the request-context cancellation bug in the async writer, may fail consistently). The mode-3 runs need polling/eventually-style assertions against the legacy API.

Unit tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes

None of the new mode-3 unit tests (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the legacy write or assert that it happened — e.g., TestMode3_Create registers a legacy Create expectation but never blocks on the goroutine nor calls `m.AssertExpectations`. The tests pass even if the legacy write is never executed, so the core behavior this PR adds (async dual write to legacy) is effectively untested at the unit level; a regression that drops the legacy call entirely would go unnoticed.

Create error test registers the storage failure on the legacy mock and only works via the shared mock instance

In TestMode3_Create's case "error when creating object in the unified store fails", the failing Create expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` on the legacy mock, but mode 3 calls unified storage first and the legacy expectation is never used intentionally — the test only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage Create call accidentally matches the legacy-registered expectation. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, the storage Create call will panic as unexpected. Register the failing expectation on the storage mock (setupStorageFn) so the test models what it claims to test.

true_positives.golden_comment: In the next action, capping the next offset at user_count can produce an empty page (e.g., total equal to limit results in offset == total, showing 2/2 with no members). This can cause confusing UX on the last page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit

totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which yields an extra page when user_count divides evenly (e.g. 100 users with limit 50 gives 3 pages instead of 2). On the real last page "next" stays enabled (showingLast compares currentPage to the inflated totalPages); clicking it requests offset == user_count, the server returns an empty member list, and the admin sees an empty "3/3" page. Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the exact same pagination bug where `user_count` being an exact multiple of `limit` allows navigating to an extra, empty page because the offset reaches `user_count`. While the golden comment frames it around capping the offset in the `next` action and the candidate frames it around the `totalPages` calculation enabling the `next` button, they identify the exact same underlying bug and UX manifestation.

false_positives.candidate:
Members endpoint now caps all groups at 50, but the public group members page has no pagination

Before this change, GroupsController#members returned every member for non-automatic groups and only applied limit/offset to automatic groups (default 200). Now every group is limited to 50 by default. The public group members page (discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6 calling model.findMembers() once, rendering templates/group/members.hbs) has no next/previous or load-more controls — only the admin template got pagination. As a result, any group with more than 50 members (and any automatic group with more than 50, previously 200) now only ever shows the first 50 alphabetically, and the remaining members are unreachable. Either keep returning the full roster for the public page or add pagination there.

PATCH /admin/groups/:id now silently ignores incremental membership changes and resets visible to false

The old update dispatched PATCH requests to update_patch, which applied params[:changes] (add/delete usernames) and touched nothing else. This PR removes that branch, so PATCH and PUT both run the single update action: params[:changes] is silently ignored while success_json is returned, and because visible is computed unconditionally as params[:visible] == "true", any legacy client sending an incremental membership PATCH without a visible param will silently flip the group to invisible. If the incremental API is being removed, the action should reject such requests rather than report success, and visible should not be forced to false when the parameter is absent.

automatic does not resolve inside the member item view, so the remove link is rendered for automatic groups too

This template is rendered as the itemView of {{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}, so its scope is the member item view (which only has `member` set via the each keyword), not the adminGroup controller. `automatic` is a property of the group, so {{#unless automatic}} is always truthy and the × remove link renders even for automatic groups. Clicking it sends DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members; the server correctly returns 422, but Group#removeMember has no rejection handler, so the admin gets no feedback and the row simply stays. The group's automatic flag needs to be passed into the item view explicitly, and/or the failure should be surfaced.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count is incremented per validation pass, so one signup attempt is counted twice

should_block? has a database write side effect (match_count += 1 and save) and is invoked from EmailValidator, meaning it runs every time a User is validated. UsersController#create validates the user twice per attempt: once explicitly in `if user.valid? && SiteSetting.call_discourse_hub?` (users_controller.rb line 168) and again inside `user.save` (line 172). Because the record is new and unsaved, email_changed? is true for both passes, so a single blocked signup attempt increments match_count by 2 and updates last_match_at twice. Any other code that calls user.valid? and then user.save (or calls valid? as a dry-run check) also mutates these statistics. Match tracking should live outside the validation cycle (e.g. in the controller after a failed save) or otherwise be per-attempt rather than per-validation, otherwise the match_count/last_match_at audit data this feature exists to collect is unreliable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same underlying architectural flaw: the `should_block?` / `should_block_email?` query method has a database write side effect (updating `match_count` and `last_match_at` statistics) during a read/validation check. The candidate issue goes further in explaining a specific concrete symptom of this design flaw (double-counting during validation passes).

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive, so a block is trivially bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact-match lookup: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first. On PostgreSQL string equality is case-sensitive, and nothing normalizes case anywhere in the flow: User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] exactly as typed, BlockedEmail.set_defaults only sets action_type, and EmailValidator passes the raw value through. An admin who blocks spammer@example.com will not block Spammer@example.com or SPAMMER@example.com, even though those deliver to the same mailbox, so a blocked spammer can re-register simply by changing letter case. Normalize the address (e.g. strip + downcase) both when writing blocked_emails rows and when checking in should_block?, or query with a case-insensitive comparison such as lower(email) = lower(?). The added specs only exercise exact-case matches, so this gap is not covered by tests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both the golden comment and the candidate issue identify the exact same vulnerability: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` performs a case-sensitive email lookup, which allows blocked users to bypass the block simply by altering the casing of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write

should_block? does record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save. That is a read-modify-write: two concurrent requests matching the same blocked email can both read the same counter value, and one increment is silently lost. If these statistics are meant to be accurate, use an atomic update such as BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_counters(match_count: 1) plus an update of last_match_at, instead of incrementing an in-memory attribute and saving the whole record.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin passes standard keywords verbatim to legacy properties that use different value names

The new `align-items($alignment)` mixin copies its argument into `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`, but those legacy properties do not accept the standard `flex-start`/`flex-end` keywords — they expect `start`/`end`. The mixin compiles silently and the declaration is simply dropped by those engines, so the first time someone uses `@include align-items(flex-start)` (the most common value in real layouts) alignment will be silently broken in old WebKit and IE10. Current usages only pass `center`/`baseline`, which happen to be valid in both syntaxes, so this is latent rather than an active bug — but the mixin should map the values (or the limitation should be documented) since it is being introduced for codebase-wide reuse. Additionally, `-ms-align-items` on line 121 is not a property that exists in any browser (IE10's 2012 spec only has `-ms-flex-align`), so that line is dead code.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue explicitly mentions the exact issue described in the golden comment in its final sentence: '-ms-align-items on line 121 is not a property that exists in any browser (IE10's 2012 spec only has -ms-flex-align), so that line is dead code.'

false_positives.candidate:
float: right on .small-action button is ignored now that .small-action is a flex container

This PR adds `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action`, but the `button` rule inside it still relies on `float: right` to pin the small-action undo/recover button to the right edge of the row. Floats have no effect on flex items, so the button will now render immediately after the `.small-action-desc` text instead of at the far right of the row whenever the description is short (e.g. "closed the topic"). The header change in this same PR solves the equivalent problem for `.panel` by adding `margin-left: auto`; the same fix (or `justify-content: space-between`) is needed here for the button.

margin-left: auto used to right-align .panel does not work in the 2009-spec flexbox fallback the new mixin emits

`.panel` is now pushed to the right edge of the header with `margin-left: auto` instead of `float: right`. The `flexbox()` mixin added in this PR emits `display: -webkit-box`/`display: -moz-box` as fallbacks, and in that 2009 flexbox spec (old iOS Safari, old Android stock browser) auto margins on box children are treated as 0, so on exactly the browsers those fallback lines exist for, the header panel (user menu / login / signup buttons) will sit immediately after the logo instead of at the right edge. At the same time the float fallbacks were removed (`.title { float: left }` deleted, `.panel { float: right }` deleted), so those engines get the degraded layout with no fallback. Either drop the old-spec prefixes or add a fallback such as `-webkit-box-pack: end` / keeping a float fallback.

Bullet category badge in the scrolled header loses its 5px top offset with no replacement

This PR removes `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }`. That offset was what aligned the small inline-flex bullet badge with the topic title text in the header's extra-info (scrolled) state. The new `@include align-items(center)` is applied to `.d-header .contents`, which only centers the `.extra-info-wrapper` as a whole within the header bar; `.extra-info-wrapper` itself is not a flex container and the badge inside it still uses `float: left`, so nothing replaces the intra-wrapper alignment the 5px margin provided. In the scrolled header the category bullet badge will sit higher than the title text baseline. The added `line-height: 1.5` does not compensate for the badge-to-title alignment. This should be verified in the scrolled header and either kept or replaced with an equivalent adjustment.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' so ActiveModelSerializers never calls it

AMS conditional-inclusion hooks must be named `include_<attribute>?`. The method defined here is `include_website_name` (no question mark), so it is dead code and `website_name` is always serialized — including as `null` for users with no website. Rename it to `include_website_name?` (and, per the related finding, have it also check `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` so the privacy behavior matches `website`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate issue accurately identifies the main bug described in the golden comment: the `include_website_name` method is missing the trailing `?` suffix required by Rails/ActiveModelSerializers for conditional attribute inclusion. Although the golden comment also mentions a secondary issue about string concatenation, the core issue is clearly matched.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the untrusted_attributes restriction that hides website from anonymous viewers of TL0 users

This serializer deliberately strips profile fields like `website` for TL0 users viewed anonymously via `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which returns false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true. The newly added `website_name` attribute is declared as a plain attribute and is not part of that mechanism, so for a restricted (e.g. spammy TL0) user the JSON payload still contains `website_name` with the website's host/path even though `website` itself is removed. That defeats the purpose of the restriction: anonymous viewers (and crawlers) still see the website domain. `website_name` should get the same guard — either add it to `untrusted_attributes` or make its inclusion conditional on `!scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`.

Non-ASCII (IDN) website URLs make website_name nil, hiding the user's website entirely

Ruby's `URI()` only accepts ASCII; a website like `http://münchen.de/page` raises URI::InvalidURIError, which the inline `rescue nil` turns into a nil host, causing `website_name` to return nil. The template (`{{#if model.website_name}}`) then hides the website block completely. Previously the display name was computed client-side with `website.split('/')[2]`, which handled such URLs fine, so this is a display regression for users with internationalized domains. Consider a tolerant fallback (e.g. string splitting, or falling back to the raw website string) when URI parsing fails.

The sibling-subdomain branch of website_name (elsif) has no test coverage

The most intricate condition added in `website_name` — the `elsif` that strips the first DNS label of both hosts when they have the same label count (e.g. website `www.example.com` vs instance `forum.example.com`) — is not exercised by any spec. The three added tests only cover equal hosts, unrelated hosts, and the parent-domain suffix case. Add a test with `Discourse.current_hostname` returning 'forum.example.com' and website 'http://www.example.com/user' expecting 'www.example.com/user', plus a negative case (same label count, different parent, e.g. www.other.com) to lock in the comparison behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Unauthenticated endpoint triggers remote fetch and topic creation; referer check is trivially spoofable

GET /embed/best enqueues a RetrieveTopic job for any embed_url with no existing embed, with no authentication and no rate limiting. The only gate is that the Referer host matches embeddable_host, which any non-browser client can spoof (curl -H 'Referer: http://blog.example.com' ...). The 60-second Redis throttle in TopicRetriever is per-URL, so an attacker can supply unlimited distinct URLs on the embeddable host: each one makes the server fetch that page and create a forum topic as the embed_by_username user (topic spam, bandwidth/CPU amplification), and when feed_polling_enabled is on each request also triggers a synchronous full PollFeed run inside the job. Consider per-IP rate limiting and/or restricting which paths are importable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify that the Referer header validation used as a security gate in the embed endpoint is trivially spoofable/bypassable. While the golden comment also mentions X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL and nil referer handling, and the candidate elaborates on the downstream DoS/spam impact of spoofing the referer, they share the core security concern regarding the reliance on spoofable Referer headers.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Unescaped URL interpolated into a single-quoted href in the imported footer TopicEmbed.import appends a footer to every imported post: #{url}. The only validation on url is a /^https?:\/\// prefix check, so a URL containing a single quote (e.g. from a malicious feed or a fetched page URL) breaks out of the attribute and injects arbitrary HTML into the post body, which is then rendered raw via the raw_html cook path. Because the footer is appended after Readability extraction, this vector bypasses even the limited tag/attribute filtering that import_remote applies to article content. The URL should be HTML/attribute-escaped before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment mentions two issues in `TopicEmbed.import`: a potential `NoMethodError` if `contents` is nil, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped `url` interpolation in the generated HTML. The candidate issue accurately identifies the exact XSS vulnerability from the unescaped `url` interpolation in `TopicEmbed.import`. Even though it omits the nil `contents` check, it directly matches the primary security concern described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content is nil for RSS items without content:encoded, crashing the hourly job

i.content.scrub raises NoMethodError when a feed item has no content:encoded/content element — plain RSS 2.0 feeds that only provide <description> are common, and SimpleRSS returns nil for absent elements. Because the job sets sidekiq_options retry: false, the exception kills the run silently until the next hour and any remaining items are never imported. Fall back to i.description (and/or i.summary) when content is absent. The new poll_feed_spec only exercises the site-setting gates and never parses a feed item, so this path is untested.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the exact same bug: calling `i.content.scrub` will raise a nil/NoMethodError exception when an RSS feed item lacks a `content` element, and both suggest falling back to `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
Feed HTML is stored and rendered completely unsanitized (stored XSS)

Feed item content is imported with no sanitization: poll_feed unescapes entities via CGI.unescapeHTML, then TopicEmbed.import stores the string as the post raw with cook_method raw_html, and Post#cook returns raw unchanged for raw_html posts. The result is rendered unsanitized both on the forum (the app renders post.cooked unescaped, trusting the normal cooking pipeline to have sanitized it) and in app/views/embed/best.html.erb via <%= raw post.cooked %>, which is served from the Discourse origin inside the iframe. Any <script> or event handler attribute in a feed entry — from a hostile or compromised blog/feed, a rogue author on a multi-author blog, or a MITM on a plaintext feed URL — becomes stored XSS executing in the forum origin as viewing users/admins. CGI.unescapeHTML makes it worse by converting the feed's safely entity-escaped markup into live tags. Imported content must be sanitized (e.g., with the already-bundled sanitize gem) before being stored as raw HTML.

embed.js/embed.css are never added to config.assets.precompile — feature 404s/500s in production

The PR adds app/assets/javascripts/embed.js and app/assets/stylesheets/embed.css.scss and references them via stylesheet_link_tag 'embed' (in the embed layout) and as the script embedding sites load, but no config change adds 'embed.js' or 'embed.css' to the asset precompile list. With the application's explicit precompile list and assets.compile disabled in production, /embed/best will raise AssetNotPrecompiledError and the embed snippet URL will 404, so the entire feature is broken in production. Add both assets to config.assets.precompile.

add_column with default on posts rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock

add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false causes PostgreSQL (pre-11) to rewrite every row of the posts table to materialize the default, holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration. posts is typically the largest table in a Discourse database, so on busy installs this migration can block all writes to posts for minutes during deploy. Add the column without a default/NOT NULL, backfill in batches, then apply the default and constraint.

open(url) used without requiring open-uri on the retrieve path

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url), but this file never requires 'open-uri' — only poll_feed.rb does. The HTTP-retrieve path (EmbedController → RetrieveTopic job → TopicRetriever#fetch_http → TopicEmbed.import_remote) therefore only works if Jobs::PollFeed happened to be loaded already; in lazy-loading environments (dev/test, or any process that never referenced PollFeed) Kernel#open treats the URL as a filename and raises Errno::ENOENT. Add require 'open-uri' to topic_embed.rb (or lib/topic_retriever.rb) so the dependency is explicit.

embeddable_host is compared as an exact string against URI#host with no normalization

The check URI(request.referer).host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host compares the parsed host against free-form admin text. Values admins commonly paste — 'http://example.com', 'example.com/', or 'example.com:8080' — never equal URI#host ('example.com'), so every legitimate embed is rejected with 'invalid referer host' and no diagnostics. The same strict comparison in TopicRetriever.invalid_host? also fails when the blog's canonical URL host differs from the page host (www vs apex), producing the infinite loading screen. Parse/normalize the setting (compare host and port explicitly, and consider allowing subdomains) or validate its format when saved.

X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value

ALLOWALL is not a permitted X-Frame-Options value (the spec defines DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM uri). Browsers currently ignore unrecognized values, which is why framing happens to work, but the behavior is undefined and stricter user agents or normalizing proxies may handle it differently. To allow cross-origin framing for this action, remove the X-Frame-Options header instead of setting an invalid value.

Edits an already-deployed migration and adds force: true, which silently drops the table

This changes 20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb — a migration that has already run in deployed environments — to create_table :top_topics, force: true. force: true issues DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating, so anywhere the table exists while the migration is considered pending (db:schema:load followed by migrate, restored backups, staging/dev databases) the existing top_topics table is silently dropped and recreated. Where the migration already ran, the edit has no effect at all, making it misleading. Old migrations should not be edited; the new create_topic_embeds migration also does not need force: true.

Blank embed_by_username silently no-ops, leaving an infinite reload/job loop

When SiteSetting.embed_by_username is blank, fetch_http looks up User.where(username_lower: '') and returns without creating anything or logging why. The embed controller then keeps rendering loading.html.erb, which reloads the iframe every 30 seconds and enqueues a new RetrieveTopic job on every reload — forever, for every open browser tab on the embedding site. The controller or retriever should fail fast with a clear error (or gate the embed on embed_by_username being configured) instead of looping silently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

OptimizedImage.downsize is defined twice; the first definition is dead code and its callers break

In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the width/height variant can never be executed. Any existing caller still using the old signature breaks: a 5-argument call raises ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments), and a 4-argument call downsize(from, to, w, h) silently mis-binds so the integer height lands in opts, where optimize then calls opts[:allow_animation] on an Integer. Remove the leftover 145-147 definition and update any remaining callers instead of shipping two.

Letting images up to 10 MB through is the point of this feature (the server downsizes them), but attachments are not downsized by the new server code (it only touches FileHelper.is_image? files), so: (a) an admin who set max_attachment_size_kb below 10 MB loses client-side enforcement and nothing in create_upload re-validates attachment size, and (b) an admin who set it above 10 MB has users wrongly rejected by the client.
