Controller specs dispatch straight to the action, so the test passes anyway, but it no longer reflects real traffic and would not fail if the route/verb mapping were broken. Use `xhr :delete` here, matching the other remove_member example.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same HTTP verb mismatch: the remove_member test uses xhr :put, while the route requires DELETE. The candidate also recommends the matching fix, xhr :delete.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `totalPages` calculation using `Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1` produces an extra page when `user_count` is an exact multiple of `limit`, leading to incorrect pagination. For example, with 100 users and a limit of 50, it reports 3 pages instead of 2, allowing navigation to an empty page.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
totalPages is off by one when user_count is an exact multiple of limit

totalPages is computed as Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1, which yields an extra page when user_count divides evenly (e.g. 100 users with limit 50 gives 3 pages instead of 2). On the real last page "next" stays enabled (showingLast compares currentPage to the inflated totalPages); clicking it requests offset == user_count, the server returns an empty member list, and the admin sees an empty "3/3" page. Use Math.ceil(user_count / limit).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same off-by-one bug: Math.floor(user_count / limit) + 1 adds an extra page when user_count is an exact multiple of limit, allowing navigation to an empty page.

false_positives.candidate:
Members endpoint now caps all groups at 50, but the public group members page has no pagination

Before this change, GroupsController#members returned every member for non-automatic groups and only applied limit/offset to automatic groups (default 200). Now every group is limited to 50 by default. The public group members page (discourse/routes/group-members.js.es6 calling model.findMembers() once, rendering templates/group/members.hbs) has no next/previous or load-more controls — only the admin template got pagination. As a result, any group with more than 50 members (and any automatic group with more than 50, previously 200) now only ever shows the first 50 alphabetically, and the remaining members are unreachable. Either keep returning the full roster for the public page or add pagination there.

PATCH /admin/groups/:id now silently ignores incremental membership changes and resets visible to false

The old update dispatched PATCH requests to update_patch, which applied params[:changes] (add/delete usernames) and touched nothing else. This PR removes that branch, so PATCH and PUT both run the single update action: params[:changes] is silently ignored while success_json is returned, and because visible is computed unconditionally as params[:visible] == "true", any legacy client sending an incremental membership PATCH without a visible param will silently flip the group to invisible. If the incremental API is being removed, the action should reject such requests rather than report success, and visible should not be forced to false when the parameter is absent.

automatic does not resolve inside the member item view, so the remove link is rendered for automatic groups too

This template is rendered as the itemView of {{each member in members itemView="group-member"}}, so its scope is the member item view (which only has `member` set via the each keyword), not the adminGroup controller. `automatic` is a property of the group, so {{#unless automatic}} is always truthy and the × remove link renders even for automatic groups. Clicking it sends DELETE /admin/groups/:id/members; the server correctly returns 422, but Group#removeMember has no rejection handler, so the admin gets no feedback and the row simply stays. The group's automatic flag needs to be passed into the item view explicitly, and/or the failure should be surfaced.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The findMembers() call is now asynchronous and unhandled. The controller may not have member data immediately available, creating a race condition.
Expected to return a value at the end of function - code paths without explicit returns will return undefined

The route provides the group's ID in params[:id], but the code attempts to read it from params[:group_id], causing the action to fail. This results in a broken feature when trying to access group memberships.

true_positives.golden_comment: BlockedEmail.should_block_email? method has side effects during a read operation - it updates statistics even when just checking if an email should be blocked. This could cause race conditions in concurrent environments and makes the method name misleading.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
match_count is incremented per validation pass, so one signup attempt is counted twice

should_block? has a database write side effect (match_count += 1 and save) and is invoked from EmailValidator, meaning it runs every time a User is validated. UsersController#create validates the user twice per attempt: once explicitly in `if user.valid? && SiteSetting.call_discourse_hub?` (users_controller.rb line 168) and again inside `user.save` (line 172). Because the record is new and unsaved, email_changed? is true for both passes, so a single blocked signup attempt increments match_count by 2 and updates last_match_at twice. Any other code that calls user.valid? and then user.save (or calls valid? as a dry-run check) also mutates these statistics. Match tracking should live outside the validation cycle (e.g. in the controller after a failed save) or otherwise be per-attempt rather than per-validation, otherwise the match_count/last_match_at audit data this feature exists to collect is unreliable.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same underlying issue: the blocking-check method writes match statistics during a read/validation operation. Its emphasis on repeated validations and double counting is a concrete consequence of the side effect highlighted by the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The case-sensitive email lookup in `BlockedEmail.should_block?` creates a bypass risk, allowing 'User@Example.com' to bypass a block on 'user@example.com'. This can lead to unauthorized access to blocked users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive, so a block is trivially bypassed

BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact-match lookup: BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first. On PostgreSQL string equality is case-sensitive, and nothing normalizes case anywhere in the flow: User.new_from_params assigns params[:email] exactly as typed, BlockedEmail.set_defaults only sets action_type, and EmailValidator passes the raw value through. An admin who blocks spammer@example.com will not block Spammer@example.com or SPAMMER@example.com, even though those deliver to the same mailbox, so a blocked spammer can re-register simply by changing letter case. Normalize the address (e.g. strip + downcase) both when writing blocked_emails rows and when checking in should_block?, or query with a case-insensitive comparison such as lower(email) = lower(?). The added specs only exercise exact-case matches, so this gap is not covered by tests.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same case-sensitive email lookup in BlockedEmail.should_block?, which allows blocked users to bypass the block by changing the capitalization of their email address.

false_positives.candidate:
match_count increment is a non-atomic read-modify-write

should_block? does record.match_count += 1 followed by record.save. That is a read-modify-write: two concurrent requests matching the same blocked email can both read the same counter value, and one increment is silently lost. If these statistics are meant to be accurate, use an atomic update such as BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_counters(match_count: 1) plus an update of last_match_at, instead of incrementing an in-memory attribute and saving the whole record.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The regex pattern @(#{domains}) in email_in_restriction_setting? method only matches domain suffixes, not full domains with proper boundary anchoring. An attacker can register evil.example.com to bypass a whitelist entry for example.com.

true_positives.golden_comment: -ms-align-items never existed in any version of IE/Edge; the correct legacy property is -ms-flex-align.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
align-items mixin passes standard keywords verbatim to legacy properties that use different value names

The new `align-items($alignment)` mixin copies its argument into `-webkit-box-align` and `-ms-flex-align`, but those legacy properties do not accept the standard `flex-start`/`flex-end` keywords — they expect `start`/`end`. The mixin compiles silently and the declaration is simply dropped by those engines, so the first time someone uses `@include align-items(flex-start)` (the most common value in real layouts) alignment will be silently broken in old WebKit and IE10. Current usages only pass `center`/`baseline`, which happen to be valid in both syntaxes, so this is latent rather than an active bug — but the mixin should map the values (or the limitation should be documented) since it is being introduced for codebase-wide reuse. Additionally, `-ms-align-items` on line 121 is not a property that exists in any browser (IE10's 2012 spec only has `-ms-flex-align`), so that line is dead code.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly identifies that -ms-align-items does not exist and that the correct legacy IE property is -ms-flex-align, matching the golden issue despite also discussing keyword mapping.

false_positives.candidate:
float: right on .small-action button is ignored now that .small-action is a flex container

This PR adds `@include flexbox()` to `.small-action`, but the `button` rule inside it still relies on `float: right` to pin the small-action undo/recover button to the right edge of the row. Floats have no effect on flex items, so the button will now render immediately after the `.small-action-desc` text instead of at the far right of the row whenever the description is short (e.g. "closed the topic"). The header change in this same PR solves the equivalent problem for `.panel` by adding `margin-left: auto`; the same fix (or `justify-content: space-between`) is needed here for the button.

margin-left: auto used to right-align .panel does not work in the 2009-spec flexbox fallback the new mixin emits

`.panel` is now pushed to the right edge of the header with `margin-left: auto` instead of `float: right`. The `flexbox()` mixin added in this PR emits `display: -webkit-box`/`display: -moz-box` as fallbacks, and in that 2009 flexbox spec (old iOS Safari, old Android stock browser) auto margins on box children are treated as 0, so on exactly the browsers those fallback lines exist for, the header panel (user menu / login / signup buttons) will sit immediately after the logo instead of at the right edge. At the same time the float fallbacks were removed (`.title { float: left }` deleted, `.panel { float: right }` deleted), so those engines get the degraded layout with no fallback. Either drop the old-spec prefixes or add a fallback such as `-webkit-box-pack: end` / keeping a float fallback.

Bullet category badge in the scrolled header loses its 5px top offset with no replacement

This PR removes `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }`. That offset was what aligned the small inline-flex bullet badge with the topic title text in the header's extra-info (scrolled) state. The new `@include align-items(center)` is applied to `.d-header .contents`, which only centers the `.extra-info-wrapper` as a whole within the header bar; `.extra-info-wrapper` itself is not a flex container and the badge inside it still uses `float: left`, so nothing replaces the intra-wrapper alignment the 5px margin provided. In the scrolled header the category bullet badge will sit higher than the title text baseline. The added `line-height: 1.5` does not compensate for the badge-to-title alignment. This should be verified in the scrolled header and either kept or replaced with an equivalent adjustment.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' so ActiveModelSerializers never calls it

AMS conditional-inclusion hooks must be named `include_<attribute>?`. The method defined here is `include_website_name` (no question mark), so it is dead code and `website_name` is always serialized — including as `null` for users with no website. Rename it to `include_website_name?` (and, per the related finding, have it also check `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` so the privacy behavior matches `website`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same primary issue: include_website_name lacks the required '?' suffix for conditional serialization. It omits the golden comment's additional string-literal mutation concern, but directly matches the conditional-inclusion bug.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the untrusted_attributes restriction that hides website from anonymous viewers of TL0 users

This serializer deliberately strips profile fields like `website` for TL0 users viewed anonymously via `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which returns false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true. The newly added `website_name` attribute is declared as a plain attribute and is not part of that mechanism, so for a restricted (e.g. spammy TL0) user the JSON payload still contains `website_name` with the website's host/path even though `website` itself is removed. That defeats the purpose of the restriction: anonymous viewers (and crawlers) still see the website domain. `website_name` should get the same guard — either add it to `untrusted_attributes` or make its inclusion conditional on `!scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`.

Non-ASCII (IDN) website URLs make website_name nil, hiding the user's website entirely

Ruby's `URI()` only accepts ASCII; a website like `http://münchen.de/page` raises URI::InvalidURIError, which the inline `rescue nil` turns into a nil host, causing `website_name` to return nil. The template (`{{#if model.website_name}}`) then hides the website block completely. Previously the display name was computed client-side with `website.split('/')[2]`, which handled such URLs fine, so this is a display regression for users with internationalized domains. Consider a tolerant fallback (e.g. string splitting, or falling back to the raw website string) when URI parsing fails.

The sibling-subdomain branch of website_name (elsif) has no test coverage

The most intricate condition added in `website_name` — the `elsif` that strips the first DNS label of both hosts when they have the same label count (e.g. website `www.example.com` vs instance `forum.example.com`) — is not exercised by any spec. The three added tests only cover equal hosts, unrelated hosts, and the parent-domain suffix case. Add a test with `Discourse.current_hostname` returning 'forum.example.com' and website 'http://www.example.com/user' expecting 'www.example.com/user', plus a negative case (same label count, different parent, e.g. www.other.com) to lock in the comparison behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Unescaped URL interpolated into a single-quoted href in the imported footer TopicEmbed.import appends a footer to every imported post: #{url}. The only validation on url is a /^https?:\/\// prefix check, so a URL containing a single quote (e.g. from a malicious feed or a fetched page URL) breaks out of the attribute and injects arbitrary HTML into the post body, which is then rendered raw via the raw_html cook path. Because the footer is appended after Readability extraction, this vector bypasses even the limited tag/attribute filtering that import_remote applies to article content. The URL should be HTML/attribute-escaped before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS vulnerability caused by unescaped URL interpolation in TopicEmbed.import's generated HTML. It does not mention the nil contents NoMethodError, but it matches one of the underlying issues explicitly described in the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content is nil for RSS items without content:encoded, crashing the hourly job

i.content.scrub raises NoMethodError when a feed item has no content:encoded/content element — plain RSS 2.0 feeds that only provide <description> are common, and SimpleRSS returns nil for absent elements. Because the job sets sidekiq_options retry: false, the exception kills the run silently until the next hour and any remaining items are never imported. Fall back to i.description (and/or i.summary) when content is absent. The new poll_feed_spec only exercises the site-setting gates and never parses a feed item, so this path is untested.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: calling i.content.scrub when an RSS item lacks content causes a nil-related exception, and both recommend falling back to description.

false_positives.candidate:
Feed HTML is stored and rendered completely unsanitized (stored XSS)

Feed item content is imported with no sanitization: poll_feed unescapes entities via CGI.unescapeHTML, then TopicEmbed.import stores the string as the post raw with cook_method raw_html, and Post#cook returns raw unchanged for raw_html posts. The result is rendered unsanitized both on the forum (the app renders post.cooked unescaped, trusting the normal cooking pipeline to have sanitized it) and in app/views/embed/best.html.erb via <%= raw post.cooked %>, which is served from the Discourse origin inside the iframe. Any <script> or event handler attribute in a feed entry — from a hostile or compromised blog/feed, a rogue author on a multi-author blog, or a MITM on a plaintext feed URL — becomes stored XSS executing in the forum origin as viewing users/admins. CGI.unescapeHTML makes it worse by converting the feed's safely entity-escaped markup into live tags. Imported content must be sanitized (e.g., with the already-bundled sanitize gem) before being stored as raw HTML.

Unauthenticated endpoint triggers remote fetch and topic creation; referer check is trivially spoofable

GET /embed/best enqueues a RetrieveTopic job for any embed_url with no existing embed, with no authentication and no rate limiting. The only gate is that the Referer host matches embeddable_host, which any non-browser client can spoof (curl -H 'Referer: http://blog.example.com' ...). The 60-second Redis throttle in TopicRetriever is per-URL, so an attacker can supply unlimited distinct URLs on the embeddable host: each one makes the server fetch that page and create a forum topic as the embed_by_username user (topic spam, bandwidth/CPU amplification), and when feed_polling_enabled is on each request also triggers a synchronous full PollFeed run inside the job. Consider per-IP rate limiting and/or restricting which paths are importable.

embed.js/embed.css are never added to config.assets.precompile — feature 404s/500s in production

The PR adds app/assets/javascripts/embed.js and app/assets/stylesheets/embed.css.scss and references them via stylesheet_link_tag 'embed' (in the embed layout) and as the script embedding sites load, but no config change adds 'embed.js' or 'embed.css' to the asset precompile list. With the application's explicit precompile list and assets.compile disabled in production, /embed/best will raise AssetNotPrecompiledError and the embed snippet URL will 404, so the entire feature is broken in production. Add both assets to config.assets.precompile.

add_column with default on posts rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock

add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false causes PostgreSQL (pre-11) to rewrite every row of the posts table to materialize the default, holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration. posts is typically the largest table in a Discourse database, so on busy installs this migration can block all writes to posts for minutes during deploy. Add the column without a default/NOT NULL, backfill in batches, then apply the default and constraint.

open(url) used without requiring open-uri on the retrieve path

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url), but this file never requires 'open-uri' — only poll_feed.rb does. The HTTP-retrieve path (EmbedController → RetrieveTopic job → TopicRetriever#fetch_http → TopicEmbed.import_remote) therefore only works if Jobs::PollFeed happened to be loaded already; in lazy-loading environments (dev/test, or any process that never referenced PollFeed) Kernel#open treats the URL as a filename and raises Errno::ENOENT. Add require 'open-uri' to topic_embed.rb (or lib/topic_retriever.rb) so the dependency is explicit.

embeddable_host is compared as an exact string against URI#host with no normalization

The check URI(request.referer).host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host compares the parsed host against free-form admin text. Values admins commonly paste — 'http://example.com', 'example.com/', or 'example.com:8080' — never equal URI#host ('example.com'), so every legitimate embed is rejected with 'invalid referer host' and no diagnostics. The same strict comparison in TopicRetriever.invalid_host? also fails when the blog's canonical URL host differs from the page host (www vs apex), producing the infinite loading screen. Parse/normalize the setting (compare host and port explicitly, and consider allowing subdomains) or validate its format when saved.

X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value

ALLOWALL is not a permitted X-Frame-Options value (the spec defines DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM uri). Browsers currently ignore unrecognized values, which is why framing happens to work, but the behavior is undefined and stricter user agents or normalizing proxies may handle it differently. To allow cross-origin framing for this action, remove the X-Frame-Options header instead of setting an invalid value.

Edits an already-deployed migration and adds force: true, which silently drops the table

This changes 20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb — a migration that has already run in deployed environments — to create_table :top_topics, force: true. force: true issues DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating, so anywhere the table exists while the migration is considered pending (db:schema:load followed by migrate, restored backups, staging/dev databases) the existing top_topics table is silently dropped and recreated. Where the migration already ran, the edit has no effect at all, making it misleading. Old migrations should not be edited; the new create_topic_embeds migration also does not need force: true.

Blank embed_by_username silently no-ops, leaving an infinite reload/job loop

When SiteSetting.embed_by_username is blank, fetch_http looks up User.where(username_lower: '') and returns without creating anything or logging why. The embed controller then keeps rendering loading.html.erb, which reloads the iframe every 30 seconds and enqueues a new RetrieveTopic job on every reload — forever, for every open browser tab on the embedding site. The controller or retriever should fail fast with a clear error (or gate the embed on embed_by_username being configured) instead of looping silently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedImage.downsize is defined twice; the first definition is dead code and its callers break

The file defines self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) at line 145 and then redefines self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}) at line 149. In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the width/height variant can never be executed. Any existing caller still using the old signature breaks: a 5-argument call raises ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments), and a 4-argument call downsize(from, to, w, h) silently mis-binds so the integer height lands in opts, where optimize then calls opts[:allow_animation] on an Integer. Remove the leftover 145-147 definition and update any remaining callers instead of shipping two.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify duplicate downsize definitions where the dimensions-string version overrides the separate width/height version, making it unreachable and breaking callers using the original signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size check no longer honors max_image_size_kb / max_attachment_size_kb

validateUploadedFile used to enforce Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']; it now hardcodes 10 MB for every upload type. Letting images up to 10 MB through is the point of this feature (the server downsizes them), but attachments are not downsized by the new server code (it only touches FileHelper.is_image? files), so: (a) an admin who set max_attachment_size_kb below 10 MB loses client-side enforcement and nothing in create_upload re-validates attachment size, and (b) an admin who set it above 10 MB has users wrongly rejected by the client. Additionally the 413 handler at line 246 now always reports a 10 MB maximum in the error message, which is wrong whenever the web server or site setting has a different limit. The 10 MB cap should apply to images; attachments should still be validated against their own setting.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that hardcoding the upload limit to 10 MB ignores per-type site settings, causing client-side limits to diverge from configured limits. The candidate also identifies the same incorrect hardcoded limit in the 413 handler.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated downsize passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which only accepts WxH geometry

downsize_instructions_animated delegates to resize_instructions_animated, producing `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. gifsicle's --resize-fit requires explicit WIDTHxHEIGHT pixel dimensions and does not understand ImageMagick-style percentages, so any animated downsize through this path exits non-zero and convert_with returns false without resizing. Previously the animated path only ever received "WxH" strings; the new percentage-based flow needs its own animated instructions (e.g. gifsicle --scale 0.8) or computed pixel dimensions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: animated GIF downsizing passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which requires WxH geometry, causing resizing to fail in the animated thumbnail path.

false_positives.candidate:
Large animated GIFs are silently flattened to their first frame

The new auto-downsize code calls OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: ...). OptimizedImage.optimize only selects the animated (gifsicle) instructions when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but uploaded tempfiles (e.g. /tmp/RackMultipart...) have no extension, so the check never matches the original filename or the file content. Large animated GIFs therefore go through `convert <path>[0] ...`, which keeps only the first frame; the upload then succeeds with a static image and the user's animation is silently destroyed (previously the file was rejected for size and the user kept their original). The allow_animation option passed here is effectively dead for direct uploads; detect the format from the original filename or image content instead of the tempfile path.

Downsize failures are ignored and the possibly-oversized original is uploaded anyway

The while loop stops after 5 attempts regardless of whether tempfile.size is now within SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb, the boolean result of OptimizedImage.downsize is ignored, and nothing is logged when it returns false (e.g. when convert/gifsicle errors out). The possibly-still-oversized file then flows straight into Upload.create_for. A large image that resists reduction (very high resolution source, missing/broken ImageMagick) is therefore either silently stored far above the configured limit or fails later with an unrelated error. Check the size after the loop and log or reject when the attempts are exhausted.

Every 80% retry also runs the full ImageOptim pipeline on the intermediate file

Each loop iteration calls OptimizedImage.downsize -> convert_with, which runs ImageOptim.new.optimize_image! (jpegoptim/pngcrush/etc.) on the intermediate result, only for the next iteration to overwrite it. Worst case that is five full optimization passes per upload where one final pass would suffice; for multi-megabyte PNGs this adds tens of seconds of CPU in the deferred job and can push the synchronous API upload path (is_api? && params[:synchronous]) toward request timeouts. Resize without optimizing inside the loop and optimize once at the end.

No specs cover the new auto-downsize upload flow

The PR changes upload size enforcement on both client and server, adds a resize loop in create_upload, and changes OptimizedImage.downsize's signature, but no spec files are touched. Controller/model specs that upload an image larger than max_image_size_kb would catch the regressions visible here (animated GIFs flattened to one frame, the duplicate downsize definition, the loop storing oversized originals when attempts run out). The feature currently ships untested.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

In the working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` computation — it was clearly meant to use slotEndTime. As a result `end > workingHour.endTime` can only fire when the slot's start is already past the end of working hours, and a slot that starts within working hours but ends after the host's availability end is treated as available. Example: fixed host works until 17:00, a round-robin co-host works until 19:00, and a 60-minute slot starts at 16:45 (aligned to the co-host's schedule) — the fixed host gets booked 16:45–17:45 despite being unavailable after 17:00.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: the slot end time is calculated using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime, causing incorrect working-hours validation.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`===` comparison between two Dayjs objects is always false (dead blocked-day branch)

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares object references, so it is never true — the author presumably meant `.isSame()`. This branch is meant to detect a fully blocked day (an override whose start equals its end, typically midnight, which is how "unavailable" date overrides are stored). Because it never fires, blocked days are only rejected incidentally via the surrounding before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the start==end timestamp of a blocked-day override (e.g., exactly 00:00 UTC) is reported as available on a day the host marked unavailable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug: using === to compare separately created Dayjs objects compares references rather than date values, so the condition is always false. Both recommend .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override return early and skip the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a host has a date override on the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the new `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` returns "available" before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom of the function ever runs. checkIfIsAvailable is the only place busy times (calendar events and existing bookings) are consulted — getTimeSlots never sees them. Consequence: for any host with a date override on a given day (fixed hosts via the new fixed-host filter, round-robin hosts via the loose-host filter, and single-user events since users default to isFixed), all of their existing bookings and calendar conflicts on that day are ignored, so the slot is offered and the host can be double-booked. Before this PR the busy check always ran, so this is a regression. The override-branch should fall through to the busy check instead of returning true.

Working-hours gate fails open when the host has no working hours on the slot's day

The new working-hours check treats a slot as "within working hours" whenever `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined. The find callback only returns true when a workingHour entry matches the slot's UTC day AND the slot is outside its range; if the host has no working-hour entry at all for that weekday (their day off), the callback returns undefined for every entry, find returns undefined, the `return false` is skipped, and the host is considered available. For round-robin events, slots are generated from the union of all hosts' hours, so a slot on a fixed host's day off (generated from a round-robin host who works that day) passes the fixed-host filter and becomes bookable — exactly the kind of booking this PR is meant to prevent. The check should fail closed: if no workingHour covers the slot's day, the slot should be unavailable.

Date-override containment check accepts slots that only partially overlap the override

The new override-range logic only rejects slots that are entirely outside the override: it returns "not within" when slotEndTime <= override.start or when slotStartTime > override.end. Two cases slip through and are treated as within the override (and therefore available): (1) a slot that starts before the override start but ends inside it, because slotStartTime.isBefore(override.start) is never checked; (2) a slot that starts before the override end but ends after it, because the end-side check is the strict `slotStartTime.isAfter(override.end)` — a slot starting at 17:30 with an override ending 18:00 (and even a slot starting exactly at 18:00, since isAfter is not inclusive) passes. Hosts with non-aligned schedules (e.g., fixed host override 14:00–18:00, co-host hours starting at :30) can be booked partially or fully outside their override window. The check should require the slot to be fully contained: slotStartTime >= override.start && slotEndTime <= override.end.

Timezone conversion of date overrides drops the date component; overrides land on the wrong invitee day when timezones straddle midnight

The new conversion shifts the stored override time by (inviteeOffset - organizerOffset) and then reads only `.hour()`/`.minute()`, discarding any day rollover, and the `activeOverrides` filter (line 207) still matches the override's stored-as-UTC date against the invitee's calendar day. When the organizer's and invitee's local dates differ, the override is applied on the wrong invitee day and never on the correct one. Concrete example: organizer in Honolulu (UTC-10) with an override Mar 10 08:00–09:00, invitee in Auckland (UTC+13). The true window is Mar 11 07:00–08:00 Auckland time, but the code offers Mar 10 07:00–08:00 Auckland (offset +1380 min rolls 08:00 to 07:00 the next day, and .hour() truncates it back onto Mar 10), while for inviteeDate Mar 11 the filter no longer matches the stored Mar 10 date so the override is missing entirely. The same happens for e.g. Tokyo organizer / Los Angeles invitee. This is the timezone-adjustment scenario the PR sets out to fix, still broken for large timezone gaps.

dayjs.tz(override.timeZone) silently falls back to the server's timezone when timeZone is undefined

TimeRange.timeZone is optional (packages/types/schedule.d.ts marks it `timeZone?: string`), and getSlots is a shared library function, but the new code calls `dayjs(...).tz(override.timeZone)` unconditionally. When timeZone is undefined, dayjs.tz does not throw — it falls back to the runtime's local timezone (typically UTC on servers/containers). The offset calculation then becomes inviteeOffset - serverOffset instead of inviteeOffset - organizerOffset, silently shifting the override's slots for any caller that passes date overrides without a timeZone. Either make the field required for date overrides or handle the undefined case explicitly.

No test covers the headline fix: date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin events

The PR's primary change is the new fixed-host/loose-host availability enforcement in checkIfIsAvailable (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts), but the only added test exercises a single-user event with a date override viewed from a different invitee timezone. There is no ROUND_ROBIN scenario with an isFixed host that has a date override, and no scenario where a host with a date override also has busy times/bookings on the override day — which is why the regression where the busy check is skipped on override days (the `dateOverrideExist` early return) is not caught: the new test would pass even with that bug. Please add tests for a round-robin event with a fixed host override (including timezones where organizer/invitee dates differ) and for a host with an override plus a conflicting booking on the same day.

Today only this file writes retryCount so there is no immediate data loss, but retryCount is a column on the shared WorkflowReminder model; if any other reminder type ever sets it (e.g. a similar retry mechanism for email), this SMS cron would silently delete those reminders. The condition should be `AND: [{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]` (and probably `scheduled: false`).
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same missing SMS method filter in the retryCount > 1 deletion OR branch, which allows non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp to be deleted. The candidate's caveat about current usage does not change the underlying issue.

Reminders that never reach the Twilio call never get their retryCount incremented

The retry-count increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. When a reminder fails before reaching `twilio.scheduleSMS` — e.g. the booking has no `smsReminderNumber` so `sendTo` is null, or the resolved message is empty — the guard fails, no SMS is attempted, and no retryCount increment happens. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0, so it is re-fetched and fully reprocessed (template rendering, profile lookup, etc.) on every cron run until `scheduledDate` passes. That is exactly the repeated-rescheduling behavior this PR is meant to stop, and a missing/invalid phone number is the failure mode called out in the PR description. There should be an `else` that increments retryCount (or otherwise marks the reminder) so the two-strike deletion applies to these reminders too.

The try block itself contains prisma calls (`prisma.profile.findFirst`, the update marking a reminder scheduled, and the new else-branch increment), so a database error lands in this catch where the update is likely to throw again. Additionally, if the reminder row is deleted concurrently (e.g. by a booking-cancellation flow between the findMany at the top and this update), the update raises Prisma P2025 'record not found'. In both cases the exception propagates out of the handler: the request returns 500 and the for-loop aborts, so every reminder after the failing one is skipped for the run. Before this PR the catch only logged the error, so this is a new failure mode. Wrap the increment in a nested try/catch (and consider using `retryCount: { increment: 1 }`).

No tests cover the new retry increment and deletion threshold

The PR adds branching logic that permanently deletes data (retryCount > 1 cleanup) and increments retryCount on two different failure paths (scheduleSMS returning falsy, and exceptions), but no tests were added or updated. A regression here either leaves users receiving duplicate SMS attempts indefinitely or silently deletes legitimate reminders. At minimum the behavior 'failure increments retryCount once per run', 'reminder is deleted on the run after the second failure', and 'successful scheduling leaves retryCount untouched' should be covered.

Diff-snippet computation can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException instead of reporting the violation In the "Illegal HTML" reporting branch, start (common prefix length) and end (common suffix length) are computed independently, so they can overlap: when the sanitizer output contains the entire input as a prefix and also shares its tail (e.g. input value "" that the sanitizer normalizes to "" yields start=3 and end=2), then value.substring(start, value.length() - end) is invoked with begin (3) > end (1) and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Instead of the intended "Illegal HTML in key …" message, the verification aborts with an unhandled exception and a bare stack trace, and no further keys/files are checked. Clamp the values so start + end never exceeds the string length for both strings, e.g. end = Math.min(end, value.length() - start) and end = Math.min(end, sanitized.length() - start).

First, the condition is inverted: it returns false (no match) when the extracted shortcut EQUALS the expected one, instead of when it does not. Second, the offsets are wrong: in the 6-character prefix (2 chars session type, 2 chars token type, 2 chars grant type) the grant shortcut occupies indexes 4-5, so it should be substring(4, 6); substring(3, 5) takes the second token-type character and the first grant-type character. false_positives.candidate:
Access tokens issued together with an offline refresh token get the wrong ("online") session-type prefix in their ID

initToken() encodes the token ID, including the session-type prefix, from the user session that exists at token-creation time. For an authorization-code or direct-grant request with scope=offline_access that session is the ONLINE session, so the ID gets the "on" prefix. However, afterwards TokenManager.AccessTokenResponseBuilder.generateRefreshToken() creates the offline user session and re-points accessToken.sessionState to the offline session (OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse even removes the online session for first-time offline access, which only works because the access token has been re-bound to the offline session). The result is that an access token bound to an OFFLINE session carries the "on" (online) prefix until the next refresh (refresh-minted tokens correctly get "of"). This corrupts exactly the data this PR exists to provide: a consumer relying on the session-type prefix to pick the right session lookup (follow-up #37662) would search online sessions, miss the offline session, and either reject a valid token or need the old fallback lookup anyway. The session type must be determined after the offline-session switch, or the token ID re-encoded when generateRefreshToken() rebinds the token to the offline session.

Adding a non-default method to the OAuth2GrantTypeFactory interface is a hard breaking change for any deployment with a custom grant type: DefaultTokenContextEncoderProviderFactory.postInit() iterates ALL registered OAuth2GrantType factories and calls getShortcut() on each of them during server startup, so a custom factory compiled against the previous version of the interface will throw AbstractMethodError and prevent the server from booting. This should be a default method (e.g. deriving a shortcut from the factory id, or returning null that the encoder factory tolerates). Note also that a custom implementation returning null would currently kill startup as well, because ConcurrentHashMap.put() throws NullPointerException for the null shortcut in postInit().

Any caller that swaps the form parameters after construction will have getGrantType() return the value from the original params, and that stale value is exactly what OAuth2GrantTypeBase.createTokenResponse() stores into the ClientSessionContext under Constants.GRANT_TYPE and what ends up encoded into the access-token ID. Either recompute grantType in setFormParams() or drop the cached field and read it from formParams in getGrantType().

The new test `BackwardsCompatibilityUserStorageTest.testRecoveryKeysSetupAndLogin` only logs in once with a single code and never asserts that the same code is rejected on a second login, so the regression is not caught. getGroupIdsWithViewPermission collects authz resource IDs instead of group IDs and never evaluates per-group permissions

Round-trip test only proves the two converters are consistent inverses of each other

false_positives.candidate:

The FixedQueuePool is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ (result_consumer.py, mode == 'thread-queue-parallel') and the same pool object is handed to every strategy built by create_with_partitions. However, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which sets worker.shutdown=True, shuts down every queue, and joins the worker threads. Arroyo's StreamProcessor closes and joins the current strategy on every partition revocation and creates a new one on the next assignment, so after the first routine consumer-group rebalance (deploy, autoscaling, another group member joining) the new strategy is built on a dead pool. From then on every submit() reaches work_queue.put(), which raises queue.ShutDown; SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() catches that with a broad 'except Exception', logs it, and then calls offset_tracker.add_offset + complete_offset for the message. The commit thread therefore commits offsets for messages that were never enqueued or processed, and since this consumer has no DLQ configured the data is silently lost until the process is restarted. Nothing recreates the pool (ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() is never invoked by the StreamProcessor). Fix by creating the pool per create_with_partitions call (or not shutting it down from the strategy), and by not marking offsets complete when the work item was never actually queued.

The SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy docstring claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but put() on an unbounded queue never blocks, so the Kafka consumer thread keeps polling and buffering messages in memory no matter how far behind the workers fall. A single slow group — the exact scenario this mode is built to tolerate — grows its queue without bound and the partition's entire backlog accumulates in the process heap, eventually OOM-killing the consumer pod. The queues should be bounded (maxsize) and/or poll() should raise MessageRejected when total depth exceeds a threshold.

FixedQueuePool.shutdown() sets worker.shutdown = True before calling q.shutdown(immediate=False). OrderedQueueWorker.run loops on 'while not self.shutdown', so each worker exits immediately after its current item and never drains the remaining queued items — the immediate=False 'graceful' drain is dead code. Additionally, SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()/join() never waits for queued work (wait_until_empty exists but is unused) and performs no final commit after workers finish: the commit thread is joined before the pool is shut down, and its last pass races with in-flight items. The result is that on every deploy or partition revocation the queued backlog plus roughly the last commit-interval's worth of completed-but-uncommitted work is redelivered by Kafka and processed a second time. join(timeout) should drain the queues within the timeout and then stage a final commit of all completed offsets.

test_different_groups_distributed is flaky due to per-process string hash randomization

The test submits 20 group keys and asserts len(queue_indices) == 3, i.e. that they cover all 3 queues. Queue assignment is hash(group_key) % num_queues, and CPython randomizes str hash values per process (PYTHONHASHSEED), so each test run is effectively a random draw: the probability that 20 keys land in only 1–2 of 3 buckets is about 0.09% (3*(2/3)^20). With no code change at all, roughly 1 in 1100 CI runs will fail this assertion. Use a looser assertion (e.g. indices are within range and ordering per key is stable), pin the hash seed, or mock hash().

false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
"Advanced" negative-offset pagination always 500s: Django rejects negative slices

In OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, when enable_advanced_features is set and the client supplies a cursor with a negative offset (Cursor.from_string accepts e.g. "0:-5:0"), the code evaluates queryset[cursor.offset : cursor.offset + limit + extra]. Django's QuerySet raises ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported") for negative slice bounds, so the request errors with a 500. The comments above the branch are false: Django does not "properly handle negative slicing automatically", and the statement "This is safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" is meaningless. This advertised feature cannot work as written and is reachable via a crafted cursor query parameter on the audit log endpoint.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the negative-offset branch in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result, where cursor.offset is passed directly into queryset slicing when advanced features are enabled. The candidate describes the consequence as Django raising an error, but the underlying code issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator crashes with TypeError when used with datetime ordering

OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key is copied from the numeric Paginator and does math.floor/math.ceil on the raw attribute value. Its only caller, OrganizationAuditLogsEndpoint, uses it with order_by="-datetime", so the value is a datetime and math.floor(datetime) raises TypeError. build_cursor calls get_item_key on every non-empty page, so any request with optimized_pagination=true that returns at least one audit log row will 500. Additionally, value_from_cursor returns the raw numeric cursor value, so even if the first page worked, page 2 would compare a timestamp column against a float in the extra WHERE clause and raise a database error. The class needs DateTimePaginator-style key conversion (or should subclass DateTimePaginator). No test covers this path, which is why it wasn't caught.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/ceil on a datetime key from order_by '-datetime', which raises a TypeError.

false_positives.candidate:
SET to ZSET type change on existing span-buf:s:* keys will cause WRONGTYPE errors during rolling deploys

The PR changes the Redis type of the existing span-buf:s:{project_id:trace_id}:span_id keys from SET (sadd/sscan/sunionstore/scard) to ZSET (zadd/zscan/zunionstore/zcard/zpopmin) while keeping the exact same key names. Segment keys live up to redis_ttl (3600s) and consumers are upgraded in a rolling fashion, so old and new code will operate on the same keys concurrently: old consumers' SADD/SSCAN against newly created ZSET keys, and new consumers' ZADD/ZCARD/ZPOPMIN/ZSCAN against SET keys created minutes earlier, both raise redis WRONGTYPE errors. That crashes span processing and flushing and drops spans. The migration needs a new key prefix or an explicit transition plan rather than reusing the live keyspace.

Spans evicted by ZPOPMIN are dropped silently with no metric or log

When a segment exceeds 1000 spans, the script now evicts the excess with ZPOPMIN, permanently discarding span payloads from the segment. The previous behavior (skip oversized segments at flush time) emitted the metric spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded and an error log; that check is removed from _load_segment_data in this PR, and the new eviction emits nothing: the script doesn't return the evicted count and process_spans records no metric. Operators lose all visibility into truncated segments and the associated data loss. Return the evicted count from the script and emit a metric/log from Python.

max_segment_spans option is now dead; the cap is hardcoded to 1000 in Lua

SpansBuffer.__init__ still accepts and stores max_segment_spans (default 1001), but the only remaining enforcement is a hardcoded `if span_count > 1000` in add-buffer.lua. The flush-time check that used self.max_segment_spans was removed from _load_segment_data, so configuring this option now silently does nothing (and the default 1001 doesn't even match the Lua 1000). Either pass the limit into the script as an ARGV or delete the parameter.

Redirect resolution limit lowered 10000 to 1000; deep traces will silently split into multiple segments

The redirect-following loop limit was reduced from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. For trace trees deeper than 1000 redirects, the loop now stops early and the span is written to whatever set the partial resolution landed on, splitting one logical segment into multiple flushed segments (partial/duplicated output downstream). This tradeoff is 10x more reachable than before; if intentional for script latency, the consequence should stay documented and a metric should be emitted when the limit is actually hit.

No test coverage for the eviction feature or the new paginator

The headline behavior of this PR — capping segments at 1000 spans via ZPOPMIN during insert — has no test: the buffer tests were only updated to add the newly required end_timestamp_precise field. A test inserting more than 1000 spans into one segment should assert which spans survive (lowest end_timestamp_precise evicted), that the segment still flushes, and that TTLs are intact. Likewise, the new OptimizedCursorPaginator / audit-log optimized_pagination path has no tests at all; even a trivial smoke test would have caught that it 500s on the first page due to the datetime TypeError.

Added comment falsely claims negative cursor offsets are supported

The new comment in Cursor.__init__ says "Allow negative offsets for advanced pagination scenarios", but no code was changed and negative offsets are not actually usable: Django querysets raise ValueError on negative slices, and BasePaginator.get_result clamps negative next-cursor offsets to 0. This misdocuments the Cursor contract for anyone building on it and should be removed or corrected.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.
Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling eligibility is computed from the outer `dataset` and raw request query instead of the scoped dataset and query actually executed

Inside `_get_event_stats(scoped_dataset, query_columns, query, ...)`, the eligibility check calls `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` using the closure variable `dataset` from `get()`, not the `scoped_dataset` argument, and `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`/`_is_error_focused_query` re-read `request.GET["query"]` instead of the `query` argument. The dashboard-widget split path calls `_get_event_stats(discover, ..., split_query, ...)` where `split_query` is rewritten to `(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction`; that error-only query is never upsampled because the decision was made against the original (metrics) dataset and the unmodified request query. The transform decision should be based on the dataset and query string actually being executed, otherwise upsampling is silently skipped (or could be misapplied) for exactly the requests the function arguments describe.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. The eligibility check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset, so upsampling is skipped in the dashboard split path, where the query runs on discover while the original dataset is metrics. The candidate also raises an extra point about the query string, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidental git submodule (gitlink) added without .gitmodules

The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290...`, i.e. a git submodule/gitlink pointing at the base commit of this same repository, but no `.gitmodules` entry is added. This is almost certainly an accidental commit of a nested checkout. It breaks any workflow that initializes submodules: `git submodule update --init` fails with `fatal: no submodule mapping found in .gitmodules for path 'sentry-repo'`, which affects CI checkouts that run with `--recurse-submodules` and fresh clones. It should be removed from the PR.

upsampled_count uses sum(sample_weight) without coalescing NULLs, silently undercounting unsampled errors

The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function is defined as `toInt64(sum(Column("sample_weight")))`. In snuba, `sample_weight` on the errors/discover storage is Nullable and is only populated for error events that carry a client sample rate; error events ingested before a project was allowlisted, from SDKs that don't sample, or server-side have NULL `sample_weight`. ClickHouse `sum()` ignores NULL rows and returns NULL if every row is NULL, so (a) any unsampled error events are silently excluded from the returned count (e.g. 10 unsampled errors + 1 error sampled at 0.1 returns 10 instead of the correct 20), and (b) a time bucket containing only unsampled events returns NULL/0 instead of the true count. The added tests never exercise events without a client_sample_rate, so this is not caught. The aggregate should treat missing weights as 1, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`; the code comment's assumption that sample_weight always exists for allowlisted projects is not guaranteed by the schema.

_is_error_focused_query substring-matches event.type:error, misfiring on negations and quoted text

`_is_error_focused_query` decides whether to rewrite `count()` into `sum(sample_weight)` by checking `if "event.type:error" in query.lower()`. This substring test ignores search semantics: a discover query like `!event.type:error` (the standard way to select transaction-like events) contains the substring and will be treated as error-focused, so its `count()` is rewritten to sum(sample_weight) over non-error rows that have no sample_weight — returning NULL/incorrect counts. A free-text search such as `message:"event.type:error"` also false-positives. For allowlisted projects this silently returns wrong data on common discover queries; the check should parse the query and inspect the actual event.type filter (including its negation) rather than doing a substring match.

Cache key built with Python hash() of project ids is collision-prone

The eligibility cache key is `f"error_upsampling_eligible:{organization.id}:{hash(tuple(sorted(snuba_params.project_ids)))}"`. Python's `hash()` is not collision-free: two different project-id sets within the same organization can produce the same hash and therefore share a cache entry, causing the wrong allowlist eligibility (and thus wrong counts) to be served for up to 60 seconds. The key should encode the ids directly (e.g. comma-joined sorted ids) rather than a hash digest of them.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code; allowlist changes have no invalidation path

`invalidate_upsampling_cache(organization_id, project_ids)` is introduced with a docstring saying it "should be called when the allowlist configuration changes", but nothing in this PR (or elsewhere) calls it, and there is no signal/hook wired to the `issues.client_error_sampling.project_allowlist` option. As shipped, every allowlist change takes up to the full 60-second TTL to take effect with no supported way to invalidate. Either wire the invalidation to the option update path or remove the unused helper and rely on the documented TTL.

No tests for the caching behavior that is the PR's stated performance optimization

The unit tests only exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `transform_query_columns_for_error_upsampling`); the main entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects` — which contains the new 60-second cache, the cache key construction, and the interaction between cached eligibility and the per-request dataset/query check — is never called. Cache hit/miss behavior, the TTL, and stale-cache regressions (the headline "performance optimization" of this PR) are therefore completely unverified.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.

Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Deny-cache test does not actually prove the denial cache short-circuits

In TestService_CacheCheck/'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry', the permission cache is seeded with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} and the comment claims this 'allows access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked'. A scope-map value of false does not allow anything, so the test returns Allowed=false even if the denial-cache logic were removed entirely: the cached perms would deny, the DB fallback (empty fakeStore) would also deny, and the assertion would still pass. To prove the denial cache is consulted, the cached value must be true — then the test would fail if the permDenialCache check in Check were removed or bypassed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point out the same problem. The test comment claims the cached permissions allow access, but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so the cached entry still denies. The candidate adds that this means the test doesn't actually prove the denial cache short-circuits, which builds on the same underlying issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Denial cache can persist denials computed from stale data and is never invalidated

In Check, when the DB fallback still denies, the denial is stored in permDenialCache for shortCacheTTL (30s) and short-circuits all later checks for that (namespace, user, action, name, folder) tuple. Two problems follow: (1) The deny decision may depend on the cached folder tree (checkInheritedPermissions -> buildFolderTree uses folderCache, also 30s TTL), which the DB fallback does NOT refresh. If a teammate of a folder creator checks a dashboard inside a folder created seconds ago, the fresh permission re-query returns the same scopes (e.g. only folders:uid:<grandparent>) and the stale tree has no ancestors for the new folder, so the request is denied and that deny is now cached for another 30s — extending the deny window up to ~60s after folder creation, longer than before this change, for exactly the 'newly created folder' scenario this PR is meant to fix. (2) When the fallback re-fetch does update permCache with fresh scopes, any pre-existing denial entry for a resource covered by those fresh scopes is not deleted, so the stale denial still wins over fresher permission data. Consider refreshing/invalidating the folder tree (or skipping denial caching) when the deny relied on folder-tree evaluation, and/or keying denials so a fresh allow can supersede them.

Every denied check for a distinct resource name now triggers a full DB permission fetch

With the new fallback, whenever the cached permission map does not contain the requested scope, Check unconditionally re-queries the full permission set from the database (getIdentityPermissions -> getUserPermissions -> permissionStore.GetUserPermissions). The denial cache only deduplicates repeats of the exact same (user, action, name, parentFolder) tuple, so a caller that polls N distinct resources it cannot access (dashboard listing integrations, scanners, a user clicking through an org where most content is restricted) now issues N full permission queries per 30s window, where before this change the permission cache answered all of them with a single query per user/action. Singleflight only collapses concurrent identical user+action fetches, not sequential distinct names. Consider bounding the fallback (e.g., a short 'permissions fresh as of' marker per user/action so repeated denials on different names within a few seconds don't each hit the DB).

Permission-cache hits that result in denial are recorded as cache misses

When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission map (cache hit) but checkPermission returns allowed=false, execution falls out of the if-block and reaches s.metrics.permissionCacheUsage.WithLabelValues("false", ...) — recording a cache miss even though the permission cache was hit. Denied checks are precisely the traffic pattern this PR optimizes, so this mislabeling systematically skews the cache hit-rate metric downward and makes the new caching behavior look less effective than it is. The hit/miss label should be recorded based on whether the cache lookup succeeded, before evaluating the allow/deny outcome.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code attempts to access integration.metadata[sender][login] without checking for the existence of the sender key. This causes a KeyError for integrations where the sender metadata was not set during creation
true_positives.matched_candidate:
KeyError crash when an existing Integration has no "sender" in metadata

In GitHubInstallation.dispatch, when an Integration row exists for the installation_id but has no OrganizationIntegration, the new verification does `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`. The "sender" key is only written into metadata by the installation webhook; `build_integration` adds it only when the pipeline state contains "sender", and nothing in the pipeline ever binds that key, so every integration created through the pipeline path (e.g. when the webhook was delayed or lost) lacks it, as do older rows created before the webhook recorded the sender. If such an integration later loses its OrganizationIntegration (e.g. the region-side org integration is deleted while the control-side Integration row is still ACTIVE during deletion propagation) and a user tries to install again, this line raises KeyError and returns a 500 instead of the intended failure page, blocking legitimate reinstalls. Use a guarded lookup such as `integration.metadata.get("sender", {}).get("login")` and explicitly fail closed with the error page when the sender is unknown.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe a KeyError from accessing integration.metadata['sender']['login'] when the sender key is missing for integrations created without it. The candidate raises the same issue as the golden comment.

false_positives.candidate:
Unguarded GitHub API calls in OAuthLoginView can 500 the install pipeline

The code exchange (`safe_urlopen(url=ghip.get_oauth_access_token_url(), data=data)`) and the profile fetch (`get_user_info(payload["access_token"])`) are not wrapped in any exception handling. safe_urlopen raises requests exceptions on connection errors/timeouts, and get_user_info can raise if GitHub returns a non-JSON error response. Any of these transient failures propagate as unhandled exceptions and the user gets a 500, which is inconsistent with the goal of this PR to show the "Invalid installation request" page whenever GitHub verification cannot be completed. Wrap both calls and render `error(request, self.active_organization)` on failure.

No test covers the sender-match success path of the new verification

test_github_user_mismatch only exercises the failure branch of the new check (authenticated GitHub user differs from the recorded installation sender). No test covers the complementary case where the Integration exists without an OrganizationIntegration and the authenticated user matches `integration.metadata["sender"]["login"]`, verifying that installation then proceeds. In all success-path tests the Integration row is absent at check time, so the verification code is never exercised positively. Given that this check reads nested metadata that may be missing on some rows, a success-path test with an existing sender-recorded integration would catch regressions in both directions.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup in testCacheIDPForLogin registers removal of a literal IdP named "alias" instead of the created providers

In testCacheIDPForLogin the creation loop does getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) with the literal string "alias" (same again at line 425 for idp-alias-20). No identity provider with alias "alias" exists, so the 21 providers the test creates (idp-alias-0 .. idp-alias-20, ten of them linked to orga) are never cleaned up, and the deferred remove() call will hit a 404 during cleanup. Because the test realm is shared across the class, the leftover org-linked IDPs contaminate other tests that assert exact counts — e.g. testCacheIDPByOrg asserts orga's cached IDP list has exactly 6 entries, which fails if testCacheIDPForLogin ran first and left 10 more IDPs linked to orga. The cleanup should reference the actual alias created in each iteration (and "idp-alias-20" for the later one), e.g. by capturing final String alias = "idp-alias-" + i and using get(alias).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate flags the same problem as the golden comment: the cleanup uses the literal "alias" when it should use "idp-alias-" + i.

false_positives.candidate:
Login cache invalidation is skipped for IDPs whose organization is disabled, leaving stale entries after the org is re-enabled

registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate compares getLoginPredicate() on the 'original' and 'updated' models to decide whether the .idp.login caches must be invalidated. The 'original' model comes from getById() (line 91), which returns the organization-aware wrapper whose isEnabled() returns false whenever the linked organization is disabled. The cached login ID sets, however, are built from the JPA query which only looks at the raw flags (enabled, hideOnLogin, linkOnly, BROKER_PUBLIC). So an org-linked IDP with enabled=true in a disabled org IS present in the cached login sets, yet predicate(original) is false. If an admin then updates that IDP so it no longer qualifies for login (sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or BROKER_PUBLIC=false, or moves it to another org), predicate(updated) is also false and no invalidation is registered (the early return at line 405-407). When the organization is later re-enabled (an org update does not invalidate these caches), the stale cached ID set is served: getById returns the fresh model whose org-aware isEnabled() is now true, and the only consumer-side re-check added in this PR (OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean) filters on isEnabled() only, so an IDP that should be hidden, link-only, or private to an org is displayed on the login page. The predicate for the 'original' state should be evaluated against the unwrapped/raw stored model (as remove() already does with idpDelegate.getByAlias) so the comparison matches what is actually in the cache.

true_positives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

Existing SQL expression tests are left in place and will now fail against the "not implemented" stub

This PR makes DB.RunCommands and DB.QueryFramesInto unconditionally return errors.New("not implemented"), which means sql.TablesList (pkg/expr/sql/parser.go) and NewSQLCommand (pkg/expr/sql_command.go) now fail for every input.
