It frames the impact as test failures, but the flagged code problem is the same stubbed DB methods.

false_positives.candidate:
Error message "sqlExpressions is not implemented" is misleading — the feature is deliberately disabled

When a dashboard or alert rule contains a SQL expression, the query now fails with the error "sqlExpressions is not implemented". The feature is in fact implemented but has been intentionally disabled in response to CVE-2024-9264 (RCE/LFI), which is exactly the situation users and support staff will need to understand when previously working SQL expressions start failing. The message text is wrong and will generate confusion; it should say something like "SQL expressions are disabled" (ideally referencing the security advisory) instead of claiming the feature does not exist.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of the cache after acquiring the write lock (double-checked locking)

After taking the exclusive lock, GetWebAssets does not re-check whether another goroutine already populated entryPointAssetsCache. At startup (or whenever the cache is empty), every concurrent request observes a nil cache under the read lock, then queues on the write lock; each one in turn re-reads and re-parses assets-manifest.json from disk (or fetches it over HTTP if the CDN path at line 56 is ever enabled) and overwrites the cache, with all but the last result discarded. This is the standard double-checked-locking pattern with the second check missing. Adding `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock avoids the redundant serialized I/O.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug in GetWebAssets: the double-checked locking pattern is missing its second check. After the write lock is acquired, the function does not re-check whether another goroutine already populated the cache.

false_positives.candidate:
Exclusive lock held across manifest I/O serializes all callers

The write lock acquired at line 48 is held (via defer) for the entire recompute, including the disk read of assets-manifest.json and, if enabled, the CDN HTTP fetch. While any writer holds it, all other callers block on the initial RLock at line 41. In dev mode the cache is deliberately bypassed on every call, so every request to GetWebAssets is now serialized through this single global mutex plus a disk read. The same happens in non-dev mode whenever the manifest read persistently fails, because the cache then stays nil and every request retries under the exclusive lock, turning a missing-file misconfiguration into a global serialization point for index page loads. Consider doing the read outside the lock and taking the write lock only to publish the result (combined with the re-check from the previous point).

Race fix ships without a regression test exercising concurrent access

This PR fixes a data race on the global entryPointAssetsCache but adds no test. Nothing guards the new synchronization: if someone later removes the mutex or accesses the global without it, nothing in the test suite would catch it. A simple test that calls GetWebAssets from many goroutines (against a temp assets-manifest.json) and is run under `go test -race` would fail if the synchronization regresses and would document the concurrency contract of this function.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists

CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags contain six r.log.Error calls (lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, 579) that log normal, successful operation: "Annotations to clean by time", "cleaned annotations by time", "Tags to clean", "cleaned tags". Combined with the cleanup ticker being changed to 1 minute in this PR, this floods error-level logs during healthy operation, breaks any alerting based on error logs, and can produce enormous log lines for large batch sizes. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: debug or routine information logged at Error level, which pollutes the error logs. Both recommend switching to Debug.

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, running all cleanup jobs 10x more often

The Run loop ticker was changed from time.Minute * 10 to time.Minute * 1. clean() does not only run annotation cleanup — on every tick it runs the entire job list: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, old annotations, expiring user invites, deleting stale short URLs, two query-history enforcement queries, and re-scanning the temp file directories. This change therefore multiplies the database and filesystem load of all background cleanup jobs by 10, yet the PR description (about avoiding MySQL deadlocks in annotation cleanup) never mentions it. If the intent is to keep annotation cleanup batches small and frequent, that should be scoped to the annotation job or at least called out explicitly; as written this is an undocumented behavior change affecting every cleanup task.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same change: the cleanup ticker went from 10 minutes to 1 minute. Both say this raises database load because all cleanup jobs now run more often. The candidate adds more detail about which jobs are affected, but the core concern is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
SQLite literal IN-list built with O(n^2) string concatenation

In deleteByIDs, the SQLite fallback for batch sizes over 999 builds the ID list with `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` inside a loop over ids. Each iteration allocates and copies the entire accumulated string, so building the list is quadratic in the number of IDs. With the batch size exercised in the new test (32767 IDs) this copies on the order of gigabytes per batch, and it runs on every batch iteration of the cleanup loop. Use a strings.Builder with strconv.AppendInt (or strings.Join on pre-converted strings) to make it linear.

Parameter-limit guard only covers SQLite; large batch sizes break on Postgres

deleteByIDs only sidesteps bind-parameter limits when the dialect is SQLite and AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize > 999; every other database gets a `DELETE FROM ... WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...)` statement with one placeholder per ID. Postgres rejects statements with more than 65535 bind parameters, and very large placeholder lists can also hit MySQL's max_allowed_packet. Since AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable and the PR itself tests a value of 32767, a batch size above 65535 on Postgres would make the delete fail on every cleanup cycle (the job errors out and nothing is cleaned). Consider chunking the ID list into fixed-size DELETE batches for all dialects instead of special-casing SQLite.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes derive their context from the request context and will be canceled immediately

In Create (and identically in Delete at line 110, Update at line 135 and DeleteCollection at line 163), the goroutine performing the asynchronous legacy write builds its context from the incoming request context: `ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, time.Second*10, ...)`. The dual writer returns immediately after spawning the goroutine, and the HTTP request context is canceled as soon as the handler returns, so the derived context is already (or almost immediately) canceled when the legacy write actually runs. The legacy store will therefore fail with context.Canceled in the common case, silently defeating the purpose of mode 3 ("write to legacy as a safe measure") — unified storage will have the data but legacy will not. Use `context.WithoutCancel(ctx)` (keeping the log values) before applying the 10s timeout so the legacy write survives request completion.

Delete no longer cleans up legacy storage when unified storage returns NotFound

The previous Mode 3 Delete tolerated a NotFound error from unified storage (`apierrors.IsNotFound`) and still attempted the legacy delete; the new code returns immediately on any storage delete error, including NotFound. An object that exists only in legacy (e.g., written before the unified copy existed, or whose unified copy was lost during migration) can now never be deleted through the API: unified returns NotFound, the client sees a failure, and the stale legacy record is left behind, where it will resurface if the installation rolls back to a legacy-first mode. The NotFound special-case for proceeding with the legacy delete should be preserved.

Create records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails

In the error path of Create, when `d.Storage.Create` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` even though the legacy store was never contacted and the measured start time belongs to the unified-storage call. This should be `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`; as written, unified-storage create failures pollute the legacy-storage error/duration metrics and the actual storage failure is never recorded, which will mislead the dashboards this mode is meant to feed.

Update records a legacy-storage duration metric when unified storage fails

In the error path of Update, when `d.Storage.Update` fails, the code calls `d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage)` instead of `d.recordStorageDuration(true, ...)`. The legacy store was never called and the duration measured is the unified-storage call's, so unified-storage update errors are misreported as legacy-storage errors in the dual-writer metrics.

DeleteCollection records the legacy delete result as a unified-storage metric

Inside the async goroutine of DeleteCollection, the result of `d.Legacy.DeleteCollection` is recorded with `d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startLegacy)` instead of `d.recordLegacyDuration(...)`. Errors and durations of the legacy delete-collection are therefore attributed to unified storage, masking real legacy failures and inflating storage timings in the metrics.

No draining of in-flight async legacy writes on shutdown

The async legacy writes are fire-and-forget goroutines with a 10s timeout, and `Destroy()` does not wait for any of them. On pod shutdown or rollout, every legacy write still in flight is silently abandoned, so the legacy copy can diverge from unified storage exactly during deploys — the window in which the "legacy as a safe measure" guarantee matters most. Consider tracking in-flight writes with a WaitGroup and draining them in Destroy.

Mode 3 integration subtests assert synchronous legacy visibility of async legacy writes

The new subtests "with dual write (file, mode 3)" and "with dual write (unified storage, mode 3)" reuse doPlaylistTests, which asserts that objects written via the k8s API are immediately visible through the legacy REST API (the `/api/playlists` list comparison in "Do CRUD via k8s" and the legacy GET in getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously in a goroutine with no synchronization point, so there is no guarantee the legacy store has caught up when those assertions run — these subtests will be flaky under CI load (and, given the request-context cancellation bug in the async writer, may fail consistently). The mode-3 runs need polling/eventually-style assertions against the legacy API.

Unit tests never wait for or assert the asynchronous legacy writes

None of the new mode-3 unit tests (Create, Update, Delete, DeleteCollection) synchronize with the goroutine that performs the legacy write or assert that it happened — e.g., TestMode3_Create registers a legacy Create expectation but never blocks on the goroutine nor calls `m.AssertExpectations`. The tests pass even if the legacy write is never executed, so the core behavior this PR adds (async dual write to legacy) is effectively untested at the unit level; a regression that drops the legacy call entirely would go unnoticed.

Create error test registers the storage failure on the legacy mock and only works via the shared mock instance

In TestMode3_Create's case "error when creating object in the unified store fails", the failing Create expectation is registered via `setupLegacyFn` on the legacy mock, but mode 3 calls unified storage first and the legacy expectation is never used intentionally — the test only passes because `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` wrap the same `*mock.Mock`, so the storage Create call accidentally matches the legacy-registered expectation. If the two mocks are ever given separate mock instances, the storage Create call will panic as unexpected. Register the failing expectation on the storage mock (setupStorageFn) so the test models what it claims to test.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Device limit check-then-insert is not atomic; concurrent new devices can exceed the limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by running CountDevices and then, only if count < deviceLimit, executing the INSERT. These are two separate statements with no transaction or locking. Concurrent anonymous requests carrying distinct new device IDs — or requests landing on different Grafana replicas in an HA setup — can all observe a count below the limit and then all insert, so the stored device count can exceed deviceLimit by an arbitrary margin under a burst of new devices (e.g., bot/scraper traffic). If the limit is meant to be a hard cap, the count-and-insert must be done atomically (single transaction with locking), or the overshoot should be explicitly accepted and documented.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem. The device count check and the insert are not atomic, so concurrent requests can all pass the check and exceed the limit. Both suggest using a transaction or lock as the fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. Cache is set before the limit check, so a retry bypasses the device limit entirely

tagDeviceUI writes the device key into the local cache (29-minute TTL) before calling anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice. When the configured device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached for a new device and Anonymous.Authenticate (client.go) rejects the request — but the cache entry has already been written and is never removed. Any subsequent request from the same device within 29 minutes hits the cache in tagDeviceUI, returns nil, and Authenticate succeeds, even though the device was never persisted and is never counted toward the limit. A brand-new device therefore only has to send its request twice to get anonymous access past the limit, and this is repeatable after each cache expiry (first request fails, then ~29 minutes of access). The cache key should be set only after a successful store call, or explicitly deleted when CreateOrUpdateDevice returns an error.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same bug: tagDeviceUI sets the cache before CreateOrUpdateDevice. On ErrDeviceLimitReached the entry stays, so later requests bypass the device limit for the 29-minute TTL.

In GrafanaBootConfig, the new field is declared as `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` with no type annotation, so TypeScript infers the class property's type as `undefined` (the `implements GrafanaConfig` clause does not widen inferred member types). Fallback locales are only loaded for HTTP requests; jobs, mailers and rake tasks cannot fall back

This PR removes `.extra-info-wrapper .badge-wrapper.bullet { margin-top: 5px; }`. That offset was what aligned the small inline-flex bullet badge with the topic title text in the header's extra-info (scrolled) state. The new `@include align-items(center)` is applied to `.d-header .contents`, which only centers the `.extra-info-wrapper` as a whole within the header bar; `.extra-info-wrapper` itself is not a flex container and the badge inside it still uses `float: left`, so nothing replaces the intra-wrapper alignment the 5px margin provided. In the scrolled header the category bullet badge will sit higher than the title text baseline. The added `line-height: 1.5` does not compensate for the badge-to-title alignment. This should be verified in the scrolled header and either kept or replaced with an equivalent adjustment.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Mixing float: left with flexbox causes layout issues. Further this PR removes the float-based right alignment for .d-header .panel, which may cause the login panel in the non-Ember/noscript header (where .panel is nested inside .row and not a flex item) to stack under the title instead of remaining right-aligned.
-webkit-box-ordinal-group and -moz-box-ordinal-group require values starting from 1, not 0. If $val is 0, this will cause incorrect rendering in older browsers, leading to layout issues.

true_positives.golden_comment: The include_website_name method is missing the required ? suffix. Rails serializers expect include_ methods to end with ? for conditional attribute inclusion, a convention followed by other methods in this serializer. Without it, the website_name attribute may not be conditionally included as intended. Additionally, the '.' << website_host string concatenation should be replaced with '.' + website_host or '.#{website_host}' to avoid mutating string literals, which can lead to issues.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
include_website_name is missing the trailing '?' so ActiveModelSerializers never calls it

AMS conditional-inclusion hooks must be named `include_<attribute>?`. The method defined here is `include_website_name` (no question mark), so it is dead code and `website_name` is always serialized — including as `null` for users with no website. Rename it to `include_website_name?` (and, per the related finding, have it also check `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` so the privacy behavior matches `website`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core issue: include_website_name is missing its '?' suffix, so conditional inclusion does not work. It does not mention the string mutation point, but the primary issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
website_name bypasses the untrusted_attributes restriction that hides website from anonymous viewers of TL0 users

This serializer deliberately strips profile fields like `website` for TL0 users viewed anonymously via `untrusted_attributes` (lines 105-111), which returns false when `scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)` is true. The newly added `website_name` attribute is declared as a plain attribute and is not part of that mechanism, so for a restricted (e.g. spammy TL0) user the JSON payload still contains `website_name` with the website's host/path even though `website` itself is removed. That defeats the purpose of the restriction: anonymous viewers (and crawlers) still see the website domain. `website_name` should get the same guard — either add it to `untrusted_attributes` or make its inclusion conditional on `!scope.restrict_user_fields?(object)`.

Non-ASCII (IDN) website URLs make website_name nil, hiding the user's website entirely

Ruby's `URI()` only accepts ASCII; a website like `http://münchen.de/page` raises URI::InvalidURIError, which the inline `rescue nil` turns into a nil host, causing `website_name` to return nil. The template (`{{#if model.website_name}}`) then hides the website block completely. Previously the display name was computed client-side with `website.split('/')[2]`, which handled such URLs fine, so this is a display regression for users with internationalized domains. Consider a tolerant fallback (e.g. string splitting, or falling back to the raw website string) when URI parsing fails.

The sibling-subdomain branch of website_name (elsif) has no test coverage

The most intricate condition added in `website_name` — the `elsif` that strips the first DNS label of both hosts when they have the same label count (e.g. website `www.example.com` vs instance `forum.example.com`) — is not exercised by any spec. The three added tests only cover equal hosts, unrelated hosts, and the parent-domain suffix case. Add a test with `Discourse.current_hostname` returning 'forum.example.com' and website 'http://www.example.com/user' expecting 'www.example.com/user', plus a negative case (same label count, different parent, e.g. www.other.com) to lock in the comparison behavior.

true_positives.golden_comment: The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
true_positives.matched_candidate: Unescaped URL interpolated into a single-quoted href in the imported footer TopicEmbed.import appends a footer to every imported post: #{url}. The only validation on url is a /^https?:\/\// prefix check, so a URL containing a single quote (e.g. from a malicious feed or a fetched page URL) breaks out of the attribute and injects arbitrary HTML into the post body, which is then rendered raw via the raw_html cook path. Because the footer is appended after Readability extraction, this vector bypasses even the limited tag/attribute filtering that import_remote applies to article content. The URL should be HTML/attribute-escaped before interpolation.
true_positives.reasoning: The golden comment raises two issues: a nil contents NoMethodError and an XSS from the unescaped url. The candidate clearly identifies the XSS from the unescaped url interpolation in TopicEmbed.import, which is a substantive part of the golden comment. It does not mention the nil issue, so the match is partial but on the same location and problem.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
i.content is nil for RSS items without content:encoded, crashing the hourly job

i.content.scrub raises NoMethodError when a feed item has no content:encoded/content element — plain RSS 2.0 feeds that only provide <description> are common, and SimpleRSS returns nil for absent elements. Because the job sets sidekiq_options retry: false, the exception kills the run silently until the next hour and any remaining items are never imported. Fall back to i.description (and/or i.summary) when content is absent. The new poll_feed_spec only exercises the site-setting gates and never parses a feed item, so this path is untested.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: `i.content.scrub` crashes when an RSS item has no content field and `i.content` is nil. Both also propose falling back to `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
Feed HTML is stored and rendered completely unsanitized (stored XSS)

Feed item content is imported with no sanitization: poll_feed unescapes entities via CGI.unescapeHTML, then TopicEmbed.import stores the string as the post raw with cook_method raw_html, and Post#cook returns raw unchanged for raw_html posts. The result is rendered unsanitized both on the forum (the app renders post.cooked unescaped, trusting the normal cooking pipeline to have sanitized it) and in app/views/embed/best.html.erb via <%= raw post.cooked %>, which is served from the Discourse origin inside the iframe. Any <script> or event handler attribute in a feed entry — from a hostile or compromised blog/feed, a rogue author on a multi-author blog, or a MITM on a plaintext feed URL — becomes stored XSS executing in the forum origin as viewing users/admins. CGI.unescapeHTML makes it worse by converting the feed's safely entity-escaped markup into live tags. Imported content must be sanitized (e.g., with the already-bundled sanitize gem) before being stored as raw HTML.

Unauthenticated endpoint triggers remote fetch and topic creation; referer check is trivially spoofable

GET /embed/best enqueues a RetrieveTopic job for any embed_url with no existing embed, with no authentication and no rate limiting. The only gate is that the Referer host matches embeddable_host, which any non-browser client can spoof (curl -H 'Referer: http://blog.example.com' ...). The 60-second Redis throttle in TopicRetriever is per-URL, so an attacker can supply unlimited distinct URLs on the embeddable host: each one makes the server fetch that page and create a forum topic as the embed_by_username user (topic spam, bandwidth/CPU amplification), and when feed_polling_enabled is on each request also triggers a synchronous full PollFeed run inside the job. Consider per-IP rate limiting and/or restricting which paths are importable.

embed.js/embed.css are never added to config.assets.precompile — feature 404s/500s in production

The PR adds app/assets/javascripts/embed.js and app/assets/stylesheets/embed.css.scss and references them via stylesheet_link_tag 'embed' (in the embed layout) and as the script embedding sites load, but no config change adds 'embed.js' or 'embed.css' to the asset precompile list. With the application's explicit precompile list and assets.compile disabled in production, /embed/best will raise AssetNotPrecompiledError and the embed snippet URL will 404, so the entire feature is broken in production. Add both assets to config.assets.precompile.

add_column with default on posts rewrites the whole table under an exclusive lock

add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false causes PostgreSQL (pre-11) to rewrite every row of the posts table to materialize the default, holding an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock for the duration. posts is typically the largest table in a Discourse database, so on busy installs this migration can block all writes to posts for minutes during deploy. Add the column without a default/NOT NULL, backfill in batches, then apply the default and constraint.

open(url) used without requiring open-uri on the retrieve path

TopicEmbed.import_remote calls open(url), but this file never requires 'open-uri' — only poll_feed.rb does. The HTTP-retrieve path (EmbedController → RetrieveTopic job → TopicRetriever#fetch_http → TopicEmbed.import_remote) therefore only works if Jobs::PollFeed happened to be loaded already; in lazy-loading environments (dev/test, or any process that never referenced PollFeed) Kernel#open treats the URL as a filename and raises Errno::ENOENT. Add require 'open-uri' to topic_embed.rb (or lib/topic_retriever.rb) so the dependency is explicit.

embeddable_host is compared as an exact string against URI#host with no normalization

The check URI(request.referer).host != SiteSetting.embeddable_host compares the parsed host against free-form admin text. Values admins commonly paste — 'http://example.com', 'example.com/', or 'example.com:8080' — never equal URI#host ('example.com'), so every legitimate embed is rejected with 'invalid referer host' and no diagnostics. The same strict comparison in TopicRetriever.invalid_host? also fails when the blog's canonical URL host differs from the page host (www vs apex), producing the infinite loading screen. Parse/normalize the setting (compare host and port explicitly, and consider allowing subdomains) or validate its format when saved.

X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL is not a valid header value

ALLOWALL is not a permitted X-Frame-Options value (the spec defines DENY, SAMEORIGIN, and ALLOW-FROM uri). Browsers currently ignore unrecognized values, which is why framing happens to work, but the behavior is undefined and stricter user agents or normalizing proxies may handle it differently. To allow cross-origin framing for this action, remove the X-Frame-Options header instead of setting an invalid value.

Edits an already-deployed migration and adds force: true, which silently drops the table

This changes 20131223171005_create_top_topics.rb — a migration that has already run in deployed environments — to create_table :top_topics, force: true. force: true issues DROP TABLE IF EXISTS before creating, so anywhere the table exists while the migration is considered pending (db:schema:load followed by migrate, restored backups, staging/dev databases) the existing top_topics table is silently dropped and recreated. Where the migration already ran, the edit has no effect at all, making it misleading. Old migrations should not be edited; the new create_topic_embeds migration also does not need force: true.

Blank embed_by_username silently no-ops, leaving an infinite reload/job loop

When SiteSetting.embed_by_username is blank, fetch_http looks up User.where(username_lower: '') and returns without creating anything or logging why. The embed controller then keeps rendering loading.html.erb, which reloads the iframe every 30 seconds and enqueues a new RetrieveTopic job on every reload — forever, for every open browser tab on the embedding site. The controller or retriever should fail fast with a clear error (or gate the embed on embed_by_username being configured) instead of looping silently.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
The current origin validation using indexOf is insufficient and can be bypassed. An attacker could use a malicious domain like evil-discourseUrl.com to pass this check.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: The downsize method is defined twice. The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedImage.downsize is defined twice; the first definition is dead code and its callers break

The file defines self.downsize(from, to, max_width, max_height, opts={}) at line 145 and then redefines self.downsize(from, to, dimensions, opts={}) at line 149. In Ruby the second definition silently replaces the first, so the width/height variant can never be executed. Any existing caller still using the old signature breaks: a 5-argument call raises ArgumentError (wrong number of arguments), and a 4-argument call downsize(from, to, w, h) silently mis-binds so the integer height lands in opts, where optimize then calls opts[:allow_animation] on an Integer. Remove the leftover 145-147 definition and update any remaining callers instead of shipping two.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same issue. The downsize method is defined twice, and the second definition (taking a single dimensions argument) overrides the first (taking width and height). This makes the original unreachable and breaks callers that use the old signature.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Client-side upload size check no longer honors max_image_size_kb / max_attachment_size_kb

validateUploadedFile used to enforce Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']; it now hardcodes 10 MB for every upload type. Letting images up to 10 MB through is the point of this feature (the server downsizes them), but attachments are not downsized by the new server code (it only touches FileHelper.is_image? files), so: (a) an admin who set max_attachment_size_kb below 10 MB loses client-side enforcement and nothing in create_upload re-validates attachment size, and (b) an admin who set it above 10 MB has users wrongly rejected by the client. Additionally the 413 handler at line 246 now always reports a 10 MB maximum in the error message, which is wrong whenever the web server or site setting has a different limit. The 10 MB cap should apply to images; attachments should still be validated against their own setting.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate raises the same problem as the golden comment. It notes the hardcoded 10MB limit replaces the per-type Discourse.SiteSettings max_*_size_kb check, which lets client and server limits diverge. It also flags that the 413 handler has the same hardcoding.

true_positives.golden_comment: Passing 80% as the dimensions can fail for animated GIFs when allow_animated_thumbnails is true, since the animated path uses gifsicle --resize-fit which expects WxH geometry, not a percentage; downsizing would then silently fail.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Animated downsize passes "80%" to gifsicle --resize-fit, which only accepts WxH geometry

downsize_instructions_animated delegates to resize_instructions_animated, producing `gifsicle --resize-fit 80%`. gifsicle's --resize-fit requires explicit WIDTHxHEIGHT pixel dimensions and does not understand ImageMagick-style percentages, so any animated downsize through this path exits non-zero and convert_with returns false without resizing. Previously the animated path only ever received "WxH" strings; the new percentage-based flow needs its own animated instructions (e.g. gifsicle --scale 0.8) or computed pixel dimensions.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue: the '80%' value is passed to gifsicle --resize-fit on the animated path, which expects WxH geometry, so the animated downsize fails silently.

false_positives.candidate:
Large animated GIFs are silently flattened to their first frame

The new auto-downsize code calls OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: ...). OptimizedImage.optimize only selects the animated (gifsicle) instructions when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but uploaded tempfiles (e.g. /tmp/RackMultipart...) have no extension, so the check never matches the original filename or the file content. Large animated GIFs therefore go through `convert <path>[0] ...`, which keeps only the first frame; the upload then succeeds with a static image and the user's animation is silently destroyed (previously the file was rejected for size and the user kept their original). The allow_animation option passed here is effectively dead for direct uploads; detect the format from the original filename or image content instead of the tempfile path.

Downsize failures are ignored and the possibly-oversized original is uploaded anyway

The while loop stops after 5 attempts regardless of whether tempfile.size is now within SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb, the boolean result of OptimizedImage.downsize is ignored, and nothing is logged when it returns false (e.g. when convert/gifsicle errors out). The possibly-still-oversized file then flows straight into Upload.create_for. A large image that resists reduction (very high resolution source, missing/broken ImageMagick) is therefore either silently stored far above the configured limit or fails later with an unrelated error. Check the size after the loop and log or reject when the attempts are exhausted.

Every 80% retry also runs the full ImageOptim pipeline on the intermediate file

Each loop iteration calls OptimizedImage.downsize -> convert_with, which runs ImageOptim.new.optimize_image! (jpegoptim/pngcrush/etc.) on the intermediate result, only for the next iteration to overwrite it. Worst case that is five full optimization passes per upload where one final pass would suffice; for multi-megabyte PNGs this adds tens of seconds of CPU in the deferred job and can push the synchronous API upload path (is_api? && params[:synchronous]) toward request timeouts. Resize without optimizing inside the loop and optimize once at the end.

No specs cover the new auto-downsize upload flow

The PR changes upload size enforcement on both client and server, adds a resize loop in create_upload, and changes OptimizedImage.downsize's signature, but no spec files are touched. Controller/model specs that upload an image larger than max_image_size_kb would catch the regressions visible here (animated GIFs flattened to one frame, the duplicate downsize definition, the loop storing oversized originals when attempts run out). The feature currently ships untested.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The loop checking `tempfile.size` may never terminate correctly due to stale cached size, leading to potential infinite loops or incorrect file handling after modifications.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: Potential nil pointer exception - if no TopicUser record exists, tu will be nil and calling methods on it will crash
true_positives.matched_candidate:
NoMethodError (500) when the visitor has no TopicUser row

tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id]) can return nil. Emailed users normally have a row because send_notification_email calls TopicUser.change, but the unsubscribe URL is reachable by any logged-in user — someone who never interacted with the topic, or whose topic_users row was later removed — and the very next line calls tu.notification_level, raising NoMethodError and returning a 500 instead of the unsubscribe page. Guard the nil case or use TopicUser.change, which upserts.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: TopicUser.find_by can return nil, and calling methods such as notification_level on that nil value crashes.

false_positives.candidate: unsubscribe mutates notification state on an idempotent-unsafe GET topics#unsubscribe is wired to plain GET routes (config/routes.rb adds get "t/:slug/:topic_id/unsubscribe" and "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe") and it permanently writes the user's topic notification level before rendering the page. GET requests must not mutate state, and this one is not even idempotent: the first visit drops a watching/tracking user to regular, but simply reloading the confirmation page (or hitting back) executes the URL again and, because the level is now regular, falls into the else branch and fully mutes the topic — while the page still only claims 'You will stop receiving notifications'. It is also CSRF-able: any third-party page can embed and silently change a logged-in visitor's notification state, and any logged-in link prefetcher triggers it. The state change should happen via POST (the unsubscribe page already renders a topic-notifications-button the user can click), or the GET should render a confirmation without writing.

Direct tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change bookkeeping, allowing silent re-subscription

Assigning tu.notification_level and calling tu.save! bypasses TopicUser.change, so notifications_changed_at and notifications_reason_id are not updated and the notification_level_change MessageBus event is never published. One concrete consequence: TopicUser.update_last_read and TopicUser.auto_track only auto-subscribe users whose notifications_reason_id is null, and TopicUser.change would have stamped the reason as user_changed — because this code doesn't, a user who unsubscribes (set to regular) and later spends time reading the topic can be silently flipped back to tracking by the auto-track-on-view-time logic. Open browser tabs also won't reflect the new level in real time. Use TopicUser.change(current_user.id, topic_id, notification_level: ...) instead.

unsubscribe_link now hard-requires %{unsubscribe_url}, breaking other add_unsubscribe_link callers

The unsubscribe_link site text now interpolates %{unsubscribe_url} ('To stop receiving notifications about this particular topic, [click here](%{unsubscribe_url})'), but Email::MessageBuilder only provides unsubscribe_url when the caller passes it in opts. The in-tree caller in user_notifications was updated, but any other caller of build_email with add_unsubscribe_link: true that doesn't pass unsubscribe_url (plugins, custom mailers) will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument when building both the text body (MessageBuilder#body) and the HTML part (MessageBuilder#html_part), failing those emails entirely — the existing spec had to be changed for exactly this reason. Consider defaulting unsubscribe_url (e.g., to user_preferences_url) or making the second sentence conditional.

No specs for the new state-mutating topics#unsubscribe endpoint

The PR adds a new endpoint that mutates user state with several branches — watching/tracking → regular, regular/muted → muted, missing TopicUser row, slug-mismatch 301 redirect, login requirement — but adds no controller or request specs for it; the only spec change passes unsubscribe_url in message_builder_spec. Even basic coverage would have caught the nil-TopicUser 500 and the non-idempotent escalation to muted on repeat visits described above.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sed -i '' syntax is macOS-only and fails on GNU/Linux

The script updates GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL with `sed -i '' -E "s|...|..." "$ENV_FILE"`. The `-i ''` form (separate empty-string argument for the backup suffix) is BSD/macOS-only; on GNU sed (Linux dev machines, CI containers) the empty string is parsed as a filename and the command fails with "sed: can't read : No such file or directory", so the .env file is never updated. true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the `sed -i ''` syntax only works on macOS/BSD sed and fails on GNU sed on Linux.

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Handler throws a generic Error, surfacing as HTTP 500 instead of 404/403

When the credential does not exist or belongs to another user, deleteCacheHandler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. In tRPC a plain Error is reported to the client as INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR (HTTP 500), which is wrong for a not-found/authorization failure and will also pollute server error monitoring. The codebase convention is to throw a TRPCError with an explicit code, e.g. `new TRPCError({ code: "NOT_FOUND", message: ... })` or FORBIDDEN, so clients get the correct status code.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that throwing a generic Error for an auth/access failure produces a 500 in tRPC, and both recommend a TRPCError with a code such as FORBIDDEN. They describe the same issue.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache timestamp is hardcoded to en-US formatting, ignoring the user's locale

The 'cache_last_updated' timestamp is formatted with new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", { dateStyle: "short", timeStyle: "short" }). Every user, regardless of their configured locale, will see US-style dates (e.g. 7/15/25, 3:04 PM), which is confusing for locales that use DD/MM/YYYY or 24-hour times. Use the user's locale (e.g. navigator.language or the i18n locale from useLocale) instead of the hardcoded "en-US" string.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the date is formatted with a hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of the user's locale. The candidate also suggests using the locale from useLocale, which is the fix the golden comment implies.

false_positives.candidate:
deleteCache success does not invalidate the connectedCalendars query, leaving stale cache status on screen

The deleteCache mutation's onSuccess only shows a toast and calls the optional onSuccess prop; unlike the disconnect mutation right below it (which invalidates utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars in onSettled), it never invalidates the connectedCalendars query. The query that supplies cacheUpdatedAt is configured with refetchOnWindowFocus: false, so in any usage of SelectedCalendarsSettingsWebWrapper where the optional onChanged/onSuccess callback is not provided, the dropdown will keep showing "Cache Status / Last updated: <timestamp>" and the "Delete cached data" action for cache rows that were just deleted, until a full page reload. Add an onSettled invalidation of utils.viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars to deleteCacheMutation so the cache status disappears after deletion.

No tests for the new deleteCache mutation or the cache-status repository method

The important behavior to lock down is the authorization check: a user must not be able to delete CalendarCache rows for a credentialId owned by another user (the handler only checks prisma.credential.findFirst({ id, userId })), and the not-found path should raise the expected error. A regression here would silently let one user wipe another user's availability cache. Add handler tests covering the owner, non-owner, and missing-credential cases.

fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache now ends with SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {}), which updates (and bumps @updatedAt on) every SelectedCalendar row for the credential. fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache runs on every Google Calendar webhook notification and cache repopulation, so this adds a write query per webhook event. Per the PR's own notes, SelectedCalendar.updatedAt is not displayed or consumed anywhere in the frontend — the UI uses CalendarCache.updatedAt — so this write buys nothing and, worse, makes SelectedCalendar.updatedAt meaningless as a staleness signal for any future consumer. Consider removing it until there is an actual reader.

ENV_FILE="../.env" resolves relative to the caller's working directory and can write outside the repo

The script hardcodes ENV_FILE="../.env", which is only correct when the script is invoked from inside the scripts/ directory. A developer running `bash scripts/test-gcal-webhooks.sh` from the repository root (the natural way to run it) will have ../.env resolve to the parent directory of the checkout; the script then either edits an unrelated .env there or, per its own fallback, creates a brand-new .env outside the repository containing GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL. Resolve the path relative to the script's own location instead (e.g. ENV_FILE="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)/.env").

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Copy-paste bug: `end` is computed from slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime

In the working-hours check, `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();` duplicates the `start` computation — it was clearly meant to use slotEndTime. As a result `end > workingHour.endTime` can only fire when the slot's start is already past the end of working hours, and a slot that starts within working hours but ends after the host's availability end is treated as available. Example: fixed host works until 17:00, a round-robin co-host works until 19:00, and a 60-minute slot starts at 16:45 (aligned to the co-host's schedule) — the fixed host gets booked 16:45–17:45 despite being unavailable after 17:00.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug as the golden comment: the end time is computed from slotStartTime when it should use slotEndTime.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
`===` comparison between two Dayjs objects is always false (dead blocked-day branch)

`if (dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes"))` compares object references, so it is never true — the author presumably meant `.isSame()`. This branch is meant to detect a fully blocked day (an override whose start equals its end, typically midnight, which is how "unavailable" date overrides are stored). Because it never fires, blocked days are only rejected incidentally via the surrounding before/after checks, and a slot starting exactly at the start==end timestamp of a blocked-day override (e.g., exactly 00:00 UTC) is reported as available on a day the host marked unavailable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same bug: comparing two dayjs objects with === checks object references, so the condition is always false. Both suggest using .isSame() instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Slots inside a date override return early and skip the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, when a host has a date override on the slot's date and the slot falls inside the override window, the new `if (dateOverrideExist) { return true; }` returns "available" before the `busy.every(...)` check at the bottom of the function ever runs. checkIfIsAvailable is the only place busy times (calendar events and existing bookings) are consulted — getTimeSlots never sees them. Consequence: for any host with a date override on a given day (fixed hosts via the new fixed-host filter, round-robin hosts via the loose-host filter, and single-user events since users default to isFixed), all of their existing bookings and calendar conflicts on that day are ignored, so the slot is offered and the host can be double-booked. Before this PR the busy check always ran, so this is a regression. The override-branch should fall through to the busy check instead of returning true.

Working-hours gate fails open when the host has no working hours on the slot's day

The new working-hours check treats a slot as "within working hours" whenever `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined. The find callback only returns true when a workingHour entry matches the slot's UTC day AND the slot is outside its range; if the host has no working-hour entry at all for that weekday (their day off), the callback returns undefined for every entry, find returns undefined, the `return false` is skipped, and the host is considered available. For round-robin events, slots are generated from the union of all hosts' hours, so a slot on a fixed host's day off (generated from a round-robin host who works that day) passes the fixed-host filter and becomes bookable — exactly the kind of booking this PR is meant to prevent. The check should fail closed: if no workingHour covers the slot's day, the slot should be unavailable.

Date-override containment check accepts slots that only partially overlap the override

The new override-range logic only rejects slots that are entirely outside the override: it returns "not within" when slotEndTime <= override.start or when slotStartTime > override.end. Two cases slip through and are treated as within the override (and therefore available): (1) a slot that starts before the override start but ends inside it, because slotStartTime.isBefore(override.start) is never checked; (2) a slot that starts before the override end but ends after it, because the end-side check is the strict `slotStartTime.isAfter(override.end)` — a slot starting at 17:30 with an override ending 18:00 (and even a slot starting exactly at 18:00, since isAfter is not inclusive) passes. Hosts with non-aligned schedules (e.g., fixed host override 14:00–18:00, co-host hours starting at :30) can be booked partially or fully outside their override window. The check should require the slot to be fully contained: slotStartTime >= override.start && slotEndTime <= override.end.

Timezone conversion of date overrides drops the date component; overrides land on the wrong invitee day when timezones straddle midnight

The new conversion shifts the stored override time by (inviteeOffset - organizerOffset) and then reads only `.hour()`/`.minute()`, discarding any day rollover, and the `activeOverrides` filter (line 207) still matches the override's stored-as-UTC date against the invitee's calendar day. When the organizer's and invitee's local dates differ, the override is applied on the wrong invitee day and never on the correct one. Concrete example: organizer in Honolulu (UTC-10) with an override Mar 10 08:00–09:00, invitee in Auckland (UTC+13). The true window is Mar 11 07:00–08:00 Auckland time, but the code offers Mar 10 07:00–08:00 Auckland (offset +1380 min rolls 08:00 to 07:00 the next day, and .hour() truncates it back onto Mar 10), while for inviteeDate Mar 11 the filter no longer matches the stored Mar 10 date so the override is missing entirely. The same happens for e.g. Tokyo organizer / Los Angeles invitee. This is the timezone-adjustment scenario the PR sets out to fix, still broken for large timezone gaps.

dayjs.tz(override.timeZone) silently falls back to the server's timezone when timeZone is undefined

TimeRange.timeZone is optional (packages/types/schedule.d.ts marks it `timeZone?: string`), and getSlots is a shared library function, but the new code calls `dayjs(...).tz(override.timeZone)` unconditionally. When timeZone is undefined, dayjs.tz does not throw — it falls back to the runtime's local timezone (typically UTC on servers/containers). The offset calculation then becomes inviteeOffset - serverOffset instead of inviteeOffset - organizerOffset, silently shifting the override's slots for any caller that passes date overrides without a timeZone. Either make the field required for date overrides or handle the undefined case explicitly.

No test covers the headline fix: date overrides of fixed hosts in round-robin events

The PR's primary change is the new fixed-host/loose-host availability enforcement in checkIfIsAvailable (packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts), but the only added test exercises a single-user event with a date override viewed from a different invitee timezone. There is no ROUND_ROBIN scenario with an isFixed host that has a date override, and no scenario where a host with a date override also has busy times/bookings on the override day — which is why the regression where the busy check is skipped on override days (the `dateOverrideExist` early return) is not caught: the new test would pass even with that bug. Please add tests for a round-robin event with a fixed host override (including timezones where organizer/invitee dates differ) and for a host with an override plus a conflicting booking on the same day.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
retryCount deletion branch is not scoped to SMS reminders

In the cleanup `deleteMany`, the new second OR branch `{ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }` has no `method` (or `scheduled`) filter, so it matches every row in WorkflowReminder with retryCount > 1 — including EMAIL and WHATSAPP reminders. The first OR branch is explicitly limited to `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS`, showing the SMS-only intent of this cron, but the retryCount branch is table-wide. Today only this file writes retryCount so there is no immediate data loss, but retryCount is a column on the shared WorkflowReminder model; if any other reminder type ever sets it (e.g. a similar retry mechanism for email), this SMS cron would silently delete those reminders. The condition should be `AND: [{ method: WorkflowMethods.SMS }, { retryCount: { gt: 1 } }]` (and probably `scheduled: false`).
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same issue. The retryCount OR branch lacks an SMS method filter, so it can delete non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp. The candidate downplays the immediate impact, but the underlying bug and the proposed fix are the same.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders that never reach the Twilio call never get their retryCount incremented

The retry-count increment only happens inside `if (message?.length && message?.length > 0 && sendTo)`. When a reminder fails before reaching `twilio.scheduleSMS` — e.g. the booking has no `smsReminderNumber` so `sendTo` is null, or the resolved message is empty — the guard fails, no SMS is attempted, and no retryCount increment happens. The reminder stays `scheduled: false` with retryCount 0, so it is re-fetched and fully reprocessed (template rendering, profile lookup, etc.) on every cron run until `scheduledDate` passes. That is exactly the repeated-rescheduling behavior this PR is meant to stop, and a missing/invalid phone number is the failure mode called out in the PR description. There should be an `else` that increments retryCount (or otherwise marks the reminder) so the two-strike deletion applies to these reminders too.

Unawaited-safe DB write inside catch can throw and abort the entire cron run

The catch block now performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update(...)` without its own error handling. The try block itself contains prisma calls (`prisma.profile.findFirst`, the update marking a reminder scheduled, and the new else-branch increment), so a database error lands in this catch where the update is likely to throw again. Additionally, if the reminder row is deleted concurrently (e.g. by a booking-cancellation flow between the findMany at the top and this update), the update raises Prisma P2025 'record not found'. In both cases the exception propagates out of the handler: the request returns 500 and the for-loop aborts, so every reminder after the failing one is skipped for the run. Before this PR the catch only logged the error, so this is a new failure mode. Wrap the increment in a nested try/catch (and consider using `retryCount: { increment: 1 }`).

No tests cover the new retry increment and deletion threshold

The PR adds branching logic that permanently deletes data (retryCount > 1 cleanup) and increments retryCount on two different failure paths (scheduleSMS returning falsy, and exceptions), but no tests were added or updated. A regression here either leaves users receiving duplicate SMS attempts indefinitely or silently deletes legitimate reminders. At minimum the behavior 'failure increments retryCount once per run', 'reminder is deleted on the run after the second failure', and 'successful scheduling leaves retryCount untouched' should be covered.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

true_positives.golden_comment: The parseRefreshTokenResponse function incorrectly sets refresh_token to the hardcoded string 'refresh_token' when it's missing from the OAuth refresh token response. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing refresh_token is replaced with the literal string "refresh_token" and persisted, bricking credentials

When the parsed response has no refresh_token, the util sets `refreshTokenResponse.data.refresh_token = "refresh_token"`. Callers then merge/write this into the DB: zoom does `key.refresh_token = newTokens.refresh_token` (VideoApiAdapter.ts line 120) and office365 spreads the parsed data over the stored credentials (CalendarService.ts line 264). The real refresh token is thereby overwritten with a junk literal — both in sync mode (where the endpoint returns no refresh token) and in normal mode whenever a provider omits a rotated refresh token. Any later refresh attempt (e.g. after disabling the sync feature) will fail with invalid_grant and the user must reconnect the app. The placeholder should not be written back to the stored credential.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: a missing refresh_token is replaced with the hardcoded string 'refresh_token', which breaks later token refreshes and causes authentication failures.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
minimumTokenResponseSchema drops every field except access_token, corrupting stored credentials when sync is enabled

The computed keys `[z.string().toString()]` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]` both evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]" (Zod schemas have no meaningful toString), so the intended catch-all does not exist — the second key simply overwrites the first. Combined with zod's default behaviour of stripping unknown keys, parsing any token response with this schema keeps only `access_token` and discards expires_in/expires_in-like fields, scope, instance_url, etc. Consequences when APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED is on: zoom stores `expiry_date = Date.now() + undefined * 1000 = NaN` (zoomvideo/lib/VideoApiAdapter.ts line 122) so the token can never be considered valid again; salesforce (which always uses this parser when the flag is on, even though it calls Salesforce directly) permanently loses instance_url from the stored key, breaking future connections; office365 keeps a stale expiry. Zod's .catchall()/.passthrough() or an explicit expiry field is needed.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same flawed code: the computed property keys [z.string().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which make the schema invalid. The golden comment says this throws a runtime error. The candidate says it evaluates to "[object Object]" keys, which strips fields and corrupts credentials. The predicted consequence differs, but the root issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Google Calendar credential key is overwritten with the zod SafeParse wrapper object instead of the parsed tokens

parseRefreshTokenResponse() returns the whole zod safeParse result ({ success: true, data: {...} }), not the parsed data. Here it is assigned to `key` and written straight into the DB via prisma.credential.update({ data: { key } }), so after the first token refresh the stored credential key becomes {"success": true, "data": {access_token: ...}}. On the next instantiation the constructor runs googleCredentialSchema.parse(credential.key) (line 75), which throws because access_token/refresh_token are now nested under `data`. Every Google Calendar credential breaks (availability lookups, booking creation, event updates) after its first refresh, forcing users to disconnect and reconnect. This affects all Google Calendar users regardless of whether the new credential-sync feature is enabled. The fix is to store `parseRefreshTokenResponse(...).data` (or have the util return the parsed data).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns the safeParse wrapper, and that wrapper is persisted as the credential key instead of the parsed data. Both also give the same fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

Unhandled validation/decryption errors produce 500s, and the HTTP method is not restricted

appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body), JSON.parse(symmetricDecrypt(...)) (lines 57-59) are called without try/catch — a malformed body, bad ciphertext or a mismatched CALCOM_APP_CREDENTIAL_ENCRYPTION_KEY throws and results in an unhandled 500 (potentially with stack trace) instead of a 400. false_positives.candidate:
prisma is used but never imported, breaking the build

The newly added refresh block calls `await prisma.credential.update(...)` at line 96, but the file's imports (lines 1-20) do not include `import prisma from "@calcom/prisma"`. This is a TypeScript compile error (Cannot find name 'prisma') that will fail type-check/build for the app-store package.

appStoreMetadata is keyed by directory name, not App.slug, so the webhook 404s for most major apps

The lookup `appStoreMetadata[app.slug]` assumes the metadata map is keyed by the App table slug, but it is keyed by app-store directory names: `zoomvideo`, `googlecalendar`, `office365calendar`, `office365video`, `larkcalendar` — while the corresponding App slugs are `zoom`, `google-calendar`, `office365-calendar`, `msteams`, `lark-calendar` (see e.g. office365video using getAppKeysFromSlug("msteams") and createOAuthAppCredential({ appId: "zoom" }) in this PR). For those apps the metadata lookup returns undefined and the endpoint responds 404, making credential sync unusable for Google Calendar, Office 365, MS Teams, Zoom and Lark. The mapping from app slug to the metadata key needs to be resolved differently (e.g. match on metadata type/appId).

Webhook overwrites an arbitrary credential when a user has several for the same app, and find-then-create is racy

Cal.com allows a user to hold multiple credentials for the same appId (e.g. two Google accounts) and teams to hold their own. `prisma.credential.findFirst({ where: { userId, appId } })` picks whichever row happens to come first and overwrites its key with the pushed tokens, potentially replacing account A's tokens with account B's and silently breaking that connection; team credentials are never matched at all. Additionally the find-then-update/create sequence is not atomic and Credential has no unique constraint on (userId, appId), so two concurrent webhook deliveries for a new credential both find nothing and create duplicates. The payload should identify the exact credential (or the endpoint should enforce a uniqueness constraint and use a transaction/upsert).

Webhook secret compared with a plain !== string comparison

The shared secret is verified with `req.headers[...] !== process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, a non-constant-time comparison that is susceptible to timing attacks. For a secret that alone grants the ability to write arbitrary third-party tokens for any user, use crypto.timingSafeEqual (after length checks) instead.

Sync-path token refresh stores expiry_date = now and drops refresh_token/email from the credential key

When credential sync is enabled, the sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry (per the contract documented in refreshOAuthTokens.ts), so `responseBody.expires_in` is undefined and `expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)` becomes the current time — the token is considered expired on the very next getToken() call, so every MS Teams API call triggers another refresh request to the sync endpoint. Additionally `key: responseBody` replaces the entire stored credential key, discarding refresh_token and email; if sync is later disabled the credential can no longer be refreshed. The refreshed fields should be merged into the existing key and the expiry read from whatever the endpoint actually returns.

No tests for the credential-sync webhook or the token-refresh sync path

The PR checklist explicitly states no tests were added. The new endpoint can overwrite any user's stored third-party tokens, and the refreshOAuthTokens/parseRefreshTokenResponse utilities sit on the critical path of every calendar/video integration — a broken response shape here corrupts credentials in the DB (several such issues exist in this PR). At minimum, tests should cover: valid/invalid webhook secret, malformed and undecryptable payloads, create vs update behaviour, apps with multiple credentials per user, and both branches (sync enabled/disabled) of the refresh helpers.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
forEach made async: errors escape the surrounding try/catch and deletions are no longer started before returning

The PR changed `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => { const calendar = getCalendar(...); ... })` to `forEach(async (bookingRef) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(...); ... })`. Because `forEach` ignores the promises returned by async callbacks, (1) the `try/catch` wrapped around this loop no longer catches anything — a rejection from `getCalendar` (dynamic import) or from `calendar?.deleteEvent(...)` becomes an unhandled promise rejection (fatal by default on Node >= 15) instead of being logged by the catch block; and (2) `deleteEvent` is no longer invoked synchronously, so the function can send the reschedule email and return `true` before the calendar deletion has even started, which on serverless deployments means it may never run. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async (bookingRef) => { ... }))` so the work completes and errors remain observable.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: forEach with async callbacks leaves promises unawaited. That lets errors escape try/catch as unhandled rejections and leaves cleanup incomplete. Both also recommend Promise.all with map.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly at module load, so nothing is actually lazy-loaded

Each value in the appStore map is now a promise created when this module is evaluated (e.g. `applecalendar: import("./applecalendar")`). `import()` begins loading the target module immediately, so all 28 app packages are still fetched/parsed as soon as anything imports `@calcom/app-store` — the loading is not deferred to first use, which defeats the stated purpose of the PR. To get real lazy loading the values must be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites doing `await appStore[key]()`. Additionally, these module-scope promises float until a caller awaits them: if one of the dynamic imports ever rejects (failed/missing chunk) and that app key is never awaited, Node raises an unhandled promise rejection, which terminates the process by default on Node >= 15.

Recurring-cancel path: awaiting getCalendar inside fire-and-forget forEach defers deleteEvent past the end of the request

In the branch that cancels all remaining occurrences of a recurring event, the code does `bookingToDelete.user.credentials.filter(...).forEach(async (credential) => { const calendar = await getCalendar(credential); ... await calendar?.deleteEvent(uid, evt, externalCalendarId); ... })`. The `await getCalendar(...)` added by this PR makes each callback suspend on the dynamic import before `deleteEvent` is ever invoked; previously `getCalendar` was synchronous, so every `deleteEvent` HTTP call was started synchronously while the forEach ran. Nothing awaits the forEach callbacks, and the pushes into `apiDeletes` happen only after those callbacks resume — i.e. after the handler already executed `await Promise.all(prismaPromises.concat(apiDeletes))` (which snapshots the array) and returned success. The net effect is that deleting the calendar events for all future occurrences of a cancelled recurring booking may never start before the request completes (and may never run at all on serverless), leaving cancelled occurrences on users' calendars. Collect the promises (e.g. with `map`) and include them in the final `Promise.all`.
